Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
From Simulation to Reality


In Simulation (Python)

Perfect geometry
No friction or backlash
Instant, exact motion
Mathematical precision

# Perfect forward kinematics
T = robot.fkine(q)
# Returns exact pose

In Reality (FANUC)

Manufacturing tolerances
Gear backlash & friction
Servo lag & overshoot
Mechanical deflection

The robot almost goes where you command…


This is the central theme of today’s lecture: there is always a gap between the mathematical model and the physical robot. In our Python labs we computed forward kinematics and got exact homogeneous transformation matrices. The real robot has the same kinematic structure, but every physical parameter — link lengths, joint offsets, axis alignments — deviates slightly from the nominal CAD values. On top of that, phenomena like friction, gear backlash, and structural flex are not captured in the DH model at all. The goal today is to understand where these errors come from, how large they are, and what we can do about them.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
The Digital Twin Concept


A digital twin is a virtual replica that mirrors the physical robot as closely as possible. The idea is bidirectional: you program and simulate in the virtual model, then transfer to the real robot. Any mismatch between the twin and reality shows up as positional error. This diagram shows the flow: CAD model feeds the simulation, calibration data closes the loop back from the real robot to update the model. The better the calibration, the smaller the gap. FANUC’s Roboguide is an example of a digital twin environment we use in industry.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Why Does This Matter?
Scenario: You calculate joint angles in Python to reach a target



Step
Expected
Reality




Python IK output
q = [10°, 45°, -30°, 0°, 60°, 0°]
Same


Command to FANUC
Same angles
Same


Actual joint position
Same
Close (±0.01°)


Actual TCP position
(400, 200, 300) mm
(399.2, 200.8, 299.5) mm



Error: ~1.5 mm - significant for precision tasks!

Walk through this table row by row. The IK solver gives us joint angles — those are just numbers, so they transfer perfectly. The controller commands those exact angles. The joints get very close because the encoders and servo loops are precise — repeatability is excellent. But the TCP ends up about 1.5 mm off. Why? Because the forward kinematics mapping from joint space to Cartesian space depends on the DH parameters, and those parameters are slightly wrong. A 0.05 mm error in a link length, compounded across 6 joints, accumulates into a millimeter-scale TCP error. For tasks like assembly (inserting pins, connectors) or precision machining, 1.5 mm is unacceptable. This motivates everything we’ll cover today.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Definitions


Accuracy
How close the robot gets to the commanded position
\[\text{Accuracy} = |P_{actual} - P_{commanded}|\]

Affected by calibration
Can be improved
Typically ±0.5 to ±2 mm


Repeatability
How consistently the robot returns to the same position
\[\text{Repeatability} = \sigma(P_{measurements})\]

Inherent to mechanism
Hard to improve
Typically ±0.02 to ±0.1 mm



These are the two most important specifications for a robot arm, and students often confuse them. Accuracy measures the distance between where you told the robot to go and where it actually went — it depends on how well your kinematic model matches reality. Repeatability measures the spread when the robot tries to go to the same point many times — it depends on the mechanical precision of the gears, bearings, and encoders. Think of the classic dartboard analogy: accuracy is how close to the bullseye, repeatability is how tightly grouped the darts are. A robot can have excellent repeatability (tight cluster) but poor accuracy (cluster is offset from the bullseye). Calibration shifts the cluster toward the bullseye — it improves accuracy without changing repeatability.
Note that we define these in terms of position (XYZ), not orientation. Orientation errors also exist, but they are much smaller and harder to measure. A 0.02° axis misalignment at a joint produces only ~0.02° of orientation error at the TCP, but it gets amplified by the arm length into 1-2 mm of position error. So position error is the dominant, visible consequence. Measuring position to 0.1 mm is straightforward with a dial indicator; measuring orientation to 0.01° requires specialized equipment like autocollimators. ISO 9283 defines both position and orientation accuracy/repeatability separately, but datasheets typically only report position specs. Orientation accuracy matters for directional tools — welding torches, dispensing needles — which is why the 6-point TCP calibration method exists to calibrate tool frame orientation, not just position.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Visual Comparison


This figure shows four scenarios: high accuracy + high repeatability (tight cluster on target), high accuracy + low repeatability (spread out but centered), low accuracy + high repeatability (tight cluster but offset — this is the typical industrial robot), and low accuracy + low repeatability (spread out and offset). Most industrial robots out of the box are in the third case: very repeatable but not very accurate. Calibration moves them toward the first case.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Why Repeatability > Accuracy
For most industrial robots:



Specification
Typical Value




Repeatability
±0.02 - ±0.08 mm


Accuracy
±0.5 - ±2.0 mm









Tip


Repeatability is 10-100x better than accuracy! This is the most important specification to understand for industrial robotics.



This is why industrial robots:

Use taught positions (move to point, record)
Don’t rely on calculated positions for precision
Need calibration for offline programming


This 10-100x difference is a fundamental characteristic of serial-link robots. Repeatability is good because the encoders and gears are very precise — when you command the same joint angles, the joints go to almost exactly the same position every time. Accuracy is worse because the mapping from joint angles to Cartesian position goes through the kinematic model, and that model has parameter errors. This has a huge practical implication: if you jog the robot to a point and record the joint values, the robot will return to that exact spot reliably (exploiting repeatability). But if you calculate joint angles from a CAD model and send them, the robot goes to a slightly wrong Cartesian position (limited by accuracy). This is why most industrial programming still uses teaching — you physically move the robot to each point.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Industrial Approach


Online Teaching (Repeatability)

Jog robot to position
Record actual joint values
Robot returns to same joint values
Exploits repeatability

Used for: Pick-and-place, welding fixtures

Offline Programming (Accuracy)

Calculate positions from CAD
Convert to joint angles
Robot goes to calculated position
Depends on accuracy

Used for: Large parts, complex paths


A fixture is any physical structure — a jig, clamp, plate, or pallet — that holds a workpiece in a fixed, known position. Mention this definition if students aren’t familiar with the term.
Online teaching is the traditional approach — an operator uses the teach pendant to jog the robot to each waypoint and records it. This completely bypasses accuracy issues because you’re recording the actual joint encoder values, and the robot returns to those same encoder values with repeatability-level precision. The downside is it requires physical access to the robot and production downtime. Offline programming is done entirely in software using CAD models, which means zero downtime — but now you depend on accuracy because the positions are calculated, not taught. For large workpieces like airplane fuselages or ship hulls where you cannot practically teach thousands of points, offline programming is the only option, and that’s where calibration becomes essential.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Error Categories


We can group error sources into five main categories. Geometric errors are static deviations in the physical dimensions of the robot — link lengths, joint offsets, axis alignments. Backlash is the play in the gear trains. Compliance is structural bending under load. Thermal effects cause expansion and contraction. Servo errors come from the control system’s finite bandwidth and gain. These categories differ in whether they are constant, pose-dependent, or time-varying, which determines how we can compensate for them.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
1. Geometric Errors
Manufacturing tolerances in robot structure



Parameter
Nominal
Tolerance




Link length
400.00 mm
±0.05 mm


Joint offset
0.00°
±0.01°


Joint axis alignment
Perpendicular
±0.02°



These errors are constant and can be calibrated out.

Geometric errors are the dominant source of inaccuracy, typically accounting for 80-90% of the total positioning error. They arise because no manufacturing process is perfect — a link specified as 400.00 mm might actually be 400.04 mm. These are deviations in the DH parameters we studied in Week 3. The key property is that they are constant — they don’t change with pose, load, or temperature. This means once you measure them, you can update your kinematic model and permanently correct for them. This is exactly what kinematic calibration does: it identifies the true DH parameters by measuring the robot at many poses and fitting the model. An angular error of 0.02 degrees on an early joint gets amplified by the full arm length, so even tiny axis misalignments can produce millimeter-scale TCP errors.
To clarify the table terms: joint offset means the joint is in the right place and rotates around the right axis, but the zero reference is slightly off — like a clock that’s 10 seconds fast. Joint axis alignment means the joint’s rotation axis itself is slightly tilted or shifted from where it should be — like a door hinge that’s not perfectly vertical. Both are geometric errors (constant, correctable by calibration), but joint offset is simpler to fix — just adjust the zero reference via mastering. Axis misalignment requires full kinematic calibration to correct, because you need to update the alpha and d parameters in the DH model.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
2. Gear Backlash


What is it?
“Play” between gear teeth when changing direction
Effect:

Position depends on approach direction
Different position going CW vs CCW
Typical backlash: 0.5-2 arc-minutes

Mitigation:

Always approach from same direction
Use spring preload
Accept the error for non-critical moves





Backlash is the small gap between meshing gear teeth. When a joint reverses direction, there is a brief interval where the motor turns but the output doesn’t move — the gear teeth are crossing the gap. This creates a hysteresis effect: the joint position depends on which direction you approached from. The encoder is on the motor side of the gearbox, so it doesn’t see this dead zone. Industrial robots use harmonic drives or cycloidal reducers that have very low backlash (0.5-2 arc-minutes), but it’s never zero. The practical mitigation is to always approach a target point from the same direction — this is a common industrial best practice. Some FANUC programs explicitly add an approach move before the final position to ensure consistent directionality.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
3. Compliance (Deflection)


Structural Deflection
Robot arm bends under:

Its own weight
Payload weight
Process forces (pushing, welding)

\[\delta = \frac{F \cdot L^3}{3EI}\]

\(\delta\) — tip deflection, \(F\) — applied force
\(L\) — length, \(E\) — elastic modulus, \(I\) — moment of inertia



Characteristics:

Pose-dependent (worst at full extension)
Load-dependent
Can be 0.5-3 mm at full reach



The robot arm is essentially a cantilever beam, and like any beam, it deflects under load. The formula shown is the classic cantilever deflection equation: deflection is proportional to force times length cubed, divided by stiffness (3EI). The cubic dependence on length means deflection grows rapidly with reach — a fully extended arm deflects much more than a tucked-in configuration. This makes compliance pose-dependent, unlike geometric errors which are constant. The robot’s own weight is always there (gravity compensation), and payload adds to it. Process forces like pushing during grinding or the electromagnetic forces during arc welding also contribute. Some high-end controllers include gravity compensation models that adjust joint torques to counteract known deflection, but this requires careful modeling of mass distribution.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
4. Thermal Effects
Temperature changes cause expansion
\[\Delta L = L \cdot \alpha \cdot \Delta T\]



Material
α (×10⁻⁶/°C)




Steel
12


Aluminum
23



Example: 1 m aluminum link, 10°C rise: \[\Delta L = 1000 \times 23 \times 10^{-6} \times 10 = 0.23 \text{ mm}\]
Mitigation: Warm up robot before precision work

Thermal expansion is straightforward physics but easy to overlook. Robots heat up during operation — motor heat conducts into the links, and ambient temperature in a factory can vary by 10-20 degrees over a day. Aluminum expands almost twice as much as steel per degree. The example shows that a 1 meter aluminum link grows by 0.23 mm for a 10 degree temperature rise. Across multiple links in a 6-axis robot, this can add up to a millimeter. The standard industrial practice is to run the robot through its motion cycle for 15-30 minutes before starting precision work, so it reaches thermal equilibrium. Some advanced systems use temperature sensors on the links and apply real-time compensation. The key takeaway: if the robot was calibrated cold and you run it hot, accuracy degrades.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
5. Servo Errors
Control system limitations

Following error during motion
Settling time at stop
Servo stiffness (gain)

FANUC specifications:

Position loop gain: Adjustable
Settling time: ~50-100 ms for FINE
Following error: Depends on speed


Three concepts to explain here:
Following error is the lag between the commanded and actual joint position during motion. On a straight-line move this is just a time delay — the path shape is still accurate, just shifted in time. The real problem shows up on curved paths and direction changes: each axis has a different inertia and may lag by a different amount, so the actual path cuts corners on arcs and overshoots at sharp turns. This is called contour error, and it increases with speed. This is why welding and dispensing use slow speeds (50-200 mm/s) — not for settling, but for path shape accuracy on curves.
Settling time is how long the robot takes to stop oscillating and converge to the final position after a move completes. The FINE termination type waits for the position error to enter a small tolerance window (the “in-position” zone), typically 50-100 ms. The CNT termination type skips waiting and blends into the next move — faster cycle time but less precise at waypoints. In a 50-move program, using FINE everywhere adds 2.5-5 seconds of pure settling time. The practical rule: use FINE at pick/place points where precision matters, use CNT at transit points where speed matters.
Servo stiffness (gain) is how aggressively the controller corrects position errors. High gain means stiff response — small following error, fast settling, but risk of vibration and oscillation. Low gain means soft response — larger following error, smoother motion, but less precise. It’s a spring analogy: a stiff spring snaps back quickly but can bounce; a soft spring returns slowly but smoothly. Some applications intentionally reduce stiffness — FANUC’s “soft float” mode allows the robot to comply with external forces during contact tasks like grinding or insertion, trading position accuracy for force control.
Unlike geometric errors which only affect accuracy, servo errors can affect both accuracy and repeatability — a robot that vibrates during settling may land at slightly different positions each time.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Error Summary



Error Source
Magnitude
Correctable?




Geometric (link lengths)
0.1-1 mm
Yes (calibration)


Gear backlash
0.05-0.2 mm
Partial


Compliance
0.5-3 mm
Yes (compensation)


Thermal
0.1-0.5 mm
Yes (warm-up)


Servo
0.01-0.1 mm
Yes (tuning)




This table gives you the big picture. Geometric errors and compliance are the biggest contributors — both can be in the millimeter range. The good news is that geometric errors are fully correctable through calibration, and compliance can be compensated with a good model. Backlash is only partially correctable because it’s a nonlinear, direction-dependent phenomenon. Thermal errors are manageable with warm-up procedures. Servo errors are typically the smallest and are handled by the controller’s tuning. In practice, a well-calibrated robot with a warm-up routine can achieve sub-millimeter accuracy, which is sufficient for most offline programming applications.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
What is Calibration?
Finding the true robot parameters
The robot has a nominal kinematic model (from CAD)
Calibration finds the actual parameters:

True link lengths
True joint offsets
True axis alignments


Calibration is fundamentally a parameter identification problem. The robot manufacturer provides nominal DH parameters based on the CAD design. Every individual robot deviates from these nominals due to manufacturing tolerances. Calibration measures the robot’s actual behavior and solves for the parameter values that best explain the measurements. Once you know the true parameters, you update the kinematic model, and now your forward and inverse kinematics calculations match reality much more closely. There are different levels of calibration — from simple joint zero adjustment (mastering) all the way to full kinematic parameter identification. The more parameters you calibrate, the better the accuracy, but the more expensive and time-consuming the process.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Calibration Approaches


This diagram shows the hierarchy of calibration methods from simplest to most complex. At the bottom is mastering — just setting joint zeros. Then TCP calibration — finding the tool center point offset. User frame calibration defines workpiece coordinate systems. At the top is full kinematic calibration, which identifies all DH parameters using external measurement equipment. Each level builds on the previous ones. In practice, you always start with mastering, then TCP, then user frames. Full kinematic calibration is only done when you need high accuracy for offline programming.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Mastering (Joint Zero Calibration)
Purpose: Define the “zero” position for each joint


Process:

Move joint to mechanical reference (mark, pin)
Tell controller “this is zero”
Repeat for all joints

When needed:

After motor/encoder replacement
After collision
When positions drift significantly





Zero-position scribe marks on FANUC LR Mate 200iD (B-83574EN, Fig. 8.3a)

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
TCP Calibration (4-Point Method)
Goal: Find true Tool Center Point location

Mount tool on robot
Define a fixed point in space (pin tip)
Touch point from 4+ different orientations
System calculates TCP offset

Math: All poses → same world point: \(T_{tcp}^{0} = T_{flange}^{0} \cdot T_{tcp}^{flange}\)


TCP calibration answers the question: “where is the tool tip relative to the flange?” Without this, the controller doesn’t know where the actual working point of the tool is. The 4-point method is elegant: you place a sharp reference point (like a pin mounted on a stand) and touch the tip of your tool to that exact point from at least 4 different orientations. The key insight is that no matter how the robot is oriented, the tool tip should be at the same world-space location. The controller knows the flange pose at each orientation (from forward kinematics), so it can solve for the unknown TCP offset vector that makes all four measurements consistent. Mathematically, it’s finding the translation vector from flange to TCP that minimizes the spread of the computed world-space points. More points give a better estimate.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
User Frame Calibration (3-Point Method)


Goal: Define a coordinate system aligned with fixture/workpiece
Process:

Origin point: Touch corner of fixture
X-direction point: Touch point along X axis
Y-plane point: Touch point in XY plane

The controller calculates the transform from World to User frame.




3-point user frame teaching in Roboguide — touching fixture points from different orientations




User frame calibration creates a local coordinate system tied to a fixture or workpiece. You teach three points: the origin, a point along the desired X direction, and a point roughly in the XY plane. From these three points, the controller constructs a full rotation matrix: X-axis direction is from origin to the second point (normalized), then it uses the third point to define the XY plane, and Z comes from the cross product. This is exactly the frame construction procedure we studied in Week 1. The result is a homogeneous transformation from the world frame to the user frame. Once defined, all positions taught in that user frame are relative to the fixture — if the fixture moves, you just re-calibrate the 3 points and all your taught positions automatically update. This is extremely powerful in flexible manufacturing where workstations get repositioned.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Full Kinematic Calibration
For high-accuracy applications
Process:

Measure TCP position at many poses (50-100+)
Use external measurement system (laser tracker, CMM)
Solve for all kinematic parameters
Update robot model

Achieves: Sub-millimeter accuracy
Cost: Expensive equipment, significant time

Full kinematic calibration is the gold standard. You move the robot to 50-100 or more poses spread throughout the workspace. At each pose, an external measurement device (typically a laser tracker costing 100,000+ dollars or a coordinate measuring machine) records the true TCP position. Then an optimization algorithm — usually nonlinear least squares — adjusts all the DH parameters simultaneously to minimize the difference between the model’s predicted TCP positions and the measured ones. The result is a corrected kinematic model that matches reality to sub-millimeter accuracy. This is how automotive and aerospace manufacturers achieve the precision needed for offline programming of complex paths on large workpieces. The downside is cost and time: a full calibration can take several hours, requires expensive equipment, and must be repeated if the robot is moved or serviced. Some companies like Leica and API sell turnkey calibration systems specifically for this purpose.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Why Limit Robot Motion?
Safety and protection:

Keep robot away from fixtures
Prevent collisions with environment
Protect cables and hoses
Define safe working areas


Safety is paramount in industrial robotics. A robot moving at full speed carries enormous kinetic energy — a collision can damage the robot, destroy expensive tooling or fixtures, or injure a person. Software limits provide a safety net beyond what the programmer explicitly codes. Even if there’s a bug in the program or an operator jogs the robot in the wrong direction, the limits prevent the robot from entering dangerous regions. In our lab, we’ll set up limits to protect the robot from hitting the table or the teach pendant cable. In industry, these zones are part of the risk assessment and must be configured before a cell goes into production.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Joint Limits (Soft Limits)
Software limits on each joint



Joint
Lower Limit
Upper Limit




J1
-170°
+170°


J2
-135°
+70°


J3
-80°
+270°


J4
-190°
+190°


J5
-125°
+125°


J6
-360°
+360°



These are software limits - can be adjusted within hardware limits.

Every joint has two layers of limits. Hardware limits are physical mechanical stops — the joint physically cannot rotate past them. Software limits (soft limits) are enforced by the controller and are always set inside the hardware limits. You can tighten the software limits to restrict the robot’s workspace — for example, if J1 only needs ±90 degrees for your application, you can set tighter limits to keep it from swinging into adjacent equipment. The controller checks these before executing any motion and will refuse to move if the commanded position violates a joint limit. Note that J3 has an asymmetric range (-80 to +270) — this is because of the robot’s mechanical geometry. J6, the wrist roll, has the widest range at ±360 degrees. If your application requires the wrist to rotate more than 360 degrees (like a screw driving task), you might need to manage wrist wrap-around in your program.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Cartesian Limits (World Zones)


While joint limits restrict individual joint angles, world zones restrict where the TCP can go in Cartesian space. This is often more intuitive for safety — you can define a box around a fixture and say “the robot must not enter this region.” The figure shows how these zones appear as 3D regions in the robot’s workspace. You can define multiple zones, each with its own shape, size, and action. This is the Cartesian-space complement to the joint-space limits.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
World Zone Types
FANUC provides several zone types:








Type
Function
Action




Position Register Interference
Avoid specific position
Stop or error


Cartesian Space Interference
Avoid 3D region
Stop or signal


Safe Zone
Must stay inside
Stop if exit


Forbidden Zone
Must stay outside
Stop if enter




The distinction between safe zones and forbidden zones is important. A safe zone defines the allowed region — the robot must stay inside it. If the TCP tries to leave, the robot stops. A forbidden zone defines a prohibited region — the robot must stay outside it. If the TCP tries to enter, the robot stops. You can combine these: a large safe zone defining the overall workspace, with smaller forbidden zones carved out around fixtures, cables, or operator access areas. The “stop + signal” action is useful in automated cells because a PLC or supervisory system can detect the signal and trigger a recovery routine rather than just faulting out.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Setting Up a World Zone
Example: Forbidden Zone around fixture
MENU → SETUP → Frames → Space → Interference
Zone 1:
  Type: Cartesian
  Shape: Box
  X: 400 to 600 mm
  Y: -100 to 100 mm
  Z: 0 to 200 mm
  Action: Stop + Signal DO[10]

This is the menu path on the FANUC teach pendant to configure a world zone. You choose a zone number, specify the type (Cartesian box is the most common), and enter the min/max coordinates for X, Y, and Z — defining an axis-aligned bounding box. The box coordinates are in the world frame. The action specifies what happens if the robot enters the zone: here it stops and also sets digital output 10, which could trigger an alarm light or notify a PLC. In the lab, you’ll configure a zone like this to create a no-go region. Keep in mind that the box is axis-aligned with the world frame — if you need a tilted region, you would need to use a user frame or multiple zones to approximate it.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Interference Checking
How it works:

Robot calculates future TCP path
Checks path against defined zones
If violation predicted:

Stops motion (FINE termination)
Sets output signal
Displays error








Warning


Checks TCP position only, not the full arm envelope! The elbow can still collide even if the TCP stays outside a forbidden zone.




This is a critical limitation to understand. The interference check only looks at the TCP — the tip of the tool. It does not check the elbow, the forearm, or any other part of the arm. This means the robot’s elbow can swing into a fixture even if the TCP stays outside the forbidden zone. For comprehensive collision avoidance, you would need a full 3D collision checking system like what Roboguide provides in simulation. On the physical robot, it’s the programmer’s responsibility to ensure the entire arm path is clear, not just the TCP path. Some advanced FANUC options include elbow interference zones, but these are add-on features. Always test new programs at slow speed first and watch the full arm motion, not just the tool tip.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
What is a Digital Twin?


A virtual replica of the physical robot

Same kinematics (DH model)
Same joint limits
Same tool definition

FANUC Roboguide is our digital twin environment:

Offline programming (no production downtime)
Collision checking before running
Path optimization in simulation
Training operators without hardware risk






FANUC Roboguide — offline programming environment



Key insight: The digital twin (Roboguide) is only as good as its calibration. This is why we study accuracy, error sources, and calibration methods.

This ties everything together. The digital twin is the practical application of all the calibration concepts we’ve discussed. If your digital twin has the nominal DH parameters, it will have the same accuracy limitations as uncalibrated offline programming — positions calculated in Roboguide will be off by millimeters on the real robot. If you perform full kinematic calibration and update the Roboguide model, the virtual and physical robots converge. Roboguide also adds value beyond pure kinematics: it does full 3D collision detection (including the arm body, not just TCP), cycle time estimation, and reachability analysis. In industry, the digital twin workflow is: design the cell in Roboguide, program all the paths, simulate and optimize, then deploy to the physical robot with minimal touch-up. The calibration quality directly determines how much touch-up is needed.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Position Registers (PR[ ])
Stored Cartesian poses that programs can reference and modify
! Store current position
PR[1]=LPOS ;

! Move to a position register
L PR[1] 500mm/sec FINE ;

! Access individual components
PR[1,1]=400.0 ;   ! Set X
PR[1,2]=100.0 ;   ! Set Y
PR[1,3]=250.0 ;   ! Set Z
PR[1,4]=180.0 ;   ! Set W (Rx)
PR[1,5]=0.0 ;     ! Set P (Ry)
PR[1,6]=0.0 ;     ! Set R (Rz)
Why use PR instead of P?

P[ ] positions are local to one program
PR[ ] are global — shared across all programs
PR[ ] can be modified with math at runtime


Position registers are one of the most powerful features in FANUC TP programming. The key differences from regular position variables (P[]): first, PR[] are global — all programs on the controller share the same PR[] table, so if your PICK program sets PR[1], your PLACE program can read it. Second, you can do math on individual components — PR[1,3] accesses just the Z coordinate, which lets you compute offsets, shifts, and transforms at runtime. Third, LPOS is a special system variable that holds the robot’s current Cartesian position — assigning it to a PR captures where the robot is right now. The indices 1-3 are X, Y, Z translation and 4-6 are W, P, R rotation (FANUC’s Euler angle convention). In practice, you typically reserve a block of PR numbers for specific purposes: PR[1-10] for working positions, PR[10-20] for offsets, etc. Document which PR numbers are used where, because since they’re global, a naming collision between programs can cause subtle bugs.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Offset Positions
Computing new positions from existing ones
! Approach: 50mm above the pick point
PR[2]=PR[1] ;
PR[2,3]=PR[1,3]+50.0 ;   ! Z + 50mm

! Move sequence with approach
L PR[2] 500mm/sec FINE ;  ! Approach
L PR[1] 100mm/sec FINE ;  ! Pick
CALL HAND_CLOSE ;
L PR[2] 500mm/sec FINE ;  ! Retract
Common offset patterns:



Pattern
Offset




Approach from above
Z + height


Retract after place
Z + height


Shift along conveyor
X + distance


Pallet column offset
Y + pitch




This is the approach-pick-retract pattern, the most fundamental motion sequence in pick-and-place. Instead of teaching three separate points (approach, pick, retract), you teach just the pick point and compute the approach and retract by adding a Z offset. This has two major advantages: fewer taught points to manage, and if the pick point changes, the approach and retract automatically follow. The pattern is: copy the base position into a working PR, modify the Z component, move to the approach point, then move down to the pick point at slower speed (for safety and precision near the part), call HAND_CLOSE to grip the part, then retract. The HAND_CLOSE and HAND_OPEN macros encapsulate the gripper I/O and any necessary wait time internally — pneumatic grippers need time to physically close and build gripping force. The approach speed (500 mm/s) is fast because we’re in free space; the final approach (100 mm/s) is slow because we’re near the part and need precision.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
User Frames (UFRAME)


Problem: If the workstation moves, all taught points become wrong.
Solution: Teach points relative to a User Frame attached to the fixture.
If the fixture moves:

Re-calibrate the same User Frame (3 points)
All taught positions update automatically
For two known positions: pre-calibrate UF[1] and UF[2], switch with UFRAME_NUM

UFRAME_NUM=1 ;   ! Select User Frame 1
! All subsequent moves are in
! this frame's coordinates

Positions taught in one UF cannot be used with a different UF — frame mismatch error!





User frames are the key to portable, reusable programs. Without user frames, every position is taught in the world frame — if the fixture moves even 1 mm, every single taught position is wrong and must be re-taught. With user frames, positions are stored relative to the fixture. When the fixture moves, you re-calibrate the user frame (3 points, takes about a minute) and all the taught positions automatically transform to the new fixture location. This is the homogeneous transformation concept from Week 1 in action: positions are stored in the user frame, and the controller applies the world-to-user transform to convert them to world coordinates before commanding motion. The frame mismatch warning is important — if you teach points in UF[1] and then accidentally switch to UF[2], the robot will go to completely wrong positions because the stored coordinates are interpreted in a different frame. FANUC protects against this with a mismatch error. A common industrial setup: a fixture can be in two positions (e.g., rotary table), so you pre-calibrate UF[1] for position A and UF[2] for position B, and the program switches between them.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
section: Setting Up a User Frame (3-Point Method)
text:
Setting Up a User Frame (3-Point Method)
Three points define the frame:

Origin Point — corner of fixture
X-Direction Point — along the X edge
Y-Plane Point — roughly along Y (defines the XY plane)

MENU → SETUP → Frames → User Frame
Frame Number: 1
  Method: Three Point
  Orient Origin Point: [Record]
  X Direction Point:   [Record]
  Y Direction Point:   [Record]
The controller computes the full \(T_{User}^{World}\) transform automatically.

This is the same frame construction we did mathematically in Week 1, but now the robot does it for you. You jog the TCP to the fixture corner and record the origin. Then jog along the X edge to a second point — the controller normalizes the vector from origin to this point to get the X-axis unit vector. Then jog to a point roughly in the Y direction — it doesn’t have to be exactly along Y because the controller uses the Gram-Schmidt process to make Y perpendicular to X while staying in the plane defined by your three points. Z is computed as the cross product of X and Y. The result is stored as a 4x4 homogeneous transformation matrix. Practical tips: use physically identifiable features on the fixture for the three points (corners, edges, alignment pins) so different operators get consistent results. The further apart the points are, the more accurate the frame definition — points that are too close together amplify any touching error into angular error in the frame.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Tool Frames (UTOOL)


Defines where the Tool Center Point (TCP) is

Relative to the flange
All Cartesian moves reference TCP
Different tools = different UTOOLs

UTOOL_NUM=1 ;   ! Select Tool 1
! TCP is now at the tool tip
Why it matters:

Without correct UTOOL, linear moves curve
Orientation changes pivot around wrong point
Calibrate with 4-point or 6-point method





The tool frame defines the offset from the robot’s flange (the mounting surface at the end of J6) to the actual working point of the tool. If you have a welding torch, the TCP is at the wire tip. If you have a gripper, the TCP might be at the center of the finger pads. Without a correct UTOOL, when you command a linear move, the controller plans a straight line for the flange, but the tool tip traces a curve — because the tool tip is offset from the flange and the orientation changes along the path. Similarly, when you rotate the wrist to change orientation, the tool tip sweeps an arc instead of staying in place, because the controller pivots around the flange instead of the TCP. With the correct UTOOL, the controller plans motions so the TCP moves in a straight line and orientation changes pivot around the TCP. If your cell has multiple tools (e.g., a gripper and a welder on a tool changer), you store each as a different UTOOL number and switch with UTOOL_NUM before using each tool.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration

Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Lab 7: Offsets, Frames & Structured Programs
Objective: Practice user frames, offsets, and multi-program structure on FANUC

This lab brings together the theoretical concepts from today’s lecture into hands-on exercises. You’ll work directly with the FANUC teach pendant to calibrate frames, build offset patterns, and structure programs with subroutine calls. Focus on understanding how user frames make programs portable and how offsets reduce the number of taught points.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
What You’ll Do


Exercise 1: User Frame Setup

Calibrate a User Frame on a fixture
Teach 3 pick positions relative to it
Move the fixture, re-calibrate frame
Verify positions follow the frame

Exercise 2: Offset Patterns

Teach one base position
Use PR offsets for approach/retract
Build a 2x2 grid using calculated offsets


Exercise 3: Structured Program

Write a MAIN program that calls PICK and PLACE subprograms
PICK: approach → grip → retract
PLACE: approach → release → retract
MAIN: loop calling both

Bonus: Simple Pallet

Extend to a 3x2 pallet using registers and MOD/DIV



Exercise 1 is the most important — it will give you a visceral understanding of why user frames matter. After you teach your positions and then physically move the fixture, you’ll see those positions are now wrong. Then you re-calibrate the user frame and watch them snap back into place. Exercise 2 practices the offset patterns we discussed — approach/retract and grid offsets. Exercise 3 combines everything into a structured multi-program application. The bonus exercise implements the palletizing pattern from the slide. Start with Exercise 1 and make sure you understand it before moving on. Remember: work slowly, keep speeds low (50-100 mm/s), and always have the E-stop within reach.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Key Takeaways

Repeatability >> Accuracy for industrial robots

Teach positions when possible
Calibrate for offline programming

Error sources are multiple

Geometric, backlash, compliance, thermal, servo
Some correctable, some inherent

Calibration improves accuracy

Mastering: joint zeros
TCP calibration: tool offset
User frame calibration: fixture alignment

Advanced TP programming enables flexible automation

Position registers and offsets avoid re-teaching
User frames make programs portable
Multi-program architecture keeps code organized



The three big ideas to remember from this lecture: First, the difference between accuracy and repeatability and why industrial robots exploit repeatability through taught positions. Second, the five error sources and which ones can be calibrated out. Third, the practical programming tools — position registers, offsets, user frames, tool frames, and multi-program structure — that make industrial robot programs maintainable and adaptable. These concepts directly carry into the lab this week.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Next Week
Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics

Holonomic vs Non-holonomic constraints
Unicycle model
Bicycle model (Ackermann steering)
Lab 8: Driving a mobile robot in simulation


Next week we shift from manipulator arms to mobile robots. The key difference is that mobile robots have motion constraints — a car-like robot cannot move sideways, which is a non-holonomic constraint. We’ll derive the kinematic models for two fundamental mobile robot types: the unicycle (like a differential-drive robot) and the bicycle (like a car with Ackermann steering). These models describe how the robot’s velocity relates to its wheel speeds, analogous to how the Jacobian relates joint velocities to end-effector velocity for manipulators.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
Exit Ticket
Scenario: You have a pick-and-place station. The pick point is at P[1]. You need to:

Approach from 40mm above P[1]
Pick the part (CALL HAND_CLOSE)
Place it at a position that is 200mm to the right (+X) of P[1], at the same height

Write the TP code using Position Registers and offsets. Assume UFRAME and UTOOL are already set.

Give students 3-5 minutes to work through this on paper. The challenge is combining two types of offsets: a vertical approach offset and a horizontal placement offset. They need to think about when to use the Offset instruction versus PR math to compute a new position. Walk around and check that students are considering both the approach/retract for the pick AND for the place — a common mistake is forgetting the approach and retract at the place location.

A 3R elbow robot has: \(d_1 = 0.30\) m, \(a_2 = 0.40\) m, \(a_3 = 0.30\) m, \(\theta_1 = 45^\circ\), \(\theta_2 = 30^\circ\), \(\theta_3 = -60^\circ\)

\[

\]
\[
x = r\cos 45^\circ = 0.4287\text{ m},
\qquad

\]
\[
z = d_1 + a_2\sin 30^\circ + a_3\sin(-30^\circ)
= 0.30 + 0.20 - 0.15 = 0.35\text{ m}
\]
So,
\[
\mathbf{p}_{ee} =
\begin{bmatrix}

\end{bmatrix}\text{ m}
\]
The decomposition works because \(\theta_1\) only rotates the vertical plane around \(z_0\). Once \(\theta_1\) is fixed, the remaining 2-link chain (\(a_2\), \(a_3\)) lives in a single plane — the same geometry reappears in IK (Problem 7).

title: Week 5: Kinematics Problem-Solving Session

Problem 5: Cylindrical Manipulator IK


Same cylindrical robot as Problem 1: \(d_1 = 0.50\) m.

title: Week 5: Kinematics Problem-Solving Session
text:
Solution 5: Cylindrical Manipulator IK
Convert Cartesian to cylindrical coordinates directly:
\[
\theta_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x) = \operatorname{atan2}(0.4000, 0.3000) = 53.13^\circ
\]
\[
d_3 = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} = \sqrt{0.09+0.16} = 0.5000\text{ m}
\]
\[
d_2 = z - d_1 = 0.7500 - 0.5000 = 0.2500\text{ m}
\]
Workspace check: \(0 \le 0.25 \le 0.60\) \(\checkmark\), \(\;0.10 \le 0.50 \le 0.80\) \(\checkmark\)
The IK solution is unique — no multiple branches. This is because the cylindrical robot has no coupled revolute joints; each joint maps directly to one cylindrical coordinate.
FK check: \(x = 0.50\cos 53.13^\circ = 0.3000\), \(y = 0.50\sin 53.13^\circ = 0.4000\), \(z = 0.50 + 0.25 = 0.75\) \(\checkmark\)

title: Week 5: Kinematics Problem-Solving Session
text:
Solution 1: Frame Assignment


Step 1 — Assign z-axes (along joint axes):

\(z_0\): vertical (base revolute)
\(z_1\): vertical (prismatic slide along \(z_0\))
\(z_2\): horizontal/radial (prismatic extension)

Step 2 — Assign x-axes (DH rules):

\(x_0\): free choice (no link \(-1\)) → pick \(\hat{x}_0 = [1,0,0]\)
\(x_1\): \(z_0 \parallel z_1\) → common normal direction, choose \(\hat{x}_1 = \hat{x}_0\)
\(x_2\): \(z_1 \times z_2\) → \([0,0,1]\times[1,0,0] = [0,1,0]\)

title: Week 5: Kinematics Problem-Solving Session
text:
Solution 2: Frame Assignment


Step 1 — Assign z-axes:

\(z_0, z_1\): vertical (\(+z\)), revolute axes
\(z_2\): vertical (\(-z\)), prismatic downward
\(z_3\): vertical (\(-z\)), revolute (tool spin)

Step 2 — Assign x-axes:

\(x_0\): free choice → \([1,0,0]\)
\(x_1\): \(z_0 \parallel z_1\) → same direction, \(\hat{x}_1 = [1,0,0]\)
\(x_2\): \(z_1\) antiparallel to \(z_2\) → common normal, choose \(\hat{x}_2 = [1,0,0]\)
\(x_3\): \(z_2 \parallel z_3\) → \(\hat{x}_3 = [1,0,0]\)

All x-axes point in the same direction — a clean SCARA convention.

title: Week 5: Kinematics Problem-Solving Session
text:
Solution 3: Frame Assignment


Step 1 — Assign z-axes (ZYZ wrist):

\(z_3\): along forearm (first roll axis)
\(z_4\): perpendicular to forearm (pitch axis)
\(z_5\): along forearm (second roll axis)

\(z_3 = z_5\) — the hallmark of a ZYZ spherical wrist.
Step 2 — Assign x-axes (all axes intersect):

\(x_3\): free choice (no preceding link) → pick \([0,0,-1]\)
\(x_4\): \(z_3 \times z_4 = \hat{x}\times\hat{y} = \hat{z}\); choose \(-\hat{z}\) → \([0,0,-1]\) (gives \(\alpha_4 = -90^\circ\) for ZYZ)
\(x_5\): \(z_4 \times z_5 = \hat{y}\times\hat{x} = -\hat{z}\) → \([0,0,-1]\)

title: Week 5: Kinematics Problem-Solving Session
text:
Solution 4: Frame Assignment


Step 1 — Assign z-axes:

\(z_0\): vertical (base revolute) → \([0,0,1]\)
\(z_1, z_2\): horizontal, perpendicular to arm plane (shoulder & elbow pitch) → \([0,-1,0]\)

Step 2 — Assign x-axes:

\(x_0\): free choice → \([1,0,0]\)
\(x_1\): \(z_0 \times z_1 = [0,0,1]\times[0,-1,0] = [1,0,0]\) (natural direction)
\(x_2\): \(z_1 \parallel z_2\) → common normal, \(\hat{x}_2 = [1,0,0]\)

All x-axes point radially outward in the arm plane — simplifying the position equations.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Note on Notation
The trajectory methods in this section apply to both joint space and Cartesian space.
We write \(q(t)\) to represent either:

A joint angle \(\theta_i(t)\) — when planning in joint space
A Cartesian coordinate \(x(t)\), \(y(t)\), \(z(t)\) — when planning in Cartesian space

Each degree of freedom gets its own polynomial. The math is identical.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Where Do Polynomials Apply?
The polynomial methods in this section (cubic, quintic) are timing profiles — they control how fast you move, not what shape the path is.


Joint space — apply directly

\(q(t)\) = polynomial for each joint angle
Each joint gets its own cubic/quintic
Path in Cartesian space is generally curved
This is how J (joint) motion works


Cartesian straight line — apply to a path parameter

Define the line: \(\mathbf{p}(s) = \mathbf{p}_0 + s(\mathbf{p}_f - \mathbf{p}_0)\)
The polynomial shapes \(s(t)\): \(0 \to 1\)
Path stays straight; polynomial controls the speed along it
This is how L (linear) motion works


In the following slides, \(q(t)\) means either a joint angle or the path parameter \(s(t)\) — the math is the same.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Polynomials in Joint Space
Apply a polynomial directly to each joint angle:

\(\theta_1(t)\) = cubic/quintic, \(\theta_2(t)\) = cubic/quintic, …
Each joint follows a smooth profile independently
The end-effector path in Cartesian space is generally curved
This is how FANUC J (joint) motion works

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Polynomials in Cartesian Space
For a straight-line path, we separate geometry from timing:

Path (fixed shape): \(\mathbf{p}(s) = \mathbf{p}_0 + s \cdot (\mathbf{p}_f - \mathbf{p}_0)\)
Timing (how far along): \(s(t)\) goes from 0 at the start to 1 at the end

Here \(s(t)\) is just a number between 0 and 1 that says “how far along the line are we at time \(t\)?”
The polynomial (cubic, quintic) shapes \(s(t)\), giving smooth acceleration and deceleration — while the path stays perfectly straight.
This is how FANUC L (linear) motion works.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Notation for This Section
In the following slides we write \(q(t)\) for the polynomial — this represents:

A joint angle \(\theta_i(t)\) in joint space, or
The progress variable \(s(t)\) in Cartesian space

The math is the same in both cases.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
From Polynomials to Velocity Profiles
Instead of solving for polynomial coefficients, design the velocity shape directly around motor limits (\(v_{max}\), \(a_{max}\)):

Get to maximum speed as quickly as possible
Stay there for as long as possible
Then slow down

This is what velocity profiles do — and it’s what industrial controllers use.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Why Multi-Segment?
So far: every trajectory goes from one point to another and stops.

Real tasks need motion through intermediate points without stopping
Stopping at every point wastes time and causes velocity discontinuities
We need to blend through via points for continuous motion

In FANUC TP: FINE = stop at each point, CNT = blend through

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
The Orientation Problem
So far we interpolated positions. But a Cartesian pose also includes orientation.






Note


This section applies to Cartesian-space planning only (L motion). Joint-space interpolation (J motion) handles orientation implicitly through FK — no special treatment needed.



Why can’t we just average two rotation matrices?
\[R_{avg} = \frac{R_1 + R_2}{2} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{not orthogonal, } \det \neq 1\]
The result is not a valid rotation. We need representations that support meaningful interpolation.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
RPY Angle Interpolation
Simple approach: Interpolate roll, pitch, yaw independently
\[\phi(t) = \phi_0 + s(t) \cdot (\phi_f - \phi_0)\]
Problem: Each angle lives on a circle — naive interpolation may take the long way around.

Fix: If \(|\Delta\phi| > 180°\), add/subtract 360° to take the shortest arc.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Quaternion Interpolation (SLERP)
Better approach: Represent orientation as a unit quaternion and use SLERP (Spherical Linear Interpolation)
\[\mathbf{q}(t) = \frac{\sin((1-s)\,\Omega)}{\sin \Omega}\,\mathbf{q}_0 + \frac{\sin(s\,\Omega)}{\sin \Omega}\,\mathbf{q}_f\]
where \(\Omega = \cos^{-1}(\mathbf{q}_0 \cdot \mathbf{q}_f)\) and \(s\) goes from 0 to 1.
Why quaternions?

Shortest path on the rotation sphere (great arc)
Constant angular velocity
No gimbal lock

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Full Pose Interpolation
A pose = position + orientation. Interpolate them separately:

Position: linear interpolation (straight line) with polynomial timing \(s(t)\)
Orientation: SLERP with the same \(s(t)\)

from spatialmath import SE3, UnitQuaternion

T0 = SE3.Trans(0.4, 0, 0.3) * SE3.RPY([0, 0, 0], unit='deg')
Tf = SE3.Trans(0.4, 0.2, 0.3) * SE3.RPY([0, 0, 90], unit='deg')

# rtb.ctraj does exactly this: linear position + SLERP orientation
traj = rtb.ctraj(T0, Tf, 50)

Cartesian (L motion)

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
The Speed Problem with Polynomials

Quintic polynomial can exceed motor limits (peak 84°/s > 80°/s) and you can’t control it. Trapezoidal respects \(v_{max}\) by design, cruises there, and finishes faster.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Cubic: Derivatives and Setup
Start with \(q(t) = a_0 + a_1 t + a_2 t^2 + a_3 t^3\). Take derivatives:
\[\dot{q}(t) = a_1 + 2a_2 t + 3a_3 t^2 \qquad \ddot{q}(t) = 2a_2 + 6a_3 t\]
Now plug in the boundary conditions:



Condition
Equation
Result




\(q(0) = q_0\)
\(a_0 = q_0\)
\(a_0 = q_0\)


\(\dot{q}(0) = 0\)
\(a_1 = 0\)
\(a_1 = 0\)


\(q(t_f) = q_f\)
\(q_0 + a_2 t_f^2 + a_3 t_f^3 = q_f\)



\(\dot{q}(t_f) = 0\)
\(2a_2 t_f + 3a_3 t_f^2 = 0\)




Two equations, two unknowns (\(a_2\), \(a_3\)) → solve.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Cubic: Solve for Coefficients
Write in matrix form (\(a_0\) and \(a_1\) are already known):
\[\begin{bmatrix} t_f^2 & t_f^3 \\ 2t_f & 3t_f^2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a_2 \\ a_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} q_f - q_0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\]
Invert to get:
\[a_2 = \frac{3(q_f - q_0)}{t_f^2} \qquad a_3 = \frac{-2(q_f - q_0)}{t_f^3}\]
Final trajectory:
\[q(t) = q_0 + \frac{3(q_f - q_0)}{t_f^2} t^2 - \frac{2(q_f - q_0)}{t_f^3} t^3\]

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Quintic: Apply Boundary Conditions
At \(t = 0\) (directly gives 3 coefficients):
\[a_0 = q_0 \qquad a_1 = \dot{q}_0 \qquad a_2 = \frac{\ddot{q}_0}{2}\]
At \(t = t_f\) (3 equations in 3 unknowns \(a_3, a_4, a_5\)):
\[\begin{bmatrix} t_f^3 & t_f^4 & t_f^5 \\ 3t_f^2 & 4t_f^3 & 5t_f^4 \\ 6t_f & 12t_f^2 & 20t_f^3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a_3 \\ a_4 \\ a_5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} q_f - a_0 - a_1 t_f - a_2 t_f^2 \\ \dot{q}_f - a_1 - 2a_2 t_f \\ \ddot{q}_f - 2a_2 \end{bmatrix}\]
Matrix is square → invert to solve: \(\mathbf{a} = M^{-1} \mathbf{b}\)

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Practice: Cubic Polynomial
Problem: Move from \(q_0 = 0°\) to \(q_f = 90°\) in \(t_f = 2\) s with zero endpoint velocities.

Find the coefficients \(a_0, a_1, a_2, a_3\)
What is \(q(1)\)?
What is \(\dot{q}(1)\)?


Solution:
\(a_0 = 0\), \(a_1 = 0\), \(a_2 = \frac{3 \times 90}{4} = 67.5\), \(a_3 = \frac{-2 \times 90}{8} = -22.5\)
\[q(t) = 67.5\, t^2 - 22.5\, t^3\]

\(q(1) = 67.5 - 22.5 = 45°\) (halfway — symmetric by design)
\(\dot{q}(t) = 135\,t - 67.5\,t^2 \implies \dot{q}(1) = 67.5\) °/s

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Practice: Quintic Polynomial
Problem: Same move (\(q_0 = 0°\), \(q_f = 90°\), \(t_f = 2\) s) but now with zero endpoint velocities and zero endpoint accelerations.

What are \(a_0, a_1, a_2\)?
Set up the 3×3 system for \(a_3, a_4, a_5\)
What is the peak velocity? Compare to cubic.


Solution:
\(a_0 = 0\), \(a_1 = 0\), \(a_2 = 0\) (all BCs at \(t=0\) are zero)
\[\begin{bmatrix} 8 & 16 & 32 \\ 12 & 32 & 80 \\ 12 & 48 & 160 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a_3 \\ a_4 \\ a_5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 90 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \implies a_3 = 112.5,\; a_4 = -84.375,\; a_5 = 16.875\]
Peak velocity at \(t = 1\): \(\dot{q}(1) = 3a_3 + 4a_4 + 5a_5 = 84.4\) °/s (vs 67.5 °/s for cubic — higher peak!)

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Approach 1: RPY Angle Interpolation
Simple idea: Interpolate roll, pitch, yaw independently
\[\phi(t) = \phi_0 + s(t) \cdot (\phi_f - \phi_0)\]
Same for \(\theta(t)\) and \(\psi(t)\).
Problem — the direction ambiguity:
Each angle lives on a circle → two paths from A to B (short way and long way).

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Approach 2: Quaternion SLERP
SLERP (Spherical Linear Interpolation) — linear interpolation, but on a sphere:







LERP (on a line)
SLERP (on a sphere)




\(\mathbf{p}(s) = (1-s)\,\mathbf{p}_0 + s\,\mathbf{p}_f\)
\(\text{SLERP}(\mathbf{q}_0, \mathbf{q}_f, s) = \frac{\sin((1-s)\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}\,\mathbf{q}_0 + \frac{\sin(s\,\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}\,\mathbf{q}_f\)


Weights: \((1-s)\) and \(s\)
Weights: \(\frac{\sin((1-s)\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}\) and \(\frac{\sin(s\,\Omega)}{\sin\Omega}\)


Result on the line
Result on the sphere surface


Constant linear speed
Constant angular speed



where \(\Omega = \cos^{-1}(\mathbf{q}_0 \cdot \mathbf{q}_f)\) is half the rotation angle between the two orientations.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Why SLERP Wins

All three methods reach the same final orientation — but only SLERP progresses at constant angular velocity (straight line). RPY and Euler speed up and slow down unpredictably.

section: Quaternion Recap: What is a Quaternion?
text:
Quaternion Recap: What is a Quaternion?
A quaternion is a 4-component number: \(\;\mathbf{q} = w + x\,\mathbf{i} + y\,\mathbf{j} + z\,\mathbf{k}\)
Written as a scalar-vector pair: \(\;\mathbf{q} = (w, \;\mathbf{v})\) where \(\mathbf{v} = (x, y, z)\)
Key rules: \(\;\mathbf{i}^2 = \mathbf{j}^2 = \mathbf{k}^2 = \mathbf{i}\mathbf{j}\mathbf{k} = -1\)



Representation
Parameters
Singularities
Interpolation




Rotation matrix
9 (6 constraints)
None
Not directly


Euler / RPY
3
Gimbal lock
Direction problem


Quaternion
4 (1 constraint)
None
SLERP



(See the Quaternion Basics supplementary PDF for full details.)

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Quaternion Recap: Unit Quaternions = Rotations
A unit quaternion (\(\|\mathbf{q}\| = 1\)) encodes rotation by angle \(\theta\) about axis \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\):
\[\mathbf{q} = \left(\cos\frac{\theta}{2},\;\; \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\;\hat{\mathbf{k}}\right)\]
Examples:







Rotation
Quaternion \((w, x, y, z)\)




Identity (no rotation)
\((1,\; 0,\; 0,\; 0)\)


90° about z-axis
\((\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\; 0,\; 0,\; \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})\)


180° about x-axis
\((0,\; 1,\; 0,\; 0)\)



Note the half-angle \(\theta/2\) — both \(\mathbf{q}\) and \(-\mathbf{q}\) represent the same rotation.

Why half-angle? The rotation formula is a sandwich product: p’ = q * p * q. The angle appears twice (from q and q), so θ/2 + θ/2 = θ gives the correct rotation.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
section: Why SLERP and Not Just LERP?
text:
Why SLERP and Not Just LERP?
If you use regular LERP on quaternions: \((1-s)\,\mathbf{q}_0 + s\,\mathbf{q}_f\)

Result falls inside the sphere — not a valid unit quaternion
Speed is non-uniform — faster in the middle, slower at the ends

The sin-based weights in SLERP fix both: result stays on the sphere, angular velocity is constant.
Analogy: two cities on Earth. LERP digs a tunnel (through the interior). SLERP walks the great circle (shortest path on the surface).






Tip


If \(\mathbf{q}_0 \cdot \mathbf{q}_f < 0\), negate one quaternion to take the short path (same rotation, shorter arc).

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
SLERP vs RPY vs Euler

Only SLERP progresses at constant angular velocity (straight line). RPY and Euler speed up and slow down unpredictably.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Practice: SLERP by Hand
Problem: Interpolate halfway (\(s = 0.5\)) between:

\(\mathbf{q}_0 = (1, 0, 0, 0)\) — identity (no rotation)
\(\mathbf{q}_f = (0, 0, 0, 1)\) — 180° about z-axis


Solution:

Dot product: \(\mathbf{q}_0 \cdot \mathbf{q}_f = 1 \times 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 0\)
\(\Omega = \cos^{-1}(0) = 90°\) (half the 180° rotation)
Weights at \(s = 0.5\): \(\frac{\sin(0.5 \times 90°)}{\sin 90°} = \frac{\sin 45°}{1} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) for both
\(\mathbf{q}(0.5) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(1, 0, 0, 0) + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(0, 0, 0, 1) = (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, 0, 0, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})\)

This is a 90° rotation about z — exactly halfway, as expected.

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Quaternion Recap: Operations
Conjugate (= inverse rotation for unit quaternions): \[\mathbf{q}^* = (w, -\mathbf{v})\]
Multiplication (composes rotations — order matters): \[\mathbf{q}_1 \otimes \mathbf{q}_2 = (w_1 w_2 - \mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2,\;\; w_1 \mathbf{v}_2 + w_2 \mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_2)\]
Rotating a vector (sandwich product): \[\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{q} \otimes (0, \mathbf{p}) \otimes \mathbf{q}^*\]
In practice: convert to rotation matrix \(R\) and use \(\mathbf{p}' = R\,\mathbf{p}\) (faster for many vectors).



Use case
Best tool




Store orientation

title: Week 6: Trajectory Generation
text:
Multi-Segment Trajectory with mstraj


import roboticstoolbox as rtb
import numpy as np

# Via points (each row = waypoint), start q0=20
via = np.array([[40], [10], [30]])
q0 = np.array([20])

# Trapezoidal blending: qdmax=1, tacc=2s
traj = rtb.mstraj(via, dt=0.1, tacc=2,
                   qdmax=[1], q0=q0)

# No blending (sharp corners)
traj = rtb.mstraj(via, dt=0.1, tacc=0,
                   qdmax=[1], q0=q0)

# Faster: higher max velocity
traj = rtb.mstraj(via, dt=0.1, tacc=0,
                   qdmax=[2], q0=q0)

# Specify segment durations instead
traj = rtb.mstraj(via, dt=0.1, tacc=4,
                   tsegment=[10, 30, 20], q0=q0)

via: waypoints (each row = target), q0: start position
qdmax: max velocity per axis, dt: time step
tacc: blend time — larger = smoother corners
tsegment: segment durations (overrides qdmax)



mstraj chains trapezoidal-velocity segments between via points and blends at transitions.

title: Week 7: Industrial Sensors & Logic
text:
Digital Inputs: NPN vs PNP

What robots sense: part presence, position confirmation, safety status, machine states
When wiring sensors, match the type: PNP is standard in Europe/Asia (our lab), NPN in North America. Wrong type → input never triggers.

NPN and PNP refer to the output transistor type inside the sensor. Both are 3-wire sensors (brown = +24V, blue = 0V, black = signal).
PNP (sourcing): When the sensor detects something, it connects the signal wire to +24V internally. The controller input sees +24V = ON. The current flows FROM the sensor TO the controller input, then to ground through the input card. The sensor is the “source” of current.
NPN (sinking): When the sensor detects something, it connects the signal wire to 0V (ground) internally. The controller input is pulled to ground = ON. The current flows FROM the +24V supply through the input card TO the sensor, then to ground. The sensor is the “sink” — it provides the path to ground.
Why it matters: Our FANUC controller has PNP-compatible inputs (it expects to see +24V when active). If you accidentally buy an NPN sensor, the input will never read ON — or worse, it might float and give false readings. Always check the sensor datasheet for “PNP” or “sourcing” output.
Quick way to remember: PNP = Positive output when active. NPN = Negative (ground) output when active.

Week 7: Industrial Sensors & Logic
text:
Mechanical & Pressure Sensors





Limit switch






Vacuum switch




Limit Switch: Physical contact — object pushes lever, toggles contacts (NO↔︎NC). Confirms clamp closed, end-of-travel. Nearly indestructible.
Pressure Switch: Monitors pneumatic line pressure — if pressure drops, DI goes OFF → fault detected.
Vacuum Switch: Measures suction level at the gripper. If vacuum is below threshold → part not sealed → abort pick.



How the vacuum switch works with a suction gripper:
A vacuum gripper picks parts by suction — a vacuum pump pulls air through the suction cup, creating negative pressure that holds the part against the cup. When the cup seals properly against the part, the vacuum level rises (e.g., to -60 kPa). When there’s no part or the seal is bad (wrong shape, porous surface), the vacuum level stays low (e.g., -10 kPa) because air keeps leaking in.
The vacuum switch (like the SMC ZSE30 in the image) is a small digital pressure sensor connected to the suction line. You set a threshold (e.g., -40 kPa). When vacuum reaches that threshold, the switch outputs ON (24V on its signal wire → DI goes ON). The TP program checks this:
DO[1:Vacuum]=ON ;          ! Turn on vacuum pump
WAIT 0.50(sec) ;            ! Give time to build vacuum
IF DI[2:Vac_OK]=OFF, JMP LBL[99] ;  ! No seal → abort
L P[2:Lift] 200mm/sec FINE ;         ! Seal OK → lift part
Without this check, the robot might lift with a bad seal and drop a glass panel mid-air. The vacuum switch is essentially a “grip confirm” sensor for suction grippers, just like a force sensor confirms grip for finger grippers.
Limit switch details: Has three terminals: C (common), NO (normally open), NC (normally closed). When the lever is not pressed, C-NC is connected. When pressed, C-NO is connected. Wire to whichever logic you need. For safety applications (e.g., confirming a guard door is closed), use the NC contact — if the wire breaks, the circuit opens, which is the safe state.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
TCP Calibration Methods Compared









Method
Points
Finds
Trade-off




3-Point
3 orientations
XYZ position
Exact (3 eqns, 3 unknowns) — no way to detect a bad touch


4-Point
4+ orientations
XYZ position
Over-constrained → reports residual error; redo if too high


6-Point
4 + 2 orient.
XYZ + orientation
Extra 2 pts define tool Z & X axes




Why 4 over 3? Over-constraining lets the controller flag inaccurate touches
Why 6? Welding torches, dispensing needles — any tool where approach direction matters


The 3-point method is the simplest: you touch the reference pin from only 3 orientations. It gives a rough TCP position but is less accurate because 3 points barely constrain the solution — any measurement noise has a large effect. It’s acceptable for symmetric tools like cylindrical grippers where the exact TCP doesn’t need to be very precise.
The 4-point method is the industry standard. Four orientations over-constrain the problem, so the controller can do a least-squares fit and report a residual error. A residual under 1 mm is considered good; under 0.5 mm is excellent. If the residual is high, one of the touch points was probably inaccurate — redo it. Always use orientations as different from each other as possible (don’t just rotate 10 degrees between touches — aim for 45-90 degree changes).
The 6-point method adds tool frame orientation on top of position. After the first 4 points find where the TCP is, points 5 and 6 tell the controller which direction the tool’s Z-axis and X-axis point. This matters for tools with directional behavior — a welding torch needs its Z-axis along the wire, a dispensing needle needs Z along the flow direction, a deburring spindle needs Z along the cutting axis. Without correct orientation, the controller cannot properly execute orientation-dependent moves like “approach along tool Z.” For a simple parallel-jaw gripper, the 4-point method is usually sufficient because the grip direction is obvious and symmetric.
