text:
FANUC Mastering Methods



Method
Procedure
Accuracy




Fixture
Align joints with precision jig
Highest


Zero-position
Move to mechanical stop marks
High


Single-axis
Re-master one joint only
High


Quick
Align witness marks on housing
Moderate




Mastering establishes the relationship between encoder counts and joint angles. The encoder is an incremental or absolute sensor — it counts pulses or reads a code pattern, but it doesn’t inherently know what angle corresponds to what count. Mastering tells the controller: “at this specific encoder reading, the joint angle is defined as zero.” Without correct mastering, every position the robot has ever taught becomes wrong. This is why after a collision or motor replacement, all taught programs become unreliable until you re-master. On FANUC, the most common method is quick mastering using calibration marks — small witness marks on the joints that align at the zero position. Fixture mastering is the most accurate but requires a special jig. After a battery failure on older systems with incremental encoders, re-mastering was mandatory — modern absolute encoders retain position even without power.

title: Week 8: Digital Twinning & Calibration
text:
FANUC Mastering Methods (B-83574EN, Ch. 8)








Menu Item
What You Do
When to Use




1 — Fixture position
Align joints with precision jig
Motor/reducer replaced, disassembly


2 — Zero-position
Jog all axes to 0° using scribe marks
Quick-fix after failure (visual, less accurate)


3 — Quick master
Jog to saved reference pose, or use last power-off pose
BZAL alarm, battery died (no parts changed)


5 — Single-axis
Re-master one joint only
Single axis service or cable disconnect



Quick master has two sub-modes:

At reference position: jog to saved pose (default: 0° on all axes)
Using power off position: no jogging — uses last known pose


This table is based on B-83574EN Chapter 8 — the mechanical unit operator’s manual for the LR Mate 200iD.
Key insight: The encoder stores two values — “rotation times” and “pulse value within one revolution.” A battery run-out only loses the rotation times; the within-revolution pulse value survives. Quick mastering exploits this to recover without full re-alignment. That is why quick mastering CANNOT be used if mechanical parts (motor, reducer, pulsecoder) were replaced — the within-revolution data is only valid if the motor-to-arm relationship hasn’t physically changed.
Zero-position mastering and Quick mastering (at reference) both use the same scribe marks on the robot housing — the factory default reference position for quick mastering IS the zero position (all axes 0°). The difference is what the controller does internally with the encoder data: zero-position writes completely new mastering data from scratch, while quick mastering only recovers the lost rotation times.
Quick mastering using power off position is the simplest — no jogging needed at all. The controller uses the surviving encoder data plus the assumption that the robot hasn’t physically moved since power went off.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
This Week’s Goals

Distinguish holonomic from non-holonomic constraints and identify each in real robots
Derive the unicycle kinematic model relating body velocity to control inputs
Map a differential-drive robot onto the unicycle abstraction
Derive the bicycle (Ackermann) model for car-like robots
See how mobile-robot kinematics extends the FK/IK thinking from manipulators to velocity-level models


This is the first week of Part IV — we leave manipulator arms and FANUC behind and enter the world of mobile robotics. The mathematical tools change: instead of DH parameters and forward kinematics chains, we work with velocity constraints and kinematic models in the plane. But the underlying question is the same: how does the robot’s motion relate to its actuator inputs? By the end of today, students should be able to derive and use the two fundamental mobile robot models.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Two Worlds of Robotics


Manipulator (W01–W08)

Fixed base, serial chain of links
Configuration: joint angles \(q = [\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_n]^T\)
FK gave us: joint angles \(\to\) end-effector pose
IK gave us: desired pose \(\to\) joint angles
Workspace is limited by arm reach


Mobile Robot (W09–W13)

The base itself moves through the world
Configuration: pose \(q = (x, y, \theta)\)
New question: wheel commands \(\to\) how does the pose change?
Motion is constrained by wheel geometry
Workspace is (in principle) unbounded



Draw a clear line between the two halves of the course. In Part II–III we studied manipulators: the base was bolted to the floor, we used FK to find where the tool is, and IK to find what joint angles reach a target pose. Now in Part IV–V we study mobile robots: the entire robot moves through the environment. The core question changes: given wheel speeds or a steering angle, how does the robot’s position and heading change over time? This is a velocity-level question — we’ll build a model that maps control inputs (like left/right wheel speed) to the rate of change of (x, y, theta). The key twist: mobile robots have velocity constraints that manipulators don’t — a wheeled robot can’t slide sideways. This is the central concept of today’s lecture.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Types of Mobile Robots





Type
Examples




Wheeled
Differential drive, car-like, omnidirectional


Legged
Quadruped (Spot), biped (Atlas)


Aerial
Quadrotor, fixed-wing


Underwater
AUV, ROV



Course focus: wheeled ground robots




Give a brief survey of mobile robot types. Wheeled robots are the most common in industry — warehouse AGVs, delivery robots, autonomous cars. Legged robots handle rough terrain but are mechanically complex. Aerial and underwater robots have 3D kinematics. We focus on wheeled ground robots because: they are the most deployed, the math is clean 2D, and they perfectly illustrate the holonomic vs non-holonomic distinction. Lab 8 this week will use a simulated wheeled robot.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
The Planar Configuration


A wheeled robot on a flat surface has three configuration variables:
\[q = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ \theta \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^2 \times S^1\]

\((x, y)\): position of the robot’s reference point
\(\theta\): heading angle (orientation)
\(S^1\): the circle — \(\theta\) wraps around at \(2\pi\)

The configuration space is 3-dimensional.




Unlike a manipulator where the configuration space is n-dimensional joint space, a planar mobile robot always has a 3D C-space regardless of how many wheels it has. The reference point is usually the center of the drive axle (for differential drive) or the rear axle center (for car-like robots). The S^1 factor means theta is an angle — it wraps around, so 0 and 2*pi are the same configuration. This is topologically different from R^3: the C-space is R^2 x S^1, not R^3. We’ll see that despite having 3 configuration variables, most wheeled robots can only command 2 independent velocities at any instant — that gap is the non-holonomic constraint.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
From Jacobian to G(q)
Manipulator (what we know):
\[\dot{x}_{ee} = J(q)\,\dot{q} \qquad \text{(joint velocities } \to \text{ task velocity)}\]
Mobile robot (what we’ll derive today):
\[\dot{q} = G(q)\,u \qquad \text{(control inputs } \to \text{ configuration velocity)}\]
where \(u\) is a vector of control inputs (e.g., wheel speeds or steering commands).






Note


\(G(q)\) is the mobile robot’s “Jacobian” — it tells you which configuration velocities are achievable given the control inputs.




This is the key analogy to carry through the lecture. For a manipulator, J is typically square (n joints, n task-space DOF) or tall (redundant). For a mobile robot, G(q) is rectangular: 3 rows (configuration dimension) but only 2 columns (two independent controls). That means not all configuration velocities are instantaneously achievable — the robot can’t move in every direction at once. The null space of G(q)^T defines the forbidden directions. This is precisely the non-holonomic constraint, which we’ll formalize next.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
What is a Constraint?
A constraint limits the configurations or motions a system can achieve.
Why this matters for wheeled robots: rolling without slipping imposes a velocity-level constraint on the wheels — this is the mathematical root of why a car can’t slide sideways, and it shapes every model in the rest of this lecture.








Type
Mathematical Form
Effect




Holonomic
\(f(q) = 0\)
Reduces C-space dimension


Non-holonomic
\(A(q)\dot{q} = 0\), not integrable
Restricts velocity only









Warning


Key distinction: A holonomic constraint eliminates reachable configurations. A non-holonomic constraint restricts how you move, not where you can go.




This is the most important definition slide of the lecture. Holonomic constraints are position-level: f(q) = 0 carves out a lower-dimensional surface in C-space. Example: a pendulum of fixed length has q = (x, y) but the constraint x^2 + y^2 = L^2 reduces it to 1 DOF. Non-holonomic constraints are velocity-level: A(q)*q_dot = 0 cannot be integrated to a position constraint. The number of reachable configurations is NOT reduced — only the instantaneous velocity directions are limited. This is counterintuitive and worth spending time on. If students ask: “If I can’t move sideways, how can I reach a point to my left?” — the answer is parallel parking, which is the next key slide.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Holonomic Example: Train on Rails


Top-down view. Position: \((x, y)\) in meters.
Suppose the rail is a straight line at \(y = 3\).
The constraint:
\[f(q) = y - 3 = 0\]

\(x\) is free — the train slides along the rail
\(y\) is locked at 3
Before: 2 DOF (a plane)
After: 1 DOF (a line)

One position equation kills one degree of freedom → holonomic.




The train example is deliberately simple. The constraint y = y_track(x) is purely a function of configuration — no velocities involved. It permanently removes degrees of freedom. The train can never leave the track, no matter what sequence of inputs it receives. Contrast this with the next slide: a car also can’t move sideways instantaneously, but it CAN reach any point in the plane given enough maneuvering.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Non-Holonomic Example: The Car


A car cannot move sideways — the velocity perpendicular to the heading is zero:
\[\dot{x}\sin\theta - \dot{y}\cos\theta = 0\]
In Pfaffian form: \(\;A(q)\,\dot{q} = 0\)
\[\begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta & -\cos\theta & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \\ \dot{\theta} \end{bmatrix} = 0\]
This depends on \(q\) and \(\dot{q}\) — and it cannot be integrated to \(f(q) = 0\).




Walk through the equation carefully. The constraint says: the component of velocity perpendicular to the heading direction is zero. Expand it: x_dot * sin(theta) - y_dot * cos(theta) = 0. If theta were a constant, you could integrate this to get xsin(theta) - ycos(theta) = const, which would be holonomic. But theta itself changes over time and is coupled to x and y through the dynamics — so the constraint is not integrable. This is what makes it non-holonomic. The mathematical proof of non-integrability uses Frobenius’ theorem, which is beyond our scope, but the intuition is clear: a car can’t slide sideways, yet it can parallel park into any spot.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
The Parallel Parking Insight
Non-holonomic \(\neq\) unreachable
A car cannot move sideways instantaneously, but through a sequence of forward/reverse maneuvers, it can reach any \((x, y, \theta)\).







Tip


Key insight: A non-holonomic constraint restricts instantaneous velocity directions, not the set of reachable configurations. Parallel parking is the proof!





The technical term: the system is controllable — any configuration can be reached from any other configuration, despite the velocity constraint.

This is the “aha moment” slide. Pause and let it sink in. A non-holonomic constraint seems like it should prevent the robot from reaching certain places — but it doesn’t. The constraint only says what you can’t do RIGHT NOW; it says nothing about what you can achieve over TIME through a sequence of maneuvers. This is Chow’s theorem (or the Rashevsky-Chow theorem): if the control vector fields and their Lie brackets span the full tangent space, the system is controllable. We won’t prove this formally, but the parallel parking example makes it viscerally clear. Every student who has parallel parked a car has exploited non-holonomic controllability.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Rolling Without Slipping
The fundamental constraint behind conventional wheeled robots — two conditions:

Rolling: \(v = r\dot{\phi}\) (velocity at contact = ground velocity)     2. No lateral slip: \(\dot{x}\sin\theta - \dot{y}\cos\theta = 0\)

These are velocity-level constraints — they cannot be reduced to position constraints.







All the kinematic models we derive today rest on these two assumptions: pure rolling (no skid in the forward direction) and no lateral slip (no skid in the sideways direction). In reality, tires do slip — especially at high speed, on wet surfaces, or during aggressive maneuvers. But at low to moderate speeds (typical for indoor robots, warehouse AGVs, and careful autonomous driving), the no-slip assumption is very accurate. When it breaks down, you need dynamic models that account for tire friction — that’s a topic for an advanced course. For our purposes, rolling without slipping gives us clean, elegant kinematic models.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Pfaffian Form
Combine the no-slip constraint into a standard form:
\[A(q)\,\dot{q} = 0\]
For a single wheel with heading \(\theta\):
\[\begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta & -\cos\theta & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \\ \dot{\theta} \end{bmatrix} = 0\]

1 constraint on a 3-DOF system
Leaves 2 independent velocity directions
Therefore the robot needs exactly 2 control inputs


The Pfaffian form A(q)*q_dot = 0 is the standard mathematical representation of non-holonomic constraints. The matrix A(q) is 1x3 here (one constraint), so its null space is 2-dimensional. Those two null-space directions are the allowable velocity directions — they become the columns of the G(q) matrix we’re about to derive. The number of control inputs equals the dimension of the null space: 3 (C-space dim) minus 1 (number of constraints) = 2. This is why both the unicycle and differential-drive robots have exactly two control inputs (v and omega, or left and right wheel speeds). The bicycle model also has 2 inputs (speed and steering angle). This is not a coincidence — it’s a direct consequence of the single rolling constraint.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
The Unicycle Abstraction


The simplest non-holonomic mobile robot:

A single wheel that can roll forward/backward and pivot
Configuration: \(q = (x, y, \theta)\)
Control inputs: \(u = (v, \omega)\)

\(v\): linear velocity
\(\omega\): angular velocity (yaw rate)


Captures the essential behavior of most wheeled robots.




The unicycle is an idealization — a point robot with a heading. It abstracts away the physical details of wheels, axles, and chassis. The two control inputs are the forward speed v and the turning rate omega. Think of it as a Segway or a Roomba seen from above. The unicycle model is the “hello world” of mobile robot kinematics — simple enough to analyze completely, yet rich enough to exhibit the non-holonomic constraint. Every differential-drive robot (iRobot, TurtleBot, most warehouse AGVs) can be modeled as a unicycle.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Unicycle Kinematics


The robot moves at speed \(v\) along its heading \(\theta\):
\[\dot{x} = v\cos\theta \qquad \dot{y} = v\sin\theta \qquad \dot{\theta} = \omega\]
In matrix form:
\[\dot{q} = \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \\ \dot{\theta} \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{G(q)} \begin{bmatrix} v \\ \omega \end{bmatrix}\]




Derive this step by step. The robot is at position (x, y) heading in direction theta. If it drives forward at speed v, the x-component of velocity is vcos(theta) and the y-component is vsin(theta) — just resolving the velocity vector into components. The heading changes at rate omega, independently of position. The G(q) matrix is 3x2: 3 configuration variables, 2 control inputs. The first column [cos(theta), sin(theta), 0]^T is the “drive forward” vector field — it says what happens to q when you increase v. The second column [0, 0, 1]^T is the “turn in place” vector field — it says what happens when you increase omega. Note that G(q) depends on the configuration through theta — the direction you move depends on which way you’re facing. This is fundamentally different from a holonomic system where you could move in any direction regardless of your current state.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
section: Sanity Check: Does the Constraint Hold?
text:
Sanity Check: Does the Constraint Hold?
Recall the no-lateral-slip constraint: \(\dot{x}\sin\theta - \dot{y}\cos\theta = 0\)
Substitute the unicycle equations:
\[v\cos\theta \cdot \sin\theta - v\sin\theta \cdot \cos\theta = 0 \quad \checkmark\]
The model automatically satisfies the non-holonomic constraint — because we derived it from the constraint’s null space.

This is a quick verification that builds confidence. The unicycle model was constructed to lie in the null space of A(q), so of course it satisfies A(q)q_dot = 0. But it’s good practice to check explicitly. Point out that any linear combination of the columns of G(q) will satisfy the constraint — the columns span the null space of A(q). This is the relationship: A(q)G(q) = 0.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Worked Example: Circular Motion
Given: \(v = 1\) m/s, \(\omega = 0.5\) rad/s, \(q(0) = (0, 0, 0)\)
Step 1: Heading: \(\theta(t) = 0.5\,t\)
Step 2: Position (integrate):
\[x(t) = \int_0^t \cos(0.5\tau)\,d\tau = 2\sin(0.5\,t)\] \[y(t) = \int_0^t \sin(0.5\tau)\,d\tau = 2\bigl(1 - \cos(0.5\,t)\bigr)\]
Result: A circle of radius \(R = v/\omega = 1/0.5 = 2\) m, centered at \((0, 2)\).






Note


General rule: Constant \(v\) and \(\omega\) produce a circle of radius \(R = |v / \omega|\).




Walk through the integration on the board. The key formula is R = v/omega — the turning radius. This is the mobile robot analog of the turning radius from everyday driving. When v and omega are both constant, the path is a perfect circle. The center of the circle is offset from the starting position by R in the direction perpendicular to the initial heading. Here, starting at (0,0,0) facing right, the center is at (0, R) = (0, 2) — directly to the left. The robot traces a counterclockwise circle because omega > 0 (positive = counterclockwise by convention). If omega were negative, it would curve to the right.

Tip


The ability to spin in place (\(v = 0\), \(\omega \neq 0\)) is unique to differential-drive robots. A car cannot do this.




Go through each row. The most important insight is the spin-in-place capability: a differential-drive robot can rotate without translating. This is extremely useful — it can face any direction without moving. A car or bicycle cannot do this; they must be moving forward to change heading. This fundamental difference is why differential drive is preferred for indoor robots (tight spaces, need to turn on the spot) while car-like steering is used for outdoor vehicles (higher speed, more stable).

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
The Differential-Drive Robot


The most common physical realization of the unicycle model:

Two independently driven wheels on a common axle
Wheel radius: \(r\)
Track width (wheel separation): \(L\)
Each wheel spins at \(\dot{\phi}_R\) and \(\dot{\phi}_L\)
Often a passive caster wheel for balance

Examples: iRobot Roomba, TurtleBot, warehouse AGVs







The differential-drive robot is called “differential” because steering is achieved by the difference in wheel speeds — not by a dedicated steering mechanism. Both wheels spin forward at equal speeds: the robot goes straight. Right wheel faster: the robot turns left. Opposite wheel speeds: the robot spins in place. This is mechanically simple (just two motors) and gives full unicycle control authority. The caster wheel at the front or back is passive and just prevents the robot from tipping over. In practice, there may be two casters for stability. The reference point for the kinematic model is the midpoint of the drive axle.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Differential-Drive to Unicycle Mapping


Right wheel velocity: \(v_R = r\dot{\phi}_R\)
Left wheel velocity: \(v_L = r\dot{\phi}_L\)
Forward velocity (average):
\[v = \frac{v_R + v_L}{2} = \frac{r}{2}\bigl(\dot{\phi}_R + \dot{\phi}_L\bigr)\]
Angular velocity (difference):
\[\omega = \frac{v_R - v_L}{L} = \frac{r}{L}\bigl(\dot{\phi}_R - \dot{\phi}_L\bigr)\]

In matrix form:
\[\begin{bmatrix} v \\ \omega \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} r/2 & r/2 \\ r/L & -r/L \end{bmatrix}}_{M} \begin{bmatrix} \dot{\phi}_R \\ \dot{\phi}_L \end{bmatrix}\]
\(M\) is invertible — so we can go both ways.


Derive this from first principles. The forward velocity is the average of the two wheel velocities — if both wheels go at the same speed, v equals that speed. The angular velocity is proportional to the difference — if the right wheel is faster by delta_v, the robot turns left at rate delta_v / L, where L is the distance between the wheels. The factor R converts from angular wheel speed (rad/s) to linear wheel speed (m/s). The matrix M is 2x2 and invertible (det = -R^2/L which is nonzero), so we can uniquely recover wheel speeds from desired v and omega. This invertibility is crucial for control: given a desired trajectory, we compute the required (v, omega) and then invert M to get wheel commands.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
section: Inverse Mapping: From Commands to Wheels
text:
Inverse Mapping: From Commands to Wheels
Invert \(M\) to get wheel speeds from desired \((v, \omega)\):
\[\begin{bmatrix} \dot{\phi}_R \\ \dot{\phi}_L \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/r & L/(2r) \\ 1/r & -L/(2r) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v \\ \omega \end{bmatrix}\]
Or equivalently:
\[\dot{\phi}_R = \frac{v + \omega L/2}{r} \qquad \dot{\phi}_L = \frac{v - \omega L/2}{r}\]






Tip


This is what the motor controller uses: given a desired forward speed \(v\) and turn rate \(\omega\), compute the required wheel RPMs.




This inverse mapping is what actually runs on the robot’s microcontroller. The high-level planner outputs a desired (v, omega) — e.g., “go forward at 0.5 m/s while turning left at 0.2 rad/s” — and the low-level controller converts this to motor commands using these formulas. Note that positive omega (turning left) makes the right wheel faster and the left wheel slower, which matches our intuition. If omega = 0, both wheels spin at the same speed v/R. If v = 0 and omega > 0, the right wheel goes forward and the left wheel goes backward at equal speeds — a pure pivot turn.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Worked Example: Differential Drive
Given: \(r = 0.05\) m, \(L = 0.30\) m, \(\dot{\phi}_R = 10\) rad/s, \(\dot{\phi}_L = 5\) rad/s

Step 1 — Forward velocity:
\[v = \frac{r}{2}(\dot{\phi}_R + \dot{\phi}_L) = \frac{0.05}{2}(10 + 5) = 0.375 \text{ m/s}\]


Step 2 — Angular velocity:
\[\omega = \frac{r}{L}(\dot{\phi}_R - \dot{\phi}_L) = \frac{0.05}{0.30}(10 - 5) = 0.833 \text{ rad/s}\]


Step 3 — Turning radius:
\[R_{\text{turn}} = \frac{v}{\omega} = \frac{0.375}{0.833} = 0.45 \text{ m}\]
The robot curves left (right wheel is faster).


Go through each step slowly. Emphasize the units: r in meters, phi_dot in rad/s, so v comes out in m/s. The turning radius is less than half a meter — this is a tight turn. The right wheel (10 rad/s) is faster than the left (5 rad/s), so the robot curves to the left. Ask students: what if we swapped the wheel speeds? Answer: omega becomes negative, the robot curves right with the same radius.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Practice Problem
Given: A differential-drive robot with \(r = 0.04\) m, \(L = 0.20\) m needs to drive in a circle of radius \(1.0\) m at \(v = 0.5\) m/s.
Find \(\dot{\phi}_R\) and \(\dot{\phi}_L\).

Solution — Angular velocity:
\[\omega = \frac{v}{R_{\text{turn}}} = \frac{0.5}{1.0} = 0.5 \text{ rad/s}\]


Right wheel:
\[\dot{\phi}_R = \frac{v + \omega L/2}{r} = \frac{0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.1}{0.04} = \frac{0.55}{0.04} = 13.75 \text{ rad/s}\]


Left wheel:
\[\dot{\phi}_L = \frac{v - \omega L/2}{r} = \frac{0.5 - 0.5 \times 0.1}{0.04} = \frac{0.45}{0.04} = 11.25 \text{ rad/s}\]


Give students 2–3 minutes to work through this. Walk around and check. Common mistakes: forgetting the factor of 2 in omega*L/2, mixing up r (wheel radius) with R_turn (turning radius), or getting the sign of omega wrong. Note that the wheel speed difference is small — only 2.5 rad/s — because the turning radius (1 m) is much larger than the track width (0.2 m). For tighter turns, the difference grows.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
The ICR (Instantaneous Center of Rotation)


Every planar rigid-body motion (except pure translation) has an Instantaneous Center of Rotation (ICR):

The point about which the body instantaneously rotates
All velocity vectors are tangent to circles centered at the ICR

For a differential-drive robot:

ICR lies on the wheel axle line (extended)
Distance from center: \(d = v/\omega\)





The ICR is a fundamental concept from rigid-body mechanics. At any instant, a planar rigid body is either translating (ICR at infinity) or rotating about some point (the ICR). For a differential-drive robot, the ICR always lies on the line through the two wheel contact points. When both wheels go at the same speed, the ICR is at infinity (straight line). When they go at different speeds, the ICR is on the side of the slower wheel. When they go at equal and opposite speeds, the ICR is at the robot’s center (pivot turn). The distance from the robot center to the ICR is exactly v/omega — the turning radius. This geometric interpretation is very useful for visualizing trajectories.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Car-Like Robots


Many real-world robots have car-like geometry:

Rear wheels provide drive (fixed heading)
Front wheel(s) provide steering
Cannot spin in place
Has a minimum turning radius

Examples: Autonomous cars, forklifts, agricultural robots, golf carts
The bicycle model simplifies each axle to a single wheel.







The bicycle model is the standard kinematic model for car-like robots. It gets its name from the simplification: instead of modeling all four wheels individually, we collapse each axle into a single virtual wheel at the center. The rear wheel is the reference point (it can only roll forward/backward along the body heading). The front wheel is steerable by angle delta. This captures the essential kinematics while ignoring the Ackermann steering geometry (which we’ll discuss briefly). The bicycle model is used extensively in autonomous vehicle research and motion planning.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Bicycle Kinematics
The two “wheels” are virtual: each axle of a car is collapsed into one wheel. The Ackermann slide (next) brings the real four wheels back.


Configuration: \(q = (x, y, \theta)\) at rear axle
Controls: \(u = (v, \delta)\)

\(v\): rear-wheel speed
\(\delta\): front-wheel steering angle

Kinematic equations:
\[\dot{x} = v\cos\theta\] \[\dot{y} = v\sin\theta\] \[\dot{\theta} = \frac{v\tan\delta}{L}\]
where \(L\) is the wheelbase.

In matrix form:
\[\dot{q} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta \\ \sin\theta \\ \tan\delta / L \end{bmatrix} v\]
Compare with the unicycle:

Unicycle: \(\dot{\theta} = \omega\) (direct control)
Bicycle: \(\dot{\theta} = v\tan\delta / L\) (coupled to \(v\))







Warning


Key difference: The bicycle cannot change heading without moving (\(v = 0 \Rightarrow \dot{\theta} = 0\)).





Important framing point before the math: the “rear wheel” and “front wheel” in this diagram are NOT the wheels of a literal bicycle. They are the virtual single wheels you get by collapsing each axle of a car — the two real front wheels are averaged into one front wheel, and the two real rear wheels into one rear wheel. The next slide (Ackermann steering) brings the real four wheels back and shows how the inner and outer front wheels are steered at slightly different angles to realize this abstraction. Calling it the “bicycle model” is just a visual shorthand for “car with each axle collapsed to one wheel.” With that said, derive the kinematics. The rear wheel rolls along the body heading, so x_dot = vcos(theta), y_dot = vsin(theta) — same as the unicycle so far. The difference is in theta_dot. Draw a triangle: the rear wheel moves forward by vdt, the front wheel is steered at angle delta, and the wheelbase is L. The heading change is d_theta = vdt * tan(delta) / L. This comes from the ICR geometry: the turning radius is R = L/tan(delta), and theta_dot = v/R = v*tan(delta)/L. The crucial consequence: when v = 0, theta_dot = 0 regardless of delta. A car cannot turn its body while stationary — it must be moving. This is fundamentally different from a differential-drive robot that can pivot in place.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Turning Radius


From \(\dot{\theta} = v\tan\delta / L\), the turning radius is:
\[R_{\text{turn}} = \frac{L}{\tan\delta}\]
Minimum turning radius (maximum steering angle \(\delta_{\max}\)):
\[R_{\min} = \frac{L}{\tan\delta_{\max}}\]
Example: A typical car has \(L \approx 2.7\) m, \(\delta_{\max} \approx 35°\)
\[R_{\min} = \frac{2.7}{\tan 35°} \approx 3.86 \text{ m}\]




The minimum turning radius is a hard physical constraint — it’s determined by the wheelbase and the maximum steering angle, which is limited by the mechanical design of the steering linkage. A typical passenger car has R_min around 4-6 meters (curb-to-curb turning radius is about twice that). This constraint is critical for path planning: you can’t plan a trajectory with tighter turns than R_min. Contrast with a differential-drive robot: R_min = 0 (it can spin in place). This is why differential drive is preferred for tight indoor environments and car-like steering is used on roads where the minimum turning radius is not a practical limitation. For the FANUC LR Mate in lab, we never worried about turning radius because manipulators don’t have this constraint.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Ackermann Steering


Real cars have four wheels, not two. In a turn, the inner wheel must steer more than the outer so all wheels trace concentric circles around the ICR.
Ackermann condition:
\[\cot\delta_o - \cot\delta_i = \frac{W}{L}\]
where \(\delta_i, \delta_o\) = inner/outer wheel angles, \(W\) = track width, \(L\) = wheelbase.




Ackermann steering is named after Rudolph Ackermann who patented the idea in 1818 (though it was invented earlier by Georg Lankensperger). The geometric principle is simple: in a turn, all four wheels must trace concentric circles, otherwise the tires scrub (slide laterally), causing wear and wasted energy. The inner front wheel is closer to the ICR, so it must steer at a larger angle. The bicycle model uses an effective single steering angle delta — roughly the average of delta_i and delta_o. In practice, Ackermann geometry is implemented by a trapezoidal steering linkage. Perfect Ackermann is an idealization; real linkages approximate it, and the approximation is excellent at low speeds. At high speeds, tire slip angles become significant and the geometric model breaks down.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Worked Example: Bicycle Model
Given: Wheelbase \(L = 2.0\) m, \(v = 3.0\) m/s, \(\delta = 15°\), \(q(0) = (0, 0, 0)\)

Step 1 — Angular velocity:
\[\dot{\theta} = \frac{v\tan\delta}{L} = \frac{3.0 \times \tan 15°}{2.0} = \frac{3.0 \times 0.268}{2.0} = 0.402 \text{ rad/s}\]


Step 2 — Turning radius:
\[R = \frac{L}{\tan\delta} = \frac{2.0}{0.268} = 7.46 \text{ m}\]


Step 3 — After 1 second: \(\theta(1) \approx 0.402\) rad \(\approx 23°\)
The robot follows a circular arc of radius 7.46 m.


Walk through each step. The steering angle of 15 degrees is moderate — typical for a gentle highway curve. The resulting turning radius of 7.46 m is reasonable for a small vehicle. Note that the angular velocity (0.402 rad/s = 23 deg/s) seems fast, but at 3 m/s that’s only a gentle curve. If the speed were higher (say, 30 m/s on a highway), the same steering angle would give a much larger turning radius in practice because the driver would steer less. The model is kinematic — it doesn’t account for tire dynamics, lateral acceleration limits, or rollover. Those are dynamic effects that matter at high speeds.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Unicycle vs Bicycle: Comparison

Use this table as a summary comparison. The fundamental difference is controllability at zero speed: a differential-drive robot can control heading independently of position (omega is a direct control input), while a car-like robot’s heading is coupled to its forward velocity. This makes differential drive much easier to control in tight spaces. On the other hand, car-like steering is more stable at high speeds and is the natural choice for road vehicles. Both models satisfy the non-holonomic rolling constraint, and both can reach any configuration in the plane — they just get there differently.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Omnidirectional Robots: Removing the Constraint


What if a robot could move sideways?
Mecanum wheels (Swedish wheels) have angled rollers that enable motion in any direction:
\[\dot{q} = \begin{bmatrix} v_x \\ v_y \\ \omega \end{bmatrix}\]

3 controls for 3 DOF — the system is holonomic
No coupling between heading and velocity direction
The robot can translate sideways, diagonally, or spin — independently





Mecanum wheels are an elegant mechanical solution to the non-holonomic constraint. Each wheel has passive rollers mounted at 45 degrees to the wheel axis. When the wheel spins, the rollers allow the wheel to slip sideways. By coordinating four mecanum wheels, the robot can produce net force in any direction. This makes the robot holonomic — it can instantaneously move in any direction without first turning to face that direction. The trade-off: mecanum wheels have lower payload capacity, higher friction, less traction, and are more mechanically complex and expensive. They’re popular in RoboCup and for indoor logistics where omnidirectional mobility is valuable (e.g., hospital delivery robots that need to navigate crowded corridors). KUKA’s youBot and the Festo Robotino are well-known platforms with mecanum wheels.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Connecting Back to Manipulators








Concept
Manipulator (W01–W08)
Mobile Robot (W09–W13)




Configuration
\(q \in \mathbb{R}^n\) (joint angles)
\(q = (x, y, \theta) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \times S^1\)


Core math tool
FK: \(q \to T_{ee}\)
\(\dot{q} = G(q)\,u\)


Control inputs
Joint angles / velocities
Wheel speeds / steering


Constraints
Joint limits (holonomic)
Rolling (non-holonomic)


Workspace
Bounded by arm reach
Unbounded (in principle)


Forward problem
\(q \to T_{ee}\) (unique)
\(u \to \dot{q}\) (unique)


Inverse problem
\(T_{ee} \to q\) (IK, multiple solutions)
Path planning (W11–W12)




This table bridges Parts II–III and Part IV of the course. The deep parallel: both manipulators and mobile robots have a configuration space, a mapping between actuator inputs and motion, and constraints that limit what motions are possible. The key difference is the nature of the constraints: manipulators have holonomic joint limits (hard bounds on angles), while mobile robots have non-holonomic rolling constraints (restrictions on velocity directions). For manipulators, the forward problem is FK — plug in joint angles, get a pose. For mobile robots, the forward problem is: given wheel commands, how does the pose change? For manipulators, the inverse problem is IK. For mobile robots, the inverse problem is path planning — find a sequence of controls that takes the robot from one configuration to another while respecting the constraints. We’ll tackle that in Weeks 11–12.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Key Takeaways

Holonomic vs non-holonomic: Holonomic constraints (\(f(q) = 0\)) reduce C-space dimension; non-holonomic constraints (\(A(q)\dot{q} = 0\)) restrict instantaneous velocity but not reachable configurations
Unicycle model: \(\dot{q} = G(q)\,u\) with \(u = (v, \omega)\) — the universal abstraction for differential-drive robots
Differential-drive mapping: \(v = \frac{r}{2}(\dot{\phi}_R + \dot{\phi}_L)\), \(\quad \omega = \frac{r}{L}(\dot{\phi}_R - \dot{\phi}_L)\)
Bicycle model: \(\dot{\theta} = v\tan\delta / L\) — models car-like robots with minimum turning radius \(R_{\min} = L/\tan\delta_{\max}\)
The \(G(q)\) matrix maps control inputs to configuration velocity — it’s the velocity-level equivalent of FK, and it encodes the non-holonomic constraint


Emphasize that the unicycle and bicycle models are used throughout the rest of the course: path planning in W11–W12 assumes a kinematic model, and localization in W13 uses odometry derived from these models. The differential-drive to unicycle mapping is what students will implement in Lab 8 this week. The G(q) matrix is the conceptual bridge — FK told us “given joint angles, where is the tool?”, G(q) tells us “given wheel commands, how does the pose change?” If students internalize this, the rest of Part IV will flow naturally.

text:

Computer vision basics with OpenCV

Lab 9: Sensor simulation


Preview that next week we shift from “how the robot moves” to “how the robot perceives.” The kinematic models from this week tell us where the robot is going; sensors tell us what is around it. Together, kinematics + sensing enable path planning and autonomous navigation, which are the core topics of Weeks 11–13.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Exit Ticket
Problem: A differential-drive robot has wheel radius \(r = 0.05\) m and track width \(L = 0.25\) m. The right wheel spins at 8 rad/s, the left wheel at 4 rad/s.

Compute \(v\) and \(\omega\)
What is the turning radius?
If the robot starts at \(q(0) = (0, 0, 0)\), write the kinematic equations \(\dot{x}(t)\), \(\dot{y}(t)\), \(\dot{\theta}(t)\)


Give students 3–5 minutes. Walk around and check computations. The numerical values are chosen to give clean results. The third part checks whether students can connect the differential-drive mapping to the unicycle kinematic equations — it requires chaining both steps together.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Exit Ticket: Solution
Part 1:
\[v = \frac{r}{2}(\dot{\phi}_R + \dot{\phi}_L) = \frac{0.05}{2}(8 + 4) = 0.30 \text{ m/s}\] \[\omega = \frac{r}{L}(\dot{\phi}_R - \dot{\phi}_L) = \frac{0.05}{0.25}(8 - 4) = 0.80 \text{ rad/s}\]
Part 2:
\[R_{\text{turn}} = \frac{v}{\omega} = \frac{0.30}{0.80} = 0.375 \text{ m}\]
Part 3: Substitute into the unicycle model:
\[\dot{x} = 0.30\cos\theta, \qquad \dot{y} = 0.30\sin\theta, \qquad \dot{\theta} = 0.80 \text{ rad/s}\]

Walk through the solution. The key step is recognizing that Part 3 requires combining the differential-drive-to-unicycle mapping (Part 1) with the unicycle kinematic equations. The robot traces a circle of radius 0.375 m, turning left (right wheel faster). The angular velocity 0.80 rad/s means the robot completes a full circle in 2*pi/0.80 ≈ 7.85 seconds. Ask: what if we want the robot to go straight? Answer: set both wheels to the same speed. What speed for v = 0.30 m/s straight? Both at 0.30/0.05 = 6 rad/s.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
This Week’s Goals

Explain the sense-plan-act loop and classify sensors as proprioceptive vs exteroceptive
Describe how LiDAR works and convert a scan from polar to Cartesian coordinates
Use basic OpenCV operations (thresholding, contours) to extract information from camera images
Build a binary occupancy grid from a LiDAR scan using ray casting
Apply the log-odds update rule to fuse multiple scans into a single occupancy map


This week bridges “how the robot moves” (W09) with “how the robot decides where to move” (W11). The kinematic models from last week are useless without perception – the robot needs to know what is around it. By the end of today, students will understand the full pipeline: sensor data goes in, an occupancy grid comes out, and that grid is what path planning algorithms (W11) operate on. The occupancy grid is the single most important concept today.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
The Blind Robot Problem


Last week we derived kinematic models:
\[\dot{q} = G(q)\,u\]
We can command wheel speeds, predict how the pose changes…
But: the robot has no idea what’s around it.

Where are the walls?
Is there an obstacle ahead?
Where is the goal?

Motion without perception is useless.




Start with a motivating question. Last week we built the kinematic models: given wheel commands, how does the robot move? But we assumed the robot knows where to go. In reality, a mobile robot in an unknown environment needs to perceive the world before it can plan a path. This is the fundamental difference between industrial manipulators (known, structured environment) and mobile robots (unknown, unstructured environment). The FANUC robot in our lab doesn’t need to “see” because its workspace is carefully defined. A delivery robot on campus does.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
The Sense-Plan-Act Loop








The simplest model of autonomous behavior: sense → plan → act → repeat.

Sense (W10): perceive the environment
Plan (W11–W12): decide what to do
Act (W09): execute motion

This week we focus on SENSE.


The sense-plan-act (SPA) loop is the simplest model of autonomous robot behavior. The robot senses its environment, plans what to do based on what it perceives, then acts (moves). Then it repeats. Each cycle is one “step” of autonomy. Modern robots run this loop tens or hundreds of times per second. Our course covers each part: W09 gave us the Act model (kinematics), today is Sense (sensors + mapping), W11-W12 will cover Plan (path planning), and W13 revisits Sense with localization. The SPA loop is deliberately simplified – real systems often interleave sensing and acting (reactive control) – but it’s the right mental model for this course.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Sensor Taxonomy









Proprioceptive
Exteroceptive




Measures
Robot’s own state
External environment


Examples
Wheel encoders, IMU, battery voltage
LiDAR, camera, ultrasonic, bumper


Needs
Nothing external
Objects/surfaces to interact with









Tip


Connection to W09: Wheel encoders are proprioceptive sensors. In W09’s differential-drive model, we used encoder counts to compute \(v\) and \(\omega\) – that’s odometry, a proprioceptive measurement. Today we add exteroceptive sensors to see the world.




Proprioceptive sensors measure the robot’s own internal state: joint positions, wheel speeds, orientation (IMU), battery level. Exteroceptive sensors measure the external world: distances to objects, images of the scene, force of contact. The distinction matters because proprioceptive measurements are available regardless of the environment – encoders work whether the robot is in a warehouse or a field. Exteroceptive measurements depend on the environment and can fail (LiDAR can’t see glass, cameras can’t see in the dark). In W13 we’ll see how odometry (proprioceptive) drifts over time, which is why we need exteroceptive sensors to correct the estimate.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
How LiDAR Works


Light Detection And Ranging

Emit a short laser pulse
Pulse reflects off a surface
Measure the round-trip time \(\Delta t\)

\[d = \frac{c \cdot \Delta t}{2}\]
where \(c = 3 \times 10^8\) m/s (speed of light).
One pulse = one distance measurement.




LiDAR is the workhorse sensor for mobile robotics. The principle is simple: shoot a laser pulse, start a timer, measure how long until the reflected pulse returns. The factor of 2 is because the light travels to the target AND back. At the speed of light, a 1-meter distance corresponds to about 6.7 nanoseconds round-trip time – so LiDAR electronics need very precise timing. Modern LiDAR units can measure thousands of distances per second. The term “LiDAR” was coined in the 1960s as a portmanteau of “light” and “radar.”

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
section: From a Single Pulse to a 2D Scan
text:
From a Single Pulse to a 2D Scan


The sensor sweeps the laser beam through 360 degrees.
At each angle \(\alpha_i\), the sensor records a range \(r_i\).
One full rotation = one scan = array of \((r_i, \alpha_i)\) pairs.
Typical: 360 measurements per scan (1 degree resolution).





A single distance measurement is not very useful. The key innovation in 2D LiDAR is the rotating mirror or spinning head that sweeps the beam through a plane. Each rotation produces one complete scan – a set of range measurements at known angles. The angular resolution (spacing between consecutive measurements) and scan rate (how many full rotations per second) are the key specs. Some LiDARs use a physically spinning mechanism (like RPLIDAR), others use a fixed array with electronic beam steering (solid-state LiDAR). For our 2D case, think of it as a flat laser beam sweeping around like a lighthouse beam, measuring distance at each angle.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
What the Data Looks Like


A single scan is an array:
\[\{(r_0, \alpha_0),\; (r_1, \alpha_1),\; \ldots,\; (r_{N-1}, \alpha_{N-1})\}\]
where:

\(r_i\) = measured range (meters)
\(\alpha_i = i \cdot \Delta\alpha\) (radians)
\(N\) = number of rays per scan
\(\Delta\alpha\) = angular resolution

In Python: ranges[i] gives \(r_i\).








Show students what LiDAR data actually looks like. The raw output is just an array of numbers – one range per angle. The angles are usually evenly spaced (e.g., every 1 degree). If you plot these in polar coordinates (angle on the angular axis, range on the radial axis), you get the outline of whatever the sensor can see. The shape of a rectangular room would appear as four straight segments at different ranges. An obstacle inside the room would appear as a short-range bump. Invalid readings (too far, too close, no return) are often represented as 0 or inf. In Lab 9 this week, students will work directly with this array format.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Polar to Cartesian Conversion


Each \((r_i, \alpha_i)\) becomes an \((x_i, y_i)\) point:
\[x_i = r_i \cos(\alpha_i)\] \[y_i = r_i \sin(\alpha_i)\]
The set of all points \(\{(x_i, y_i)\}\) is called a point cloud.
In NumPy:
x = ranges * np.cos(angles)
y = ranges * np.sin(angles)





This is straightforward trigonometry – the same polar-to-Cartesian conversion students have seen since high school. The point is that polar form is how the sensor measures (range + angle), but Cartesian form is what we need for mapping and planning. The NumPy vectorized form is important to show: you never loop over individual rays in Python – you use array operations. The resulting point cloud is in the sensor’s local frame (sensor at the origin, x-axis pointing forward). To place it in the world frame, we need the robot’s pose, which we cover next.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
section: Point Clouds in the World Frame
text:
Point Clouds in the World Frame
The LiDAR gives points in the sensor frame \(\{S\}\). To build a map, we need points in the world frame \(\{W\}\).
It’s a 2D rotation and translation:
\[\begin{bmatrix} x^W_i \\ y^W_i \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{rotate by } \theta} \begin{bmatrix} x^S_i \\ y^S_i \end{bmatrix} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} x_R \\ y_R \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{translate to robot}}\]
Packed as a single matrix multiply (the 2D version of W02’s \(T_{WS}\)):
\[
\begin{bmatrix} x^W_i \\ y^W_i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & x_R \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & y_R \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{T_{WS}(x_R,\, y_R,\, \theta)}
\begin{bmatrix} x^S_i \\ y^S_i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
\]
Same math as the \(4 \times 4\) homogeneous transforms from W02, one dimension smaller.

Walk students through both forms. The first line is the “rotate then translate” form – easier to code in NumPy, and the order matters: rotating first aligns the sensor’s forward direction with the world axes; translating first would rotate the point around the world origin instead of around the robot. The second line packs exactly the same operation into a single 3x3 matrix by adding a row [0, 0, 1] and an extra “1” coordinate – bookkeeping that turns “rotate then translate” into one multiplication. The real payoff of the homogeneous form is composition: if the LiDAR is mounted 10 cm in front of the robot center, you can express that as T_RS (robot-to-sensor, a constant) and then T_WS = T_WR * T_RS. Identical trick to the 4x4 transforms we used for manipulator frames in W02-W03.

Note
