Give students a feel for real hardware. The RPLIDAR A1 is the most accessible – it’s what you’d find on a hobbyist robot or in an educational kit. The Hokuyo is the workhorse of research mobile robots. The Velodyne is what self-driving cars use (though newer models like the VLP-16 are much cheaper than the original $75K units). Key takeaway: there’s a huge range in specs and cost. For indoor robots, a 10-12m range is usually fine. For outdoor autonomous vehicles, you need 100m+. Resolution matters for detecting small obstacles – at 1 degree resolution and 10m range, two objects need to be at least 17cm apart to be distinguishable. Lab 9 will use parameters similar to the RPLIDAR A1.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
LiDAR Limitations


LiDAR is not perfect:

Glass: beam passes through
Dark / matte surfaces: weak return
Mirrors, polished metal: specular bounce
Rain, fog, dust: scatters the beam
Min range (~15 cm): too close to measure
2D scan is one plane: misses overhangs





These limitations are important for practical robotics. Glass walls are a classic failure mode – the robot’s map will show a gap where the glass door is, and it might try to drive through it. Dark surfaces (like black matte rubber) absorb the IR laser and return too little light for detection. Specular reflection is tricky: a polished metal surface acts like a mirror, bouncing the beam at the angle of incidence rather than back to the sensor, so the sensor either gets no return or a phantom return from wherever the reflected beam ends up. Rain and fog scatter the beam, reducing effective range. The minimum range is a hardware limitation – the electronics need a brief “dead time” after firing before they can listen for the return. And 2D LiDAR only scans in one horizontal plane, typically 10-20cm off the ground, so it can completely miss obstacles that are above or below that plane (table edges, overhanging shelves, steps).

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
The Camera as a Sensor


An image is an \(H \times W\) grid of pixels; each pixel stores \((B, G, R) \in [0, 255]\).
Cameras give (LiDAR doesn’t):

Color, texture, appearance
Object recognition (shape, text, faces)
High pixel resolution

Cameras lack:

Direct depth
Lighting independence





Cameras are the other major exteroceptive sensor. The key difference from LiDAR: a camera gives you rich appearance information (color, texture, shape) but NOT direct distance measurements. A LiDAR tells you “there’s something 3.2m away at 45 degrees” but nothing about what it is. A camera tells you “there’s a red ball at pixel (320, 240)” but not how far away it is. This complementarity is why many robots use both. For this course, we cover cameras briefly – just enough to understand what they can contribute to a robot’s perception. Deep computer vision is a separate course.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Image Coordinates vs World Coordinates


Image \((u, v)\): origin top-left, \(u\) = column, \(v\) = row.
World \((x, y, z)\): 3D position.
A camera projects 3D onto 2D: \[(x, y, z) \;\to\; (u, v)\]
Depth is lost — one pixel could be a small nearby object or a large distant one.




This is the fundamental issue with camera-only sensing: the projection from 3D to 2D is lossy. You cannot recover depth from a single image without additional information (known object size, stereo vision, structured light, etc.). The image coordinate system has a quirk that confuses students: v (row) increases downward, not upward. This is because images are stored as matrices where row 0 is the top. In OpenCV, an image is just a NumPy array of shape (H, W, 3), where img[v, u] gives the (B,G,R) values at pixel (u,v). Note the order: row first, column second, which is (v,u) not (u,v).

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
section: Basic OpenCV: From Image to Information
text:
Basic OpenCV: From Image to Information


import cv2
import numpy as np

# 1. Load image
img = cv2.imread('scene.jpg')

# 2. Convert BGR -> HSV
hsv = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)

# 3. Threshold: keep only red pixels
#    values are [H, S, V]
lower_red = np.array([ 0, 120,  70])  # H,S,V min
upper_red = np.array([10, 255, 255])  # H,S,V max
mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, lower_red, upper_red)

# 4. Find contours (outlines)
contours, _ = cv2.findContours(mask,
    cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
Load \(\to\) Color convert \(\to\) Threshold \(\to\) Contours

Why HSV, not BGR?
BGR mixes color and brightness — a red ball looks different in shade vs. sunlight. HSV splits them:

H — Hue (color angle) [0, 179]
S — Saturation (vividness) [0, 255]
V — Value (brightness) [0, 255]

Thresholding on H picks “red” across lighting changes.
Careful — hue is circular. In OpenCV red sits at both ends:
H=0   red         H=90   cyan
H=30  yellow      H=120  blue
H=60  green       H=179  red (wraps)
So H ∈ [0, 10] misses the reds around H ∈ [170, 179]. Build two masks and OR them.


Walk through each step. cv2.imread loads the image as a NumPy array in BGR format (not RGB – a common gotcha). cvtColor converts to HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value), which is better for color detection because it separates color (hue) from brightness (value). In HSV, “red” is a narrow range of hue values regardless of lighting conditions – in RGB, the same red object looks very different in shadow vs sunlight. inRange creates a binary mask: 255 where the pixel is in the specified range, 0 elsewhere. findContours traces the boundaries of white regions in the binary mask and returns them as lists of points. This 4-step pipeline is the bread and butter of simple vision-based robotics.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
section: Color Thresholding: Finding a Red Ball
text:
Color Thresholding: Finding a Red Ball

The binary mask isolates regions matching the target color. The contour gives us the position and size of the detected object.

Show a concrete example. A red ball on a table: the original image shows the full scene, the mask shows only the red region as white pixels, and the contour is the outline of that region overlaid on the original image. The contour tells the robot where in the image the ball is (pixel coordinates) and how large it appears (area in pixels). From the centroid of the contour, the robot knows which direction to turn to face the ball. From the area, it can estimate rough distance (a larger contour = closer object, if the object’s real size is known).

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
From Contours to Robot Decisions
if contours:
    # Largest contour = most likely our target
    c = max(contours, key=cv2.contourArea)

    # Bounding box: x, y, width, height
    x, y, w, h = cv2.boundingRect(c)

    # Center of the object in image
    cx = x + w // 2
    cy = y + h // 2

    # Robot decision: is the object left, center, or right?
    img_center = img.shape[1] // 2
    if cx < img_center - 50:
        action = "turn left"
    elif cx > img_center + 50:
        action = "turn right"
    else:
        action = "go straight"

This is a complete example of vision-based reactive control. The robot detects the largest red contour, computes its center in image coordinates, and decides whether to turn left, right, or go straight based on where the object appears in the image. This is simple but effective – it’s essentially how line-following robots work (threshold the line color, find centroid, steer toward it). The key insight for students: you don’t need deep learning or complex algorithms for basic visual servoing. A threshold + contour + centroid is often enough for structured tasks. Of course, this breaks down in unstructured environments with varying lighting, multiple objects, occlusions, etc.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Camera vs LiDAR: Trade-offs









LiDAR
Camera




Direct depth?
Yes (range per ray)
No (2D projection)


Color / texture?
No
Yes


Works in dark?
Yes (active sensor)
No (needs light)


Cost
$100–$4,000+
$10–$100


Data rate
~100K points/sec
~30 frames/sec


Best for
Mapping, obstacle avoidance
Object recognition, tracking









Note


For this course: we use LiDAR data for mapping (W10) and path planning (W11–W12). Camera-based perception is a full course on its own.




Emphasize that LiDAR and cameras are complementary, not competing. Self-driving cars use both (plus radar, ultrasonic, and more). For our course, we focus on LiDAR because it gives direct range data that maps naturally onto the occupancy grid we’re about to build. Camera-based perception requires much more processing (feature extraction, object detection, depth estimation) which is beyond the scope of this introductory robotics course. Students interested in vision should take a computer vision or deep learning course. The key takeaway: choose your sensor based on what information your task requires.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
The Representation Problem
The environment is continuous; algorithms need a discrete representation.









Representation
Idea
Pros
Cons




Feature map
List of landmarks
Compact, semantic
Hard to query “is this free?”


Topological map
Graph of places
Compact, high-level
No metric info


Occupancy grid
Grid of free/occupied cells
Full spatial info, easy planning
Memory-heavy



We use the occupancy grid — direct input to grid-based planning (W11: Dijkstra, A*).

Three main ways to represent the environment. Feature maps store a sparse set of landmarks with positions – good for localization but you can’t easily answer “can I drive through this 1m gap?” Topological maps are even more abstract – “the kitchen connects to the hallway which connects to the lab” – good for high-level planning but you lose metric information. Occupancy grids discretize the space into a regular grid and mark each cell as free or occupied. They’re the most common representation in mobile robotics because they directly support the question we care about: “is there a collision-free path from A to B?” Grid-based search algorithms (Dijkstra, A*) operate directly on this grid. The trade-off is memory: a 50m x 50m area at 5cm resolution requires a million cells.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
The Occupancy Grid


A 2D array where each cell stores:

Free (0): the robot can drive here
Occupied (1): there’s an obstacle here
Unknown (-1): not yet observed

Parameters:

Origin: \((x_{\min}, y_{\min})\)
Resolution: cell size in meters (e.g., 5 cm)
Size: \(M \times N\) cells






The occupancy grid is the single most important concept in today’s lecture. It’s a 2D NumPy array where each element represents a small square patch of the physical world. A resolution of 5cm means each cell is 5cm x 5cm. A 10m x 10m room at 5cm resolution requires a 200x200 grid = 40,000 cells – easily handled by any computer. The three states (free, occupied, unknown) are crucial: unknown means the robot hasn’t observed this region yet. Initially, the entire grid is unknown. As the robot moves and scans, cells transition to free or occupied based on sensor data. In the next few slides, we’ll derive exactly how that transition works.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Grid Coordinates
To convert between world coordinates \((x, y)\) and grid indices \((i, j)\):
\[i = \left\lfloor \frac{x - x_{\min}}{\text{resolution}} \right\rfloor, \qquad j = \left\lfloor \frac{y - y_{\min}}{\text{resolution}} \right\rfloor\]
And the reverse:
\[x = x_{\min} + (i + 0.5) \cdot \text{resolution}, \qquad y = y_{\min} + (j + 0.5) \cdot \text{resolution}\]
The \(+0.5\) gives the center of the cell.
def world_to_grid(x, y, origin, resolution):
    i = int((x - origin[0]) / resolution)
    j = int((y - origin[1]) / resolution)
    return i, j

This is the coordinate mapping that students will implement in Lab 9. It’s just a linear map with a floor operation. Common mistakes: forgetting to subtract the origin, mixing up i/j ordering (columns vs rows), off-by-one errors at grid boundaries. The reverse map uses +0.5 to return the center of the cell rather than the corner – this is conventional and avoids ambiguity. Make sure students understand that (i,j) are integer indices into a NumPy array, while (x,y) are continuous world coordinates in meters. A cell at grid index (100, 75) with origin (-5, -5) and resolution 0.05 corresponds to world point (0.025, -1.225).

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
section: Building a Grid from One LiDAR Scan
text:
Building a Grid from One LiDAR Scan


For each ray \((r_i, \alpha_i)\):

Convert endpoint to grid coords
Trace line from robot to endpoint
Mark cells along the line as free
Mark endpoint as occupied

Cells no ray touches stay unknown.





This is the core algorithm. The insight is that a LiDAR ray tells us TWO things: (1) the endpoint is occupied (something reflected the beam), and (2) everything between the sensor and the endpoint is free (otherwise the beam would have been blocked sooner). So for each ray, we trace a line from the robot’s position to the hit point and mark all cells along that line as free, then mark the endpoint cell as occupied. Cells that no ray passes through remain unknown – typically because they’re behind obstacles (occluded). This is sometimes called “inverse sensor model” because we’re going backwards from the measurement to the state of the world.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Ray Casting: Bresenham’s Line Algorithm


Problem: Given two grid cells, which cells lie on the line between them?
Bresenham’s algorithm efficiently finds the “staircase” of cells.
from skimage.draw import line

# Cells from robot to endpoint
cells_i, cells_j = line(
    robot_i, robot_j,
    end_i, end_j
)
# cells_i, cells_j are arrays
# of grid indices along the ray
No need to implement from scratch – skimage.draw.line does it.





Bresenham’s line algorithm is a classic computer graphics algorithm from 1962. It determines which pixels (cells) to color when drawing a line between two points on a grid. It uses only integer arithmetic, making it very fast. Students don’t need to implement it – the scikit-image library provides it. The important thing is understanding what it does: given start cell (i1,j1) and end cell (i2,j2), it returns a list of all grid cells that the line passes through. For our occupancy grid, all cells in this list except the last one are marked free, and the last one is marked occupied. Show the staircase pattern on the SVG – for a diagonal line, the cells form a staircase approximation.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Ray Casting a Full 360° Scan

After processing all rays: cells are white (free), black (occupied), or gray (unknown/occluded).

Show the full picture. The robot is in a room with walls and one internal obstacle. After processing all 360 rays, the grid shows the visible area as free (white), the walls and obstacle as occupied (black), and the region behind the obstacle as unknown (gray) because no rays could reach there – they were blocked by the obstacle. This occluded region is the “shadow” behind the obstacle. The robot would need to move to a different position to scan that region. This naturally leads to the idea of building the map incrementally from multiple scans, which we’ll cover after the practice problem.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
section: Practice: Building a Grid from a Scan
text:
Practice: Building a Grid from a Scan
Given: A robot at grid position \((5, 5)\) on a \(10 \times 10\) grid. Six LiDAR rays hit walls at:



Ray
\(\alpha\) (degrees)
Grid endpoint \((i, j)\)




1
0° (right)
\((9, 5)\)


2
45°
\((8, 8)\)


3
90° (up)
\((5, 9)\)


4
135°
\((2, 8)\)


5
180° (left)
\((1, 5)\)


6
270° (down)
\((5, 1)\)



Task: On paper, mark cells as Free (F), Occupied (O), or Unknown (U).

(Work on this for 3 minutes, then we’ll see the solution.)

Give students 3 minutes to work this out on paper. The key steps: for each ray, trace from (5,5) to the endpoint, marking intermediate cells as free and the endpoint as occupied. Cells not touched by any ray are unknown. This is a simplified version of what they’ll implement in Lab 9. Walk around the room while they work. Common mistakes: forgetting that the robot’s own cell is also free, not tracing diagonal rays correctly (e.g., the 45-degree ray from (5,5) to (8,8) passes through (6,6) and (7,7) which should be marked free).

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Practice: Solution








For every ray:

Free — each cell the beam crosses
Occupied — only the endpoint cell
Unknown — everything not touched by a ray

Huge unknown wedges between rays — 6 beams can’t cover a full scene.


Walk through the solution. The robot cell (5,5) is free. Ray 1 going right: cells (6,5), (7,5), (8,5) are free, (9,5) is occupied. Ray 2 at 45 degrees: (6,6), (7,7) are free, (8,8) is occupied. And so on for each ray. Everything else is unknown. Point out the large unknown regions in the corners – the robot only had 6 rays with 45-degree spacing, leaving huge gaps. In practice, a LiDAR with 360 rays at 1-degree spacing would fill in much more of the grid. But even with dense scanning, the occluded region behind an obstacle remains unknown.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
The Problem: Sensor Noise


Real sensors are noisy:

Scan 1 says cell \((5, 2)\) is free
Scan 2 says cell \((5, 2)\) is occupied

A binary grid can only store one value.
Which scan do we trust?
Neither – we need to accumulate evidence over multiple observations.




This is the motivation for moving from binary grids to probabilistic grids. Real LiDAR measurements have noise: the range measurement has a standard deviation of a few centimeters, the angular measurement has small errors, and occasionally you get completely spurious readings (multipath reflections, temporary obstacles like a person walking by). If two scans disagree about a cell, a binary grid has no good way to resolve the conflict – you either overwrite the old value or ignore the new one. What we want is to accumulate evidence: if 9 out of 10 scans say a cell is free and 1 scan says occupied, the cell is probably free (the occupied reading was noise). This requires storing a probability, not just 0 or 1.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
From Binary to Probabilistic
Instead of \(\{0, 1, -1\}\), store a probability \(p(\text{occupied})\) for each cell.





\(p\)
Meaning




0.0
Definitely free


0.5
Unknown


1.0
Definitely occupied



Update rule (Bayes):
\[p(\text{occ} \mid z_{1:t}) = \frac{p(z_t \mid \text{occ})\, p(\text{occ} \mid z_{1:t-1})}{p(z_t)}\]

where

\(z_t\) — current measurement (free / occupied)
\(z_{1:t}\) — all measurements so far (scans \(1\) → \(t\))
\(p(\text{occ} \mid z_{1:t-1})\) — prior belief
\(p(z_t \mid \text{occ})\) — sensor model (likelihood of the reading if the cell is occupied)
\(p(z_t)\) — normaliser


But repeatedly multiplying small probabilities causes numerical underflow…

The probabilistic approach stores a probability of occupancy for each cell. We start with p = 0.5 (maximum uncertainty – we have no idea). Each new observation updates the probability. If the sensor says “free,” p decreases. If it says “occupied,” p increases. The Bayesian update rule is theoretically correct but computationally problematic: multiplying many numbers between 0 and 1 eventually produces values too small for floating-point representation. We need a transformation that turns these multiplications into additions. That’s the log-odds trick, coming next.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
The Log-Odds Representation


Define the log-odds of a probability:
\[l = \log\frac{p}{1 - p}\]



\(l\)
\(p\)
Meaning




\(-\infty\)
0.0
Certain free


\(-2.2\)
0.1
Likely free


\(0\)
0.5
Unknown


\(+2.2\)
0.9
Likely occupied


\(+\infty\)
1.0
Certain occupied



Inverse: \(p = 1 / (1 + e^{-l})\) (sigmoid)



Key property: Bayesian update becomes addition — no multiplications, no underflow.


Log-odds is a monotonic transformation of probability. It maps [0,1] to (-inf, +inf). The nice thing is that 0.5 maps to 0 (our “unknown” prior), negative values mean “more likely free,” positive values mean “more likely occupied.” Students may recognize the sigmoid function from logistic regression or neural networks – it’s the same thing. The log-odds representation has been standard in occupancy grid mapping since Elfes (1989). The mathematical reason it works: in log-odds space, the Bayesian update becomes a simple addition rather than a multiplication, which is both numerically stable and computationally cheap.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Log-Odds Update Rule
The Bayesian update simplifies to \(l_{t} = l_{t-1} + l_{\text{meas}}\).


What to add? In practice, look up a fixed value based on the cell’s role in the beam — the inverse sensor model:



Cell’s role in this beam
\(l_{\text{meas}}\)
implied \(p\)




Beam endpoint (hit)
\(+0.85\)
\(0.70\)


Ray passed through
\(-0.40\)
\(0.40\)


Beyond the hit / off-beam
\(0\)
\(0.50\)




Constants are picked once at design time from chosen probabilities via \(l = \log\frac{p}{1-p}\), then hardcoded:
L_FREE = -0.40   # p(occ | pass) ≈ 0.40
L_OCC  = +0.85   # p(occ | hit)  ≈ 0.70
L_MIN, L_MAX = -2.0, +3.5   # clamp
During scans you never touch \(p\) — pure additive updates. No multiplications, no normalisation, no underflow.


This is the payoff of the log-odds representation. The full Bayesian update with priors and likelihoods reduces to a single addition per cell. The values l_free = -0.4 and l_occ = +0.85 are tuning parameters that encode how much we trust a single observation. These particular values correspond to: if the ray passes through a cell, we’re about 60% confident it’s free (p = 0.4 = exp(-0.4)/(1+exp(-0.4))); if the ray hits a cell, we’re about 70% confident it’s occupied. The asymmetry (|l_occ| > |l_free|) is intentional: occupied evidence is stronger because a single hit is more informative than a single pass-through. Students can think of l_free and l_occ as “confidence weights” – bigger magnitudes mean more aggressive updates.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Worked Example: Log-Odds Update
A cell starts at \(l_0 = 0\) (unknown, \(p = 0.5\)). Five successive observations:



Obs
Type
\(l_{\text{meas}}\)
\(l_{\text{new}}\)
\(p\)




1
free
\(-0.4\)
\(-0.4\)
0.40


2
free
\(-0.4\)
\(-0.8\)
0.31


3
occupied
\(+0.85\)
\(+0.05\)
0.51


4
free
\(-0.4\)
\(-0.35\)
0.41


5
free
\(-0.4\)
\(-0.75\)
0.32



Computation: \(l_{\text{new}} = l_{\text{old}} + l_{\text{meas}}\), then \(p = 1/(1+e^{-l_{\text{new}}})\).

Walk through each row. Start at l=0 (totally uncertain). First free observation: l drops to -0.4, p drops to 0.40 (slight lean toward free). Second free: l = -0.8, p = 0.31 (more confident it’s free). Third observation is occupied: l jumps from -0.8 to +0.05, p goes back to 0.51 (almost back to uncertain – one occupied reading nearly cancelled two free readings because l_occ > |l_free|). Fourth and fifth are free again, bringing the belief back down.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Putting It in Code
def update_occupancy_grid(grid, robot_ij, endpoints_ij, l_free=-0.4, l_occ=0.85):
    """Update occupancy grid with one full LiDAR scan."""
    for end_i, end_j in endpoints_ij:
        # Get all cells along the ray
        ray_i, ray_j = line(robot_ij[0], robot_ij[1], end_i, end_j)

        # All cells except last: free evidence
        grid[ray_i[:-1], ray_j[:-1]] += l_free

        # Last cell: occupied evidence
        grid[ray_i[-1], ray_j[-1]] += l_occ

    # Clamp to prevent saturation
    np.clip(grid, -5.0, 5.0, out=grid)

This is the complete occupancy grid update function. Students will implement a version of this in Lab 9. Note the structure: for each ray, get the cells using Bresenham’s algorithm, add l_free to all cells along the ray except the last one, add l_occ to the last cell. The clamp at the end prevents log-odds from growing without bound – without it, a cell observed 100 times as free would have l = -40, and it would take 50+ occupied observations to change the belief. Clamping to [-5, +5] means the maximum confidence is about p = 0.007 (very confident free) or p = 0.993 (very confident occupied). The function modifies the grid in-place for efficiency.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Building the Map: Multiple Scans


As the robot moves and scans from different positions, the unknown region shrinks and the map converges.

Show three panels: (1) after the first scan, most of the grid is unknown except for the area directly visible from the robot’s starting position; (2) after the robot moves and takes a second scan, more area is revealed, and cells observed from both positions have stronger evidence; (3) after several scans, the map is mostly complete with only small occluded pockets remaining unknown. This is exactly how SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) works in practice, except we’re assuming the robot knows its exact pose (from odometry or some external tracking system). In W13, we’ll address what happens when the pose estimate is uncertain.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
section: From Grid to Path Planning (Preview of W11)
text:
From Grid to Path Planning (Preview of W11)


The occupancy grid IS the planner’s input:

Free cells — nodes to visit
Occupied cells — obstacles
Cell adjacency — graph edges

Next week: Dijkstra and A* find the shortest path through this grid.




This is the payoff slide – connecting today’s content to next week’s path planning. The occupancy grid is literally a graph where each free cell is a node and adjacent free cells are connected by edges. Dijkstra’s algorithm and A* search operate on exactly this kind of graph. The path planning problem reduces to: find the shortest sequence of free cells from the start cell to the goal cell, where “shortest” is measured by the number of cells traversed (or the Euclidean distance). The conversion from occupancy grid to graph is trivial: each cell with p < 0.5 is a node, and each node is connected to its 4 or 8 neighbors (4-connected for cardinal directions only, 8-connected to allow diagonal movement). Students will see this in full detail next week.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
The Full Autonomy Pipeline

Every autonomous mobile robot runs some version of this loop. Each block uses concepts from a specific week in our course.

Step back and show the big picture. The full pipeline is: (1) Sense the environment with LiDAR/camera (today, W10); (2) Build/update a map representation (today, W10 – occupancy grid); (3) Plan a path from current position to goal (W11-W12 – Dijkstra, A*, RRT); (4) Execute the path using the kinematic model (W09 – unicycle/diff-drive); (5) Estimate where you actually ended up (W13 – localization/particle filter). Then repeat. This is the sense-plan-act loop from the beginning of the lecture, but now with concrete implementations for each block. The loop runs continuously: the robot senses, updates its map, replans if the map changed, and continues executing. In reality, these steps often run at different rates – sensing at 10Hz, planning at 1Hz, control at 50Hz – but the conceptual loop is the same.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Looking Ahead
What we didn’t cover today:








Topic
Where
Why




3D perception (point clouds, depth cams)
Advanced courses
We kept to 2D


Sensor fusion (LiDAR + camera)
Advanced courses
Needs probabilistic framework


SLAM (mapping + localization)
W13 — localization
The “L” in SLAM


Deep learning for perception
Vision courses
Needs ML background



W13 closes the loop: what if the robot doesn’t know its exact pose? That’s localization.

Be transparent about what we skipped. 3D perception is increasingly important (self-driving cars use 3D LiDAR point clouds) but the math is the same – just one more dimension. Sensor fusion combines multiple sensor modalities (e.g., using camera to classify what LiDAR detects) and requires a probabilistic framework like Kalman filters. SLAM is the holy grail of mobile robotics – building a map while simultaneously figuring out where you are in that map. We’ll touch on the “L” (localization) part in W13 with particle filters. Deep learning has revolutionized perception but requires ML prerequisites that not all students have.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Key Takeaways

Sense-Plan-Act: The robot must perceive the environment (W10) before planning paths (W11) or executing motions (W09)
LiDAR measures distances using time-of-flight. A 2D scan is an array of \((r, \alpha)\) pairs. Convert to Cartesian: \(x = r\cos\alpha\), \(y = r\sin\alpha\)
Cameras provide rich appearance data but no direct depth. A simple threshold + contour pipeline extracts object locations in the image
Occupancy grids discretize space into cells (free / occupied / unknown). Built from LiDAR scans using ray casting (Bresenham’s algorithm)
Log-odds update makes Bayesian fusion simple: just add measurement evidence to each cell. Multiple scans accumulate into a consistent map


Tie each takeaway back to the learning goals from the first slide. The occupancy grid + log-odds update is the most important skill from today – students will implement it in Lab 9 and use the resulting grid as input to path planning in W11. The LiDAR material gives them the data pipeline: raw ranges go in, a grid comes out. The camera section is awareness-level – they should know what cameras can and can’t do, but they won’t implement vision-based algorithms in the labs.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Next Week
Week 11: Path Planning I – Grid Search

Configuration space (C-space): what it means for a mobile robot
Graph search on occupancy grids
Dijkstra’s algorithm: guaranteed shortest path
A* search: faster with a heuristic
Lab 10: The Maze Solver

The occupancy grid you built today becomes the maze A* will solve next week.

Preview W11 to create anticipation. The occupancy grid from today IS the input to next week’s algorithms. Dijkstra and A* are graph search algorithms that find the shortest path from start to goal on a grid. Students who have taken a data structures or algorithms course may have seen these algorithms on abstract graphs – next week we apply them to a concrete robotics problem. Lab 10 will have students implement A* on an occupancy grid and visualize the search process. The transition from W10 to W11 is one of the cleanest in the course: the output of today (a grid) is literally the input of next week (a graph to search).

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Exit Ticket
Two LiDAR scans of a \(5 \times 5\) grid, taken from different robot poses:

Scan A: robot at \((0, 2)\), ray going right hits a wall at \((4, 2)\)
Scan B: robot at \((2, 0)\), ray going up hits a wall at \((2, 4)\)

The two rays cross at cell \((2, 2)\).
Log-odds parameters: \(l_{\text{free}} = -0.4\), \(l_{\text{occ}} = +0.85\). All cells start at \(l = 0\).
Questions:

After both scans, what is the log-odds value of the intersection cell \((2, 2)\)?
What is the log-odds value of cell \((4, 2)\) (end of Ray A)?
Convert cell \((2, 2)\)’s log-odds to a probability. Is this cell likely free or occupied?

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Exit Ticket: Solution


Part 1: Cell \((2, 2)\) is on both rays’ paths (free for each):
\[l_{(2,2)} = 0 + l_{\text{free}} + l_{\text{free}} = -0.8\]
Log-odds just add — two free observations drive the belief further toward “free.”
Part 2: Cell \((4, 2)\) is the endpoint of Ray A:
\[l_{(4,2)} = 0 + l_{\text{occ}} = +0.85\]
Part 3: Convert \(l = -0.8\) to probability:
\[p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{0.8}} = \frac{1}{1 + 2.23} = 0.31\]
Since \(p = 0.31 < 0.5\), cell \((2, 2)\) is likely free — more confidently than after a single scan.




Walk through each part. Part 1: cell (3,2) is on the path of Ray A going from (2,2) to (4,2), so it gets l_free = -0.4. Ray B goes from (2,2) to (2,4), which does NOT pass through (3,2), so only Ray A contributes. Part 2: cell (4,2) is the endpoint of Ray A, so it gets l_occ = +0.85. Part 3: the sigmoid function converts l = -0.4 to p = 0.40. Since 0.40 < 0.5, the evidence suggests this cell is free. Note that this is only slightly below 0.5 – one observation gives weak evidence. Multiple consistent observations would drive the probability further toward 0 (definitely free). This is a 3-minute exit ticket – if students can do this, they understand the core algorithm.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
This Week’s Goals

Define configuration space (C-space) and distinguish it from workspace
Convert an obstacle map to a C-space representation on a grid
Formulate path planning as a graph search problem
Implement Dijkstra’s algorithm on an occupancy grid
Extend Dijkstra to A* search with a heuristic and compare performance


Last week we gave the robot eyes (sensors, occupancy grids). This week we give it a brain: given a map, find a collision-free path from start to goal. We focus on grid-based (exact discretization) methods — Dijkstra and A. Next week (W12) will handle the case when the grid approach breaks down in high dimensions, motivating sampling-based planners like RRT. The concepts today are fundamental — A is the workhorse behind everything from video game NPCs to warehouse robot fleets.

Note


This week we focus on PLAN. The occupancy grid from W10 is our input; the kinematic model from W09 executes the output.




Remind students of the sense-plan-act loop. W10 built the occupancy grid. Today, that grid becomes the input to a planning algorithm. The output is a sequence of waypoints. W09’s kinematic controller then drives the robot along those waypoints. Emphasize that the planner assumes a known, static map — dynamic replanning is a more advanced topic.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
What Is Path Planning?


Given:

A map of the environment (occupancy grid)
A start position \(q_{\text{start}}\)
A goal position \(q_{\text{goal}}\)

Find:

A collision-free path \(q_{\text{start}} \to q_{\text{goal}}\)
Ideally the shortest (or lowest-cost) such path





This is the fundamental problem statement. The “map” could be an occupancy grid from W10, a CAD model of a warehouse, or even a configuration space for a manipulator arm. We’ll start in 2D workspace for intuition, then generalize. The key constraint is collision avoidance — the path must not pass through occupied cells.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
section: Why Not Just Draw a Straight Line?
text:
Why Not Just Draw a Straight Line?


A straight line from start to goal is the shortest path in free space…
But obstacles block the way.

We need to find a path that goes around obstacles
Among all valid paths, we want the shortest one
This is a combinatorial search problem





Simple motivating example. Show that even with just one obstacle, there are multiple valid paths (go left or go right around it), and the straight-line path is blocked. As the number of obstacles grows, the number of possible detours explodes. This motivates the need for systematic search algorithms rather than ad-hoc heuristics.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Workspace vs Configuration Space


Workspace \(W\) — what you see

The real world the robot moves in
Robot has a body; obstacles have shape

Configuration Space \(C\) — what we plan in

One point in \(C\) = one full pose of the robot
Pick the smallest set of numbers that uniquely describes the robot’s pose:

Point robot → just \((x, y)\)
Mobile robot with a heading → \((x, y, \theta)\)
2-link arm → \((\theta_1, \theta_2)\)


Each new number = one more axis to search.








This is the single most important concept in motion planning. The workspace is what we see — a floor with walls, tables, chairs. The configuration space is an abstract space where each point represents one possible pose of the robot. A 2-DOF manipulator has a 2D C-space (joint angles theta1, theta2). A mobile robot on a plane has a 3D C-space (x, y, theta). The power of C-space is that regardless of the robot’s physical shape, it becomes a single point in C-space. This simplifies collision checking enormously.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
The Point Robot Trick


Key insight: Grow obstacles by the robot’s radius, then treat the robot as a point.

Inflate each obstacle (Minkowski sum) by radius \(r\)
Inflated obstacles form \(C_{\text{obs}}\)
Free space: \(C_{\text{free}} = C \setminus C_{\text{obs}}\)

Planning now reduces to moving a point through \(C_{\text{free}}\).





For a circular mobile robot, this is exact: inflate each obstacle boundary outward by the robot’s radius r. For non-circular robots the Minkowski sum is more complex, but the idea is the same. After inflation, the physical size of the robot can be ignored — we just need to find a path for a point that stays in free space. This is the standard approach used in practice: the costmap in ROS uses exactly this inflation technique. On a grid, this means marking cells within distance r of any obstacle as also “occupied.”

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
C-Space on a Grid


Discretize \(C_{\text{free}}\) into a grid:

Each cell is free (0) or occupied (1)
Cell size = resolution (e.g., 5 cm)

Planning = finding a path of free cells from start to goal.
This is now a graph problem: free cells are nodes, and edges connect each cell to its neighbors (4- or 8-connected).




This is where W10’s occupancy grid meets graph theory. Each free cell is a node. We connect neighboring cells with edges. For 4-connectivity, each cell connects to its 4 cardinal neighbors (up, down, left, right). For 8-connectivity, we also include diagonals. The edge weight is the distance: 1 for cardinal moves, sqrt(2) for diagonals. Now the path planning problem is exactly a shortest-path problem on a graph — and we have classical algorithms for that.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
4-Connected vs 8-Connected Grids









4-Connected
8-Connected




Neighbors
Up, Down, Left, Right
+ 4 Diagonals


Edge cost
All edges cost 1
Cardinal = 1, Diagonal = \(\sqrt{2}\)


Path quality
Staircase artifacts
Smoother, more natural


Computation
Fewer neighbors to check
More neighbors per cell









Tip


We will use 8-connected grids in this course. The small overhead of checking 8 neighbors is well worth the path quality improvement.




Show both on the board or with a diagram. With 4-connectivity, a diagonal path must zig-zag (Manhattan distance). With 8-connectivity, diagonal movement is allowed, so paths look more natural and are closer to the true Euclidean shortest path. The cost for a diagonal step is sqrt(2) ≈ 1.414, which correctly reflects the greater distance traveled. Most practical grid planners use 8-connectivity.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Graph Search: The Idea
We want the shortest path from start \(s\) to goal \(g\) on a weighted graph.
Strategy: Explore outward from \(s\), always expanding the cheapest unexplored node.






Important


Dijkstra’s Algorithm (1959): Guarantees the shortest path in any graph with non-negative edge weights.



Think of it as a “flood fill” that spreads outward from the start, keeping track of the cheapest way to reach each cell.

Before diving into pseudocode, build intuition. Imagine pouring water at the start cell. The water spreads equally in all directions through free cells. The first time water reaches the goal is the shortest path. Dijkstra’s algorithm is the computational version of this: it uses a priority queue to always process the cell with the smallest known distance from the start. Named after Edsger Dijkstra, who famously designed it in about 20 minutes at a café in 1956 and published it in 1959.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Dijkstra Step by Step


Track for each cell: cheapest cost from S, and which cell we came from (parent).

Set start cost = 0
Visit the unvisited cell with the smallest cost
Update neighbors — if going through this cell is cheaper, update their cost and parent
Stop when goal is visited — its cost is final

Repeat 2–3 until goal.








Walk through the algorithm step by step on the board with a small 5x5 grid example. Key points: (1) We never revisit a node once it’s been picked — when a node is picked from the to-visit list, its distance is final. (2) The to-visit list (priority queue) ensures we always process the cheapest cell first. (3) The parent pointers let us reconstruct the path by following parent[goal] → parent[parent[goal]] → … → start. On a grid, “neighbor” means the 8 adjacent free cells. The formal term for step 3 is “relaxation” — checking if we found a cheaper route. Students will see this term in textbooks.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Dijkstra: Python Pseudocode
def dijkstra(grid, start, goal):
    INF = float('inf')
    # each cell is an (i, j) tuple used as a dict key
    cost   = {start: 0}        # best cost from start to each cell
    parent = {start: None}     # to reconstruct the path
    open_set = {start}         # cells still to explore

    while open_set:
        # 1. Pick the unexplored cell with the smallest cost so far
        current = min(open_set, key=lambda c: cost[c])
        open_set.remove(current)
        if current == goal:
            return reconstruct_path(parent, goal)
        # 2. Try every neighbor; update cost if we found a cheaper way
        #   neighbor = (i, j) of a free adjacent cell
        #   step     = 1 if cardinal, sqrt(2) if diagonal
        for neighbor, step in neighbors(grid, current):
            new_cost = cost[current] + step
            if new_cost < cost.get(neighbor, INF):
                cost[neighbor]   = new_cost
                parent[neighbor] = current
                open_set.add(neighbor)
    return None     # no path exists

Walk through the three blocks: (1) initialise — start has cost 0, all others are unknown (treated as infinity). (2) main loop — each iteration picks the cheapest unexplored cell, marks it done, and looks at its 8 neighbors. (3) relax — if we just found a cheaper way to reach a neighbor, record the new cost and remember which cell we came from. We use a Python set for open_set here for clarity; in the lab you’ll switch to heapq for speed (logarithmic vs. linear pick), but the algorithm is identical. Edge costs come from neighbors: 1 for cardinal, √2 for diagonal.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Dijkstra: Strengths and Weaknesses






Strengths



Guaranteed optimal — always finds the shortest path
Complete — if a path exists, Dijkstra will find it
Simple to implement and debug










Weakness: Explores Everywhere


Dijkstra explores in all directions equally — it has no idea where the goal is.
On a large grid, this means visiting many irrelevant cells far from the goal.
→ Can we do better? Yes — with a heuristic.




The key limitation is that Dijkstra is “blind” to the goal’s location. It just expands outward like a circle. This is fine for small grids but becomes expensive for large environments. Draw on the board: the explored region is roughly a circle centered on the start, and the goal might be far to the right — yet Dijkstra explored equally far to the left. This motivates A*, which uses a heuristic to bias the search toward the goal.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
The Idea Behind A*


Dijkstra uses: \(f(v) = g(v)\)

\(g(v)\) = cost from start to \(v\) (known)

A* uses: \(f(v) = g(v) + h(v)\)

\(g(v)\) = cost from start to \(v\) (known)
\(h(v)\) = estimated cost from \(v\) to goal (heuristic)

The heuristic biases search toward the goal, avoiding wasted exploration away from it.






Important


If \(h(v)\) never overestimates the true cost (admissible), A* is guaranteed optimal — just like Dijkstra, but faster.











A* was published by Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael in 1968. The insight is brilliant: if we have a lower bound on the remaining cost to the goal, we can use it to prioritize nodes that are likely on the shortest path. The priority queue now sorts by f = g + h instead of just g. Nodes that are far from the goal (large h) get deprioritized. Nodes that are close to the goal get explored first. The admissibility condition ensures we never skip a shorter path by overestimating.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Choosing a Heuristic
For grids, common admissible heuristics:








Heuristic
Formula
Best for




Euclidean
\(\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2}\)
8-connected or any-angle


Manhattan
\(|\Delta x| + |\Delta y|\)
4-connected grids


Chebyshev
\(\max(|\Delta x|, |\Delta y|)\)
8-connected, uniform cost


Octile
see below
8-connected, optimal



Octile distance (best for 8-connected grids):
\[h = (\sqrt{2} - 1) \cdot \min(|\Delta x|, |\Delta y|) + \max(|\Delta x|, |\Delta y|)\]

The heuristic must be admissible: it must never overestimate the true shortest-path distance. Euclidean distance is always admissible because the straight line is always the shortest. Manhattan distance is admissible for 4-connected grids but overestimates for 8-connected grids (it doesn’t account for diagonal shortcuts). Octile distance is the exact distance in an obstacle-free 8-connected grid — it accounts for the fact that you can move diagonally at cost sqrt(2). It’s the tightest admissible heuristic for our grid setup, which means A* explores the fewest nodes.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
A*: Python Pseudocode
def astar(grid, start, goal):
    INF = float('inf')
    cost   = {start: 0}        # best cost from start to each cell
    parent = {start: None}     # to reconstruct the path
    open_set = {start}         # cells still to explore

    while open_set:
        # 1. Pick the cell with the smallest f = g + h
        current = min(open_set, key=lambda c: cost[c] + heuristic(c, goal))
        open_set.remove(current)
        if current == goal:
            return reconstruct_path(parent, goal)
        # 2. Try every neighbor; update cost if we found a cheaper way
        for neighbor, step in neighbors(grid, current):
            new_cost = cost[current] + step
            if new_cost < cost.get(neighbor, INF):
                cost[neighbor]   = new_cost
                parent[neighbor] = current
                open_set.add(neighbor)
    return None     # no path exists






Tip


The only difference from Dijkstra: when picking the next cell, we sort by \(f = g + h\) instead of just \(g\).




Put this slide next to the Dijkstra slide visually — the structure is identical. Same initialisation, same main loop, same relaxation step. The single change is on the “pick” line: instead of cost[c] we use cost[c] + heuristic(c, goal). That one change makes A* dramatically faster in practice while preserving optimality (assuming an admissible heuristic). This is why A* is so widely used: it’s Dijkstra with one line changed, and it often explores an order of magnitude fewer cells. As with Dijkstra, the lab will switch to heapq for speed, but the algorithm is the same.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Dijkstra vs A*: Visual Comparison


Dijkstra

Explored: ~800 cells

A*

Explored: ~200 cells

Both find the same optimal path — but A* explores far fewer cells.

This is the key takeaway slide. Use a concrete example: same grid, same start and goal, same obstacles. Dijkstra’s explored region (shown in light blue) is roughly circular, expanding in all directions. A’s explored region is elongated toward the goal — it focuses its search in the right direction. Both find the same shortest path (they’re both optimal), but A gets there with far less computation. On large grids (e.g., a warehouse floor), this difference can be 10x or more.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Handling Real-World Complications







Challenge
Solution




Robot has physical size
Inflate obstacles by radius (C-space)


Grid resolution tradeoff
Fine grid → accurate but slow; coarse → fast but may miss narrow passages


Diagonal moves cut corners
Check both cardinal neighbors before allowing diagonal


Path is jagged (grid-aligned)
Post-process with path smoothing (line-of-sight checks)


Map changes over time
Replan periodically or use D* Lite (incremental A*)




These are the practical issues students will encounter in the lab. Obstacle inflation was covered in Part 2. The diagonal corner-cutting issue: when moving diagonally from (r,c) to (r+1,c+1), we should check that both (r+1,c) and (r,c+1) are free — otherwise the robot would clip the corner of an obstacle. Path smoothing: the grid-optimal path follows cell centers and looks jagged. A simple post-processing step removes unnecessary waypoints by checking line-of-sight between non-adjacent waypoints. Dynamic environments require replanning; D* Lite is an advanced variant that efficiently updates the path when the map changes, but that’s beyond our scope.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Path Smoothing


Grid path has unnecessary waypoints at every cell.
Smoothing algorithm:

Start at \(q_{\text{start}}\)
Check line-of-sight to farther waypoints — use Bresenham’s algorithm (W10 raycasting) to list the cells the line crosses; the line is clear if all are free
Keep the farthest visible waypoint as the next keypoint
Repeat from that keypoint → fewer waypoints, smoother trajectory









The Bresenham line algorithm (which students saw in W10 for ray casting) can be reused here for line-of-sight checks. Start at the first waypoint, draw a line to each subsequent waypoint, and check if all cells along the line are free. The farthest reachable waypoint becomes the next keypoint. This is a greedy algorithm — not necessarily globally optimal, but fast and effective in practice. The smoothed path is what gets sent to the kinematic controller from W09.

Grid dimension

Warning


Grid search works well in 2D and 3D. In higher dimensions, the number of cells grows exponentially — the curse of dimensionality.
Next week: Sampling-based methods (RRT) that handle high dimensions without discretizing the space.




This slide motivates W12. Grid-based A* is the right tool for mobile robots on a plane (2D) or drones in 3D. But for a 6-DOF robot arm, discretizing each joint angle into 100 bins gives a trillion cells — completely infeasible. Sampling-based planners like RRT work in continuous space and grow a tree of random samples, avoiding the exponential grid entirely. Emphasize that grid search isn’t “bad” — it’s the right tool for the right dimension. Know when to use each approach.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Key Takeaways

Configuration space transforms planning: grow obstacles by the robot radius, shrink the robot to a point
Grid discretization turns C-space into a graph — cells are nodes, 8-connected edges cost 1 or \(\sqrt{2}\)
Dijkstra explores outward in all directions — optimal but blind to the goal
A* = Dijkstra + heuristic \(h(v)\) → same optimal path, far fewer cells explored
Admissibility (\(h \leq h^*\)) guarantees A* optimality; octile is tight for 8-connected grids
Path smoothing (Bresenham line-of-sight from W10) removes jagged grid artifacts
Grid search scales to 2D/3D; curse of dimensionality motivates W12’s sampling methods


Tie each takeaway back to the learning goals from the first slide. Point 1 is the single most important conceptual idea — the Minkowski trick. Points 3-5 are the algorithms. Points 6-7 are the practical pieces. If students remember only one thing, it should be: “A* is Dijkstra with one line changed — the priority queue now uses f = g + h instead of just g.”

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
This Week’s Goals

Explain why grid-based planners fail in high-dimensional C-spaces
Describe the sampling-based planning philosophy: probe, don’t discretize
Implement the RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree) algorithm
Extend RRT to RRT* for asymptotically optimal paths
Apply path smoothing to turn tree paths into executable trajectories


Last week we solved path planning on grids with Dijkstra and A. Those work beautifully in 2D/3D. This week we confront the fundamental limitation: grids don’t scale. A 6-DOF arm needs a 6D grid — impossibly large. Sampling-based planners sidestep this by never building the grid at all. Instead, they randomly sample configurations and incrementally build a tree toward the goal. RRT is the foundational algorithm; RRT adds optimality. By the end of today, students will understand when to use grid search vs. sampling-based methods and be able to implement both.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
section: Recap: Grid Search Works in Low Dimensions
text:
Recap: Grid Search Works in Low Dimensions


W11 result: A* on a 2D grid is fast, optimal, complete.
But it depends on discretizing C-space into cells.



Dimension
Cells (100/axis)




2D
\(10^4\)


3D
\(10^6\)


6D
\(10^{12}\)


12D
\(10^{24}\)












Warning


The number of cells grows exponentially with dimension. A 6-DOF robot arm is already infeasible for grid search.




Review the table from W11’s last slide. 100 bins per axis is actually coarse — for a robot arm with 360 degrees of motion per joint, you might want 360 bins. That’s 360^6 ≈ 2 × 10^15 cells for a 6-DOF arm. Even storing one byte per cell would need over a petabyte of memory. And most of those cells are in free space — we’re wasting enormous resources representing empty regions. This is the curse of dimensionality, named by Richard Bellman in 1961.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
The Problem with Grids


Grid planners assume:

We can enumerate all cells (memory)
We can visit relevant cells (time)
Resolution is fine enough to find narrow passages

All three break in high dimensions:

Memory explodes exponentially
Search time explodes with it
Narrow passages require very fine resolution → even more cells





The narrow passage problem is particularly nasty. Imagine two rooms connected by a doorway. In 2D, the doorway is easy to find — a few cells wide. In 6D, the “doorway” in C-space might be a tiny sliver that only a very fine grid would capture. Making the grid finer multiplies memory by a factor of 2^d for each doubling of resolution in d dimensions. Sampling-based planners handle this much better because they don’t commit to a fixed resolution.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
A Different Philosophy


Grid search:

Build a graph from grid cells in configuration space
Search that full graph with Dijkstra/A*

Sampling-based planning:

Keep the configuration space continuous
Test sampled configurations and proposed edges for collision
Add only valid samples/edges to a growing graph or tree





This is the fundamental paradigm shift. Grid planners first create a large discrete approximation of the configuration space, then search that graph. Sampling-based planners keep the space continuous and only create states as needed. A sampled configuration is useful only if it is collision-free, and a connection between two configurations is useful only if the local motion between them is collision-free. We trade the deterministic structure of a full grid for a much smaller graph or tree that grows through the parts of free space the planner actually discovers.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT: The Core Idea


Grow a tree from the start toward the goal:

Pick a random point \(q_{\text{rand}}\) in C-space
Find the nearest node \(q_{\text{near}}\) in the tree
Extend from \(q_{\text{near}}\) toward \(q_{\text{rand}}\) by step size \(\delta\)
If the new point \(q_{\text{new}}\) is collision-free, add it to the tree
Repeat until the tree reaches the goal

The tree rapidly fills the space, biased toward unexplored regions.




RRT was introduced by Steven LaValle in 1998. The key insight is that the nearest-neighbor step creates an implicit bias: nodes in sparsely explored regions have larger Voronoi cells, so random samples are more likely to fall in those regions, causing the tree to expand toward unexplored territory. This is called the Voronoi bias. The step size delta controls the resolution — too large and we might miss obstacles, too small and growth is slow. A typical choice is a fraction of the workspace diameter.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT: Step-by-Step Visualization


Walk through each step on the board. Step 1: the tree has just the start node. A random point is sampled (shown as a hollow circle). The nearest tree node is the start. We extend by delta toward the random point and add the new node (solid circle). Step 2: another random sample. This time the nearest node might be the one we just added. Extend again. Repeat. After many iterations, the tree spans the free space. When a new node lands within delta of the goal, we still check the final segment to the goal before accepting the path. The tree doesn’t follow any predetermined pattern — it’s organic, adapting to the obstacle layout.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT Key Components








Component
What it does
Implementation




random_config()
Uniform sample in C-space
Random point within bounds


nearest(tree, q)
Find closest tree node
Brute force or KD-tree


steer(from, to, δ)
Move from → to by at most δ
Linear interpolation, clip to δ


collision_free(a, b)
Check segment a→b for collisions
Sample points along segment


goal_bias
Occasionally aim directly at goal
Speeds up convergence (typ. 5%)









Tip


Goal biasing is essential in practice. Without it, RRT wanders aimlessly. With 5–10% goal bias, it finds paths much faster.




The nearest-neighbor search is the computational bottleneck. For small trees, brute force (check every node) is fine. For large trees (thousands of nodes), a KD-tree gives O(log n) queries. Collision checking along a segment is done by discretizing the segment into small steps and checking each point — similar to ray casting in W10. The step size delta is a tuning parameter: too large and you collide with thin obstacles, too small and the tree grows slowly.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
Why Does RRT Work?


Voronoi Bias
Nodes in sparsely explored regions have large Voronoi cells.
→ Random samples are more likely to land in those cells.
→ The tree preferentially grows toward unexplored regions.
This is why RRT “rapidly explores” the space — it’s baked into the nearest-neighbor step.




Draw the Voronoi diagram of the tree nodes on the board. Each node “owns” the region of space closer to it than to any other node. When we sample uniformly, the probability that a sample falls in a node’s Voronoi cell is proportional to the cell’s area. Frontier nodes (at the boundary of explored space) have much larger cells than interior nodes. So frontier nodes get selected as q_near more often, and the tree extends outward. This is an elegant emergent property — we never explicitly compute Voronoi cells, but the algorithm behaves as if it does.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT Properties






Strengths



Avoids storing a full grid — practical in higher-dimensional spaces
Probabilistically complete — if a path exists, RRT will find it given enough time
Handles complex obstacle geometries naturally
Easy to implement (~30 lines of core code)










Weaknesses



Not optimal — the first path found is usually jagged and suboptimal
Non-deterministic — different runs give different paths
Can struggle with narrow passages (low probability of sampling through them)
Path quality varies significantly between runs





Probabilistic completeness means: as the number of iterations approaches infinity, the probability of finding a path (if one exists) approaches 1. This is weaker than the deterministic completeness of A* (which always finds a path in finite time if one exists). The non-optimality is the main practical issue — the path follows the tree structure, which is random and jagged. This motivates RRT* and path smoothing, which we’ll cover next.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
The Problem with RRT Paths


RRT finds a path, not the best path.
The tree structure creates unnecessary detours:

Nodes connect to their nearest neighbor at creation time
No rewiring afterward
Path cost can be 2–5× the optimal

Can we fix this?




Show a concrete example: an RRT path that zig-zags around obstacles vs. the straight-line optimal path. The RRT path is valid (collision-free) but much longer than necessary. The issue is that RRT is greedy — each node connects to whatever tree node was nearest when it was created, and that connection is permanent. RRT* fixes this by allowing the tree to rewire itself as new, better connections are discovered.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT*: Asymptotically Optimal RRT

RRT* = RRT + local cost repair: choose the lowest-total-cost parent for \(q_{\text{new}}\), then check nearby tree nodes inside radius \(r\) and let them switch parent if routing through \(q_{\text{new}}\) is cheaper.



The radius r is typically computed as r = gamma * (log(n)/n)^(1/d), where n is the current number of nodes, d is the dimension, and gamma is a constant. This formula ensures we check enough neighbors for optimality but not so many that the algorithm becomes slow. The key theoretical result (Karaman & Frazzoli, 2011) is that with this radius, RRT* is asymptotically optimal: the cost of the best path in the tree converges to the true optimum as n → ∞. In practice, even a few hundred iterations of RRT* produce significantly better paths than basic RRT.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT vs RRT*: Comparison









RRT
RRT*




Optimality
Not optimal
Asymptotically optimal


Path quality
Jagged, suboptimal
Converges to optimal


Per-iteration cost
O(n) nearest neighbor
O(n) + rewiring overhead


Completeness
Probabilistically complete
Probabilistically complete


When to use
Quick feasibility check
When path quality matters




Use this table to separate guarantees from practical tradeoffs. RRT is often enough when we only need a feasible path quickly. RRT* spends extra computation improving the tree, so it is the better choice when path quality matters.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
Why Smooth?


Both RRT and RRT* produce tree paths — sequences of straight segments following tree edges.
Problems:

Unnecessary turns and detours
Not executable by a robot with kinematic constraints
Much longer than needed

Solution: Post-process the path to remove redundant waypoints.




This mirrors the path smoothing we discussed in W11 for grid paths, but it’s even more important for RRT because tree paths are typically more jagged than grid paths. The tree structure imposes arbitrary turns wherever the tree happened to branch. Smoothing can reduce path length by 30-50% in typical scenarios. Two main approaches: shortcutting (try to skip waypoints via line-of-sight) and curve fitting (fit smooth curves through waypoints).

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
Shortcut Smoothing


Algorithm:

Pick two random waypoints \(w_i\) and \(w_j\) on the path (\(j > i + 1\))
Check if the straight line \(w_i \to w_j\) is collision-free
If yes, replace the sub-path \(w_i \to \ldots \to w_j\) with the direct segment
Repeat for \(N\) iterations

Simple, effective, and fast.
Each successful shortcut removes unnecessary detours.




This is a randomized algorithm — we randomly pick pairs of waypoints and try to shortcut them. The order doesn’t matter because any valid shortcut reduces path length. Typically 50-200 iterations are enough to remove most redundancy. The collision check is the same as in RRT: discretize the segment and check each point. An alternative deterministic approach is greedy smoothing (from W11): start at the beginning, find the farthest visible waypoint, jump there, repeat. The randomized approach is often better for complex paths because it can find shortcuts that greedy smoothing misses.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
When to Use What?








Scenario
Best Planner
Why




Mobile robot on a floor (2D)
A* on grid
Fast, optimal, simple


Drone in 3D space
A* or RRT
3D grid is borderline; RRT if obstacles are complex


6-DOF robot arm
RRT / RRT*
Grid is infeasible at any resolution


Real-time replanning needed
RRT + smoothing
Fast enough for online use


High-quality path needed
RRT* + smoothing
Best quality, more computation


Very narrow passages
RRT + bidirectional
Grow trees from both start and goal




This decision table is the practical takeaway. Students should be able to look at a planning problem and immediately choose the right algorithm family. The dimension of the C-space is the primary factor. For 2D, always use A* — it’s faster and gives optimal paths. For 3D, it depends on the map complexity and real-time requirements. For anything higher, sampling-based is the only option. Bidirectional RRT (grow a tree from start and from goal, connect when they meet) is particularly effective for narrow passages because both trees can find opposite ends of the passage.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
Bidirectional RRT


Grow two trees simultaneously:

Tree A from the start
Tree B from the goal

After each extension, try to connect the two trees.
Advantages:

Finds paths faster (searches from both ends)
Much better at narrow passages
Connection attempts are like aggressive goal biasing





Bidirectional RRT is the most commonly used variant in practice. The two trees meet in the middle, which dramatically reduces the expected number of iterations. For narrow passages, growing from the goal side is crucial — a single tree from the start might never find the narrow entrance, but if another tree is growing from the other side of the passage, they meet inside it. RRT-Connect (Kuffner & LaValle, 2000) is a popular variant that greedily extends toward the other tree, not just one step at a time.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
The Full Planning Pipeline

    I --> P{"Dimension?"}
    P -->|"2D/3D"| AS["A* Grid Search<br/>(W11)"]
    P -->|"≥ 4D"| RR["RRT / RRT*<br/>(W12)"]
    AS --> SM["Path Smoothing"]
    RR --> SM
    SM --> T["Trajectory<br/>(W06)"]
    T --> K["Kinematic<br/>Controller<br/>(W09)"]
    style P fill:#f39c12,color:#fff,stroke:#c0392b
    style SM fill:#8e44ad,color:#fff,stroke:#6c3483













Tip


Planning produces a path; smoothing, timing, and control turn it into motion.




This ties together everything from the course. The occupancy map from W10 feeds into obstacle inflation (C-space from W11). Based on the dimension, we choose grid search or sampling-based planning. Both produce a raw path that gets smoothed. The smoothed waypoints go to the trajectory generator from W06 (polynomial interpolation), and the trajectory is tracked by the kinematic controller from W09. This is essentially the full autonomy stack for a mobile robot. Real systems like ROS’s move_base follow exactly this pipeline.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
Key Takeaways

Curse of dimensionality makes grid-based planning infeasible above 3–4 dimensions
RRT grows a tree by random sampling — probabilistically complete, practical in high dimensions
Voronoi bias gives RRT its exploration property: frontier nodes grow faster
RRT* adds rewiring for asymptotic optimality — converges to the shortest path
Path smoothing (shortcutting) removes tree artifacts, essential for executable paths
Decision rule: use A* for 2D/3D grids, RRT/RRT* for higher dimensions







Note


Next week: The robot has a path — but where is it? Localization (W13): estimating the robot’s pose from noisy sensor data.




Recap the key ideas. Emphasize the decision rule — this is what students should take away for their projects. Also note the progression: W10 gave us maps, W11 gave us grid-based planning, W12 gave us sampling-based planning, and W13 will address the question “but where am I on this map?” The final piece of the autonomy puzzle.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
The New Question
We just built three equations by hand:
\[\dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \qquad \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \qquad \dot{\theta} = \omega\]
Stacked into matrix form, with control inputs \(u = \begin{bmatrix} v \\ \omega \end{bmatrix}\):
\[\dot{q} = \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x} \\ \dot{y} \\ \dot\theta \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 \\ \sin\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{G(q)} \begin{bmatrix} v \\ \omega \end{bmatrix}\]
This is the generic shape of mobile robot kinematics:
\[\boxed{\dot{q} = G(q)\,u}\]

\(u\): control inputs (linear speed, turn rate, wheel speeds, …)
\(G(q)\): the mapping from inputs to configuration velocity, depending on the current heading
Today’s job: derive \(G(q)\) for the common wheeled robot models

Contrast with manipulators (FK/IK were about positions): today we work with velocities — how the pose changes instant by instant.

This slide reframes q_dot = G(q) u as a summary of the derivation students just watched, not a new formula pulled from thin air. Point out the 3x2 shape: 3 rows (x, y, theta components of q_dot) and 2 columns (the two independent controls v and omega). The key insight: 3 rows but only 2 columns means the image of G is a 2D subspace of the 3D velocity space — not every direction in (x_dot, y_dot, theta_dot) space is reachable. That gap between “configuration dimension 3” and “control dimension 2” IS the non-holonomic constraint, which we formalize next. Also note: the specific G(q) on this slide is the unicycle model — we will re-derive it carefully in Part 3. For now, just plant the matrix shape.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
Configuration — Concrete Example
Suppose at some instant the robot is at:
\[q = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ \theta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \\ 30^\circ \end{bmatrix}\]
What each number tells us:

x = 2 m, y = 5 m → the robot’s reference point is 2 m east, 5 m north of the origin.
θ = 30° → the robot is rotated 30° counterclockwise from the +x axis.

Turning the heading angle into a direction vector:
\[(\cos 30^\circ,\ \sin 30^\circ) \approx (0.866,\ 0.500)\]
That’s the unit arrow the robot is facing — for every 1 m it drives forward, it moves about 0.866 m in +x and 0.500 m in +y.






Tip


The configuration stores the compact scalar θ. Whenever we need to do geometry (projections, dot products, “which way is forward?”), we convert on the fly using \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\).




This slide exists to make q = (x, y, θ) stop being abstract. Walk through the numbers one by one. First point at the (2, 5) and literally say “the robot is two meters east and five meters north of the origin” — picture a top-down room view. Then address θ = 30° carefully: stress that θ is measured counterclockwise from the +x axis, not from compass north, not from the robot’s arm, not from the y-axis. Now the key move: the configuration only stores the scalar θ, but as soon as we want to ask “which way is the robot facing as a vector?” we have to convert θ into (cos θ, sin θ) — a point on the unit circle. Compute cos 30° ≈ 0.866 and sin 30° = 0.5 on the board; tell students that if they drive 1 m forward, the x-coordinate will go up by 0.866 and y by 0.5. That single calculation primes them for the next slide where we build velocity kinematics. Emphasize that the identification S¹ = { (cos θ, sin θ) } is exactly why R² × S¹ shows up in the C-space notation — the heading “lives on a circle.”

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
section: How Does the Configuration Change When the Robot Moves?
text:
How Does the Configuration Change When the Robot Moves?
Still at \(q = (2,\ 5,\ 30^\circ)\). Imagine the robot drives 1 m forward.
Step 1 — discrete update. Forward means “along the heading arrow”:
\[x_{\text{new}} = 2 + 1 \cdot \cos 30^\circ \approx 2.866, \quad y_{\text{new}} = 5 + 1 \cdot \sin 30^\circ = 5.500, \quad \theta_{\text{new}} = 30^\circ\]
Step 2 — drive for a short time \(dt\) at speed \(v\). The distance becomes \(v\,dt\):
\[\Delta x = v\cos\theta \cdot dt, \qquad \Delta y = v\sin\theta \cdot dt, \qquad \Delta\theta = \omega\cdot dt\]
(If the robot is also turning, its heading changes at rate \(\omega\).)
Step 3 — shrink \(dt\) to zero. Divide both sides by \(dt\):
\[\dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \qquad \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \qquad \dot{\theta} = \omega\]
These three numbers are the robot’s configuration velocity — how fast each coordinate is changing right now. This is exactly the kind of model we’ll build for every wheeled robot in this lecture.

The goal of this slide is to make velocity-level thinking concrete BEFORE the non-holonomic constraint equations appear. Walk through the three steps slowly. Step 1 is a literal “ruler and protractor” calculation. Step 2 just replaces “1 m” with “v dt meters”. Step 3 is the leap to continuous time — this is where students first meet q_dot. Emphasize that x_dot, y_dot, theta_dot are NOT new state variables — they are rates of change of the existing state. Write them on the board alongside x, y, theta so students see the one-to-one pairing. Next slide compresses all this into the matrix form q_dot = G(q) u.

title: Week 9: Mobile Robot Kinematics
text:
The Mecanum Wheel


A mecanum wheel is a normal wheel with passive rollers mounted around its rim at a 45° angle to the wheel axis.

When the wheel spins, it pushes the ground forward and the rollers allow it to slip sideways.
Combining those two effects gives a force at 45° to the wheel’s rolling direction.
Four mecanum wheels arranged in a rectangle can produce any combination of \((v_x, v_y, \omega)\).

Trade-offs: lower traction, lower payload, higher friction, more mechanical complexity — but omnidirectional motion in return.




This slide introduces the physical mechanism before we get to the motion diagram. Point out the diagonal rollers in the photo — each one is a passive free-spinning cylinder mounted at 45° to the wheel’s axis. When the wheel is driven, the rollers roll freely on the ground, so the wheel doesn’t generate grip in one direction. The net force direction depends on which way you drive the wheel and how the roller is oriented. The magic of mecanum comes from the fact that two wheels have rollers at +45° and two at −45° (arranged diagonally on the robot). That lets all three velocity components be independently controlled. The main downsides are practical: the rollers wear out, the wheels don’t handle rough terrain well, and they have less traction than conventional wheels.
