title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
section: Depth Cameras: Getting the Best of Both
text:
Depth Cameras: Getting the Best of Both
Modern robots often use RGB-D cameras that give color image + per-pixel depth:



Sensor
Principle
Typical Range




Microsoft Kinect v2
Time-of-flight (ToF) IR
0.5–4.5 m


Intel RealSense D435
Stereo + IR projector
0.3–3 m


iPhone Pro / iPad Pro
Solid-state ToF LiDAR
0.1–5 m









Note


Not in this course, but worth knowing: an RGB-D camera fixes the “camera has no depth” problem. Each pixel becomes a 3D point, so you get a dense point cloud + color. Scales to hundreds of thousands of points per frame, compared to a 2D LiDAR’s ~360.




RGB-D cameras are the dominant sensor on indoor service robots (vacuums, warehouse pickers, educational robots). They give what cameras lack (depth) at a cost cameras can afford. The Kinect, originally a gaming accessory, became the workhorse of hobbyist robotics from 2010 on. RealSense is Intel’s successor. Apple’s ToF LiDAR on iPhones brought consumer-grade ToF into phones starting 2020. Limitations: indoor use mostly (IR struggles in sunlight), short range (<5m), and they still fail on the same glass/dark/specular surfaces as regular LiDAR.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Grid Coordinates: World to Grid
Let the grid origin (bottom-left corner) be \(\text{origin} = (x_{\min}, y_{\min})\).
Convert world coordinates \((x, y)\) to grid indices \((i, j)\):
\[i = \left\lfloor \frac{x - x_{\min}}{\text{resolution}} \right\rfloor, \qquad j = \left\lfloor \frac{y - y_{\min}}{\text{resolution}} \right\rfloor\]
def world_to_grid(x, y, origin, resolution):
    # origin = (x_min, y_min)
    i = int((x - origin[0]) / resolution)
    j = int((y - origin[1]) / resolution)
    return i, j

This is the world-to-grid mapping students will implement in Lab 9. It’s a linear map plus a floor. Common mistakes: forgetting to subtract the origin, mixing up i/j ordering (columns vs rows), off-by-one errors at grid boundaries. Make sure students understand that (i,j) are integer indices into a NumPy array, while (x,y) are continuous world coordinates in meters.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Grid Coordinates: Grid to World
The reverse mapping (index \(\to\) cell center in world frame):
\[x = x_{\min} + (i + 0.5) \cdot \text{resolution}, \qquad y = y_{\min} + (j + 0.5) \cdot \text{resolution}\]
The \(+0.5\) offset returns the center of cell \((i, j)\), not its corner.
def grid_to_world(i, j, origin, resolution):
    x = origin[0] + (i + 0.5) * resolution
    y = origin[1] + (j + 0.5) * resolution
    return x, y

The reverse map uses +0.5 to return the center of the cell rather than the corner – this is conventional and avoids ambiguity. A cell at grid index (100, 75) with origin (-5, -5) and resolution 0.05 corresponds to world point (0.025, -1.225). Emphasize that world_to_grid discards sub-cell precision (floor), while grid_to_world reconstructs a single representative point (the center). They are not exact inverses.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
text:
Worked Example: Takeaways
Result: 4 free + 1 occupied \(\Rightarrow\) \(p = 0.32\) (probably free).

The single occupied reading shifted the belief (jumped from 0.31 to 0.51).
Accumulated free evidence outweighs the one noisy reading.
Asymmetry \(|l_{\text{occ}}| > |l_{\text{free}}|\) means one hit is louder than one pass-through.







Warning


In practice, clamp \(l \in [-5, +5]\) to prevent saturation. Otherwise a cell observed 1000 times as free needs 1000+ occupied observations to change its mind.




This is exactly how the grid handles noisy sensors: evidence accumulates and conflicting observations partially cancel. The clamping range [-5, +5] gives max confidence p ≈ 0.007 (very free) or p ≈ 0.993 (very occupied) – enough for planning, but leaves the door open for new evidence.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy
section: Homogeneous Form: One Matrix Does Both

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
This Week’s Goals

Explain the sense-plan-act loop and classify sensors as proprioceptive vs exteroceptive
Describe how LiDAR works and convert a scan from polar to Cartesian coordinates
Use basic OpenCV operations (thresholding, contours) to extract information from camera images
Build a binary occupancy grid from a LiDAR scan using ray casting
Apply the log-odds update rule to fuse multiple scans into a single occupancy map


This week bridges “how the robot moves” (W09) with “how the robot decides where to move” (W11). The kinematic models from last week are useless without perception – the robot needs to know what is around it. By the end of today, students will understand the full pipeline: sensor data goes in, an occupancy grid comes out, and that grid is what path planning algorithms (W11) operate on. The occupancy grid is the single most important concept today.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
The Blind Robot Problem


Last week we derived kinematic models:
\[\dot{q} = G(q)\,u\]
We can command wheel speeds, predict how the pose changes…
But: the robot has no idea what’s around it.

Where are the walls?
Is there an obstacle ahead?
Where is the goal?

Motion without perception is useless.





Start with a motivating question. Last week we built the kinematic models: given wheel commands, how does the robot move? But we assumed the robot knows where to go. In reality, a mobile robot in an unknown environment needs to perceive the world before it can plan a path. This is the fundamental difference between industrial manipulators (known, structured environment) and mobile robots (unknown, unstructured environment). The FANUC robot in our lab doesn’t need to “see” because its workspace is carefully defined. A delivery robot on campus does.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
The Sense-Plan-Act Loop





The simplest model of autonomous behavior: sense → plan → act → repeat.

Sense (W10): perceive the environment
Plan (W11–W12): decide what to do
Act (W09): execute motion

This week we focus on SENSE.


The sense-plan-act (SPA) loop is the simplest model of autonomous robot behavior. The robot senses its environment, plans what to do based on what it perceives, then acts (moves). Then it repeats. Each cycle is one “step” of autonomy. Modern robots run this loop tens or hundreds of times per second. Our course covers each part: W09 gave us the Act model (kinematics), today is Sense (sensors + mapping), W11-W12 will cover Plan (path planning), and W13 revisits Sense with localization. The SPA loop is deliberately simplified – real systems often interleave sensing and acting (reactive control) – but it’s the right mental model for this course.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Sensor Taxonomy









Proprioceptive
Exteroceptive




Measures
Robot’s own state
External environment


Examples
Wheel encoders, IMU, battery voltage
LiDAR, camera, ultrasonic, bumper


Needs
Nothing external
Objects/surfaces to interact with









Tip


Connection to W09: Wheel encoders are proprioceptive sensors. In W09’s differential-drive model, we used encoder counts to compute \(v\) and \(\omega\) – that’s odometry, a proprioceptive measurement. Today we add exteroceptive sensors to see the world.




Proprioceptive sensors measure the robot’s own internal state: joint positions, wheel speeds, orientation (IMU), battery level. Exteroceptive sensors measure the external world: distances to objects, images of the scene, force of contact. The distinction matters because proprioceptive measurements are available regardless of the environment – encoders work whether the robot is in a warehouse or a field. Exteroceptive measurements depend on the environment and can fail (LiDAR can’t see glass, cameras can’t see in the dark). In W13 we’ll see how odometry (proprioceptive) drifts over time, which is why we need exteroceptive sensors to correct the estimate.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
How LiDAR Works


Light Detection And Ranging

Emit a short laser pulse
Pulse reflects off a surface
Measure the round-trip time \(\Delta t\)

\[d = \frac{c \cdot \Delta t}{2}\]
where \(c = 3 \times 10^8\) m/s (speed of light).
One pulse = one distance measurement.





LiDAR is the workhorse sensor for mobile robotics. The principle is simple: shoot a laser pulse, start a timer, measure how long until the reflected pulse returns. The factor of 2 is because the light travels to the target AND back. At the speed of light, a 1-meter distance corresponds to about 6.7 nanoseconds round-trip time – so LiDAR electronics need very precise timing. Modern LiDAR units can measure thousands of distances per second. The term “LiDAR” was coined in the 1960s as a portmanteau of “light” and “radar.”

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
section: From a Single Pulse to a 2D Scan
text:
From a Single Pulse to a 2D Scan


A rotating mirror sweeps the laser beam around 360 degrees.
At each angle \(\alpha_i\), the sensor records a range \(r_i\).
One full rotation = one scan = array of \((r_i, \alpha_i)\) pairs.
Typical: 360 measurements per scan (1 degree resolution).





A single distance measurement is not very useful. The key innovation in 2D LiDAR is the rotating mirror or spinning head that sweeps the beam through a plane. Each rotation produces one complete scan – a set of range measurements at known angles. The angular resolution (spacing between consecutive measurements) and scan rate (how many full rotations per second) are the key specs. Some LiDARs use a physically spinning mechanism (like RPLIDAR), others use a fixed array with electronic beam steering (solid-state LiDAR). For our 2D case, think of it as a flat laser beam sweeping around like a lighthouse beam, measuring distance at each angle.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
What the Data Looks Like


A single scan is an array:
\[\{(r_0, \alpha_0),\; (r_1, \alpha_1),\; \ldots,\; (r_{N-1}, \alpha_{N-1})\}\]
where:

\(r_i\) = measured range (meters)
\(\alpha_i = i \cdot \Delta\alpha\) (radians)
\(N\) = number of rays per scan
\(\Delta\alpha\) = angular resolution

In Python: ranges[i] gives \(r_i\).





Show students what LiDAR data actually looks like. The raw output is just an array of numbers – one range per angle. The angles are usually evenly spaced (e.g., every 1 degree). If you plot these in polar coordinates (angle on the angular axis, range on the radial axis), you get the outline of whatever the sensor can see. The shape of a rectangular room would appear as four straight segments at different ranges. An obstacle inside the room would appear as a short-range bump. Invalid readings (too far, too close, no return) are often represented as 0 or inf. In Lab 9 this week, students will work directly with this array format.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Polar to Cartesian Conversion


Each \((r_i, \alpha_i)\) becomes an \((x_i, y_i)\) point:
\[x_i = r_i \cos(\alpha_i)\] \[y_i = r_i \sin(\alpha_i)\]
The set of all points \(\{(x_i, y_i)\}\) is called a point cloud.
In NumPy:
x = ranges * np.cos(angles)
y = ranges * np.sin(angles)





This is straightforward trigonometry – the same polar-to-Cartesian conversion students have seen since high school. The point is that polar form is how the sensor measures (range + angle), but Cartesian form is what we need for mapping and planning. The NumPy vectorized form is important to show: you never loop over individual rays in Python – you use array operations. The resulting point cloud is in the sensor’s local frame (sensor at the origin, x-axis pointing forward). To place it in the world frame, we need the robot’s pose, which we cover next.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
section: Point Clouds in the World Frame
text:
Point Clouds in the World Frame
The LiDAR gives points in the sensor frame \(\{S\}\). To build a map, we need points in the world frame \(\{W\}\).
It’s a 2D rotation and translation:
\[\begin{bmatrix} x^W_i \\ y^W_i \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{rotate by } \theta} \begin{bmatrix} x^S_i \\ y^S_i \end{bmatrix} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} x_R \\ y_R \end{bmatrix}}_{\text{translate to robot}}\]
Packed as a single matrix multiply (the 2D version of W02’s \(T_{WS}\)):
\[
\begin{bmatrix} x^W_i \\ y^W_i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & x_R \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & y_R \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{T_{WS}(x_R,\, y_R,\, \theta)}
\begin{bmatrix} x^S_i \\ y^S_i \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
\]
Same math as the \(4 \times 4\) homogeneous transforms from W02, one dimension smaller.

Walk students through both forms. The first line is the “rotate then translate” form – easier to code in NumPy, and the order matters: rotating first aligns the sensor’s forward direction with the world axes; translating first would rotate the point around the world origin instead of around the robot. The second line packs exactly the same operation into a single 3x3 matrix by adding a row [0, 0, 1] and an extra “1” coordinate – bookkeeping that turns “rotate then translate” into one multiplication. The real payoff of the homogeneous form is composition: if the LiDAR is mounted 10 cm in front of the robot center, you can express that as T_RS (robot-to-sensor, a constant) and then T_WS = T_WR * T_RS. Identical trick to the 4x4 transforms we used for manipulator frames in W02-W03.

The Hokuyo is the workhorse of research mobile robots. The Velodyne is what self-driving cars use (though newer models like the VLP-16 are much cheaper than the original $75K units). Key takeaway: there’s a huge range in specs and cost. For indoor robots, a 10-12m range is usually fine. For outdoor autonomous vehicles, you need 100m+. Resolution matters for detecting small obstacles – at 1 degree resolution and 10m range, two objects need to be at least 17cm apart to be distinguishable. Lab 9 will use parameters similar to the RPLIDAR A1.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
LiDAR Limitations


LiDAR is not perfect:

Glass: beam passes through
Dark / matte surfaces: weak return
Mirrors, polished metal: specular bounce
Rain, fog, dust: scatters the beam
Min range (~15 cm): too close to measure
2D scan is one plane: misses overhangs






These limitations are important for practical robotics. Glass walls are a classic failure mode – the robot’s map will show a gap where the glass door is, and it might try to drive through it. Dark surfaces (like black matte rubber) absorb the IR laser and return too little light for detection. Specular reflection is tricky: a polished metal surface acts like a mirror, bouncing the beam at the angle of incidence rather than back to the sensor, so the sensor either gets no return or a phantom return from wherever the reflected beam ends up. Rain and fog scatter the beam, reducing effective range. The minimum range is a hardware limitation – the electronics need a brief “dead time” after firing before they can listen for the return. And 2D LiDAR only scans in one horizontal plane, typically 10-20cm off the ground, so it can completely miss obstacles that are above or below that plane (table edges, overhanging shelves, steps).

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
The Camera as a Sensor


An image is an \(H \times W\) grid of pixels; each pixel stores \((B, G, R) \in [0, 255]\).
Cameras give (LiDAR doesn’t):

Color, texture, appearance
Object recognition (shape, text, faces)
High pixel resolution

Cameras lack:

Direct depth
Lighting independence






Cameras are the other major exteroceptive sensor. The key difference from LiDAR: a camera gives you rich appearance information (color, texture, shape) but NOT direct distance measurements. A LiDAR tells you “there’s something 3.2m away at 45 degrees” but nothing about what it is. A camera tells you “there’s a red ball at pixel (320, 240)” but not how far away it is. This complementarity is why many robots use both. For this course, we cover cameras briefly – just enough to understand what they can contribute to a robot’s perception. Deep computer vision is a separate course.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Image Coordinates vs World Coordinates


Image \((u, v)\): origin top-left, \(u\) = column, \(v\) = row.
World \((x, y, z)\): 3D position.
A camera projects 3D onto 2D: \[(x, y, z) \;\to\; (u, v)\]
Depth is lost — one pixel could be a small nearby object or a large distant one.





This is the fundamental issue with camera-only sensing: the projection from 3D to 2D is lossy. You cannot recover depth from a single image without additional information (known object size, stereo vision, structured light, etc.). The image coordinate system has a quirk that confuses students: v (row) increases downward, not upward. This is because images are stored as matrices where row 0 is the top. In OpenCV, an image is just a NumPy array of shape (H, W, 3), where img[v, u] gives the (B,G,R) values at pixel (u,v). Note the order: row first, column second, which is (v,u) not (u,v).

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
section: Basic OpenCV: From Image to Information
text:
Basic OpenCV: From Image to Information
import cv2
import numpy as np

# 1. Load image
img = cv2.imread('scene.jpg')

# 2. Convert to HSV color space (better for color detection)
hsv = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)

# 3. Threshold: keep only red pixels
lower_red = np.array([0, 120, 70])
upper_red = np.array([10, 255, 255])
mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, lower_red, upper_red)

# 4. Find contours (outlines of detected regions)
contours, _ = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL,
                                cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
The pipeline: Load \(\to\) Color convert \(\to\) Threshold \(\to\) Find contours

Walk through each step. cv2.imread loads the image as a NumPy array in BGR format (not RGB – a common gotcha). cvtColor converts to HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value), which is better for color detection because it separates color (hue) from brightness (value). In HSV, “red” is a narrow range of hue values regardless of lighting conditions – in RGB, the same red object looks very different in shadow vs sunlight. inRange creates a binary mask: 255 where the pixel is in the specified range, 0 elsewhere. findContours traces the boundaries of white regions in the binary mask and returns them as lists of points. This 4-step pipeline is the bread and butter of simple vision-based robotics.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
section: Color Thresholding: Finding a Red Ball
text:
Color Thresholding: Finding a Red Ball


The binary mask isolates regions matching the target color. The contour gives us the position and size of the detected object.

Show a concrete example. A red ball on a table: the original image shows the full scene, the mask shows only the red region as white pixels, and the contour is the outline of that region overlaid on the original image. The contour tells the robot where in the image the ball is (pixel coordinates) and how large it appears (area in pixels). From the centroid of the contour, the robot knows which direction to turn to face the ball. From the area, it can estimate rough distance (a larger contour = closer object, if the object’s real size is known).

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
From Contours to Robot Decisions
if contours:
    # Largest contour = most likely our target
    c = max(contours, key=cv2.contourArea)

    # Bounding box: x, y, width, height
    x, y, w, h = cv2.boundingRect(c)

    # Center of the object in image
    cx = x + w // 2
    cy = y + h // 2

    # Robot decision: is the object left, center, or right?
    img_center = img.shape[1] // 2
    if cx < img_center - 50:
        action = "turn left"
    elif cx > img_center + 50:
        action = "turn right"
    else:
        action = "go straight"

This is a complete example of vision-based reactive control. The robot detects the largest red contour, computes its center in image coordinates, and decides whether to turn left, right, or go straight based on where the object appears in the image. This is simple but effective – it’s essentially how line-following robots work (threshold the line color, find centroid, steer toward it). The key insight for students: you don’t need deep learning or complex algorithms for basic visual servoing. A threshold + contour + centroid is often enough for structured tasks. Of course, this breaks down in unstructured environments with varying lighting, multiple objects, occlusions, etc.

0.1–5 m









Note


Not in this course, but worth knowing: an RGB-D camera fixes the “camera has no depth” problem. Each pixel becomes a 3D point, so you get a dense point cloud + color. Scales to hundreds of thousands of points per frame, compared to a 2D LiDAR’s ~360.




RGB-D cameras are the dominant sensor on indoor service robots (vacuums, warehouse pickers, educational robots). They give what cameras lack (depth) at a cost cameras can afford. The Kinect, originally a gaming accessory, became the workhorse of hobbyist robotics from 2010 on. RealSense is Intel’s successor. Apple’s ToF LiDAR on iPhones brought consumer-grade ToF into phones starting 2020. Limitations: indoor use mostly (IR struggles in sunlight), short range (<5m), and they still fail on the same glass/dark/specular surfaces as regular LiDAR.

text:
Camera vs LiDAR: Trade-offs









LiDAR
Camera




Direct depth?
Yes (range per ray)

Color / texture?
No

Yes (active sensor)

Note


For this course: we use LiDAR data for mapping (W10) and path planning (W11–W12). Camera-based perception is a full course on its own.




Emphasize that LiDAR and cameras are complementary, not competing. Self-driving cars use both (plus radar, ultrasonic, and more). For our course, we focus on LiDAR because it gives direct range data that maps naturally onto the occupancy grid we’re about to build. Camera-based perception requires much more processing (feature extraction, object detection, depth estimation) which is beyond the scope of this introductory robotics course. Students interested in vision should take a computer vision or deep learning course. The key takeaway: choose your sensor based on what information your task requires.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
The Representation Problem
The environment is continuous; algorithms need a discrete representation.









Representation
Idea
Pros
Cons




Feature map
List of landmarks
Compact, semantic
Hard to query “is this free?”


Topological map
Graph of places
Compact, high-level
No metric info


Occupancy grid
Grid of free/occupied cells
Full spatial info, easy planning
Memory-heavy



We use the occupancy grid — direct input to grid-based planning (W11: Dijkstra, A*).

Three main ways to represent the environment. Feature maps store a sparse set of landmarks with positions – good for localization but you can’t easily answer “can I drive through this 1m gap?” Topological maps are even more abstract – “the kitchen connects to the hallway which connects to the lab” – good for high-level planning but you lose metric information. Occupancy grids discretize the space into a regular grid and mark each cell as free or occupied. They’re the most common representation in mobile robotics because they directly support the question we care about: “is there a collision-free path from A to B?” Grid-based search algorithms (Dijkstra, A*) operate directly on this grid. The trade-off is memory: a 50m x 50m area at 5cm resolution requires a million cells.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
The Occupancy Grid


A 2D array where each cell stores:

Free (0): the robot can drive here
Occupied (1): there’s an obstacle here
Unknown (-1): not yet observed

Parameters:

Origin: \((x_{\min}, y_{\min})\)
Resolution: cell size in meters (e.g., 5 cm)
Size: \(M \times N\) cells






The occupancy grid is the single most important concept in today’s lecture. It’s a 2D NumPy array where each element represents a small square patch of the physical world. A resolution of 5cm means each cell is 5cm x 5cm. A 10m x 10m room at 5cm resolution requires a 200x200 grid = 40,000 cells – easily handled by any computer. The three states (free, occupied, unknown) are crucial: unknown means the robot hasn’t observed this region yet. Initially, the entire grid is unknown. As the robot moves and scans, cells transition to free or occupied based on sensor data. In the next few slides, we’ll derive exactly how that transition works.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Grid Coordinates: World to Grid
Let the grid origin (bottom-left corner) be \(\text{origin} = (x_{\min}, y_{\min})\).
Convert world coordinates \((x, y)\) to grid indices \((i, j)\):
\[i = \left\lfloor \frac{x - x_{\min}}{\text{resolution}} \right\rfloor, \qquad j = \left\lfloor \frac{y - y_{\min}}{\text{resolution}} \right\rfloor\]
def world_to_grid(x, y, origin, resolution):
    # origin = (x_min, y_min)
    i = int((x - origin[0]) / resolution)
    j = int((y - origin[1]) / resolution)
    return i, j

This is the world-to-grid mapping students will implement in Lab 9. It’s a linear map plus a floor. Common mistakes: forgetting to subtract the origin, mixing up i/j ordering (columns vs rows), off-by-one errors at grid boundaries. Make sure students understand that (i,j) are integer indices into a NumPy array, while (x,y) are continuous world coordinates in meters.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Grid Coordinates: Grid to World
The reverse mapping (index \(\to\) cell center in world frame):
\[x = x_{\min} + (i + 0.5) \cdot \text{resolution}, \qquad y = y_{\min} + (j + 0.5) \cdot \text{resolution}\]
The \(+0.5\) offset returns the center of cell \((i, j)\), not its corner.
def grid_to_world(i, j, origin, resolution):
    x = origin[0] + (i + 0.5) * resolution
    y = origin[1] + (j + 0.5) * resolution
    return x, y

The reverse map uses +0.5 to return the center of the cell rather than the corner – this is conventional and avoids ambiguity. A cell at grid index (100, 75) with origin (-5, -5) and resolution 0.05 corresponds to world point (0.025, -1.225). Emphasize that world_to_grid discards sub-cell precision (floor), while grid_to_world reconstructs a single representative point (the center). They are not exact inverses.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
section: Building a Grid from One LiDAR Scan
text:
Building a Grid from One LiDAR Scan


For each ray \((r_i, \alpha_i)\):

Convert endpoint to grid coords
Trace line from robot to endpoint
Mark cells along the line as free
Mark endpoint as occupied

Cells no ray touches stay unknown.





This is the core algorithm. The insight is that a LiDAR ray tells us TWO things: (1) the endpoint is occupied (something reflected the beam), and (2) everything between the sensor and the endpoint is free (otherwise the beam would have been blocked sooner). So for each ray, we trace a line from the robot’s position to the hit point and mark all cells along that line as free, then mark the endpoint cell as occupied. Cells that no ray passes through remain unknown – typically because they’re behind obstacles (occluded). This is sometimes called “inverse sensor model” because we’re going backwards from the measurement to the state of the world.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Ray Casting: Bresenham’s Line Algorithm


Problem: Given two grid cells, which cells lie on the line between them?
Bresenham’s algorithm efficiently finds the “staircase” of cells.
from skimage.draw import line

# Cells from robot to endpoint
cells_i, cells_j = line(
    robot_i, robot_j,
    end_i, end_j
)
# cells_i, cells_j are arrays
# of grid indices along the ray
No need to implement from scratch – skimage.draw.line does it.





Bresenham’s line algorithm is a classic computer graphics algorithm from 1962. It determines which pixels (cells) to color when drawing a line between two points on a grid. It uses only integer arithmetic, making it very fast. Students don’t need to implement it – the scikit-image library provides it. The important thing is understanding what it does: given start cell (i1,j1) and end cell (i2,j2), it returns a list of all grid cells that the line passes through. For our occupancy grid, all cells in this list except the last one are marked free, and the last one is marked occupied. Show the staircase pattern on the SVG – for a diagonal line, the cells form a staircase approximation.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Ray Casting a Full 360° Scan


After processing all rays: cells are white (free), black (occupied), or gray (unknown/occluded).

Show the full picture. The robot is in a room with walls and one internal obstacle. After processing all 360 rays, the grid shows the visible area as free (white), the walls and obstacle as occupied (black), and the region behind the obstacle as unknown (gray) because no rays could reach there – they were blocked by the obstacle. This occluded region is the “shadow” behind the obstacle. The robot would need to move to a different position to scan that region. This naturally leads to the idea of building the map incrementally from multiple scans, which we’ll cover after the practice problem.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
section: Practice: Building a Grid from a Scan
text:
Practice: Building a Grid from a Scan
Given: A robot at grid position \((5, 5)\) on a \(10 \times 10\) grid. Six LiDAR rays hit walls at:



Ray
\(\alpha\) (degrees)
Grid endpoint \((i, j)\)

\((9, 5)\)


2

\((5, 9)\)


4

6

Task: On paper, mark cells as Free (F), Occupied (O), or Unknown (U).

(Work on this for 3 minutes, then we’ll see the solution.)

Give students 3 minutes to work this out on paper. The key steps: for each ray, trace from (5,5) to the endpoint, marking intermediate cells as free and the endpoint as occupied. Cells not touched by any ray are unknown. This is a simplified version of what they’ll implement in Lab 9. Walk around the room while they work. Common mistakes: forgetting that the robot’s own cell is also free, not tracing diagonal rays correctly (e.g., the 45-degree ray from (5,5) to (8,8) passes through (6,6) and (7,7) which should be marked free).

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Practice: Solution





For every ray:

Free — each cell the beam crosses
Occupied — only the endpoint cell
Unknown — everything not touched by a ray

Huge unknown wedges between rays — 6 beams can’t cover a full scene.


Walk through the solution. The robot cell (5,5) is free. Ray 1 going right: cells (6,5), (7,5), (8,5) are free, (9,5) is occupied. Ray 2 at 45 degrees: (6,6), (7,7) are free, (8,8) is occupied. And so on for each ray. Everything else is unknown. Point out the large unknown regions in the corners – the robot only had 6 rays with 45-degree spacing, leaving huge gaps. In practice, a LiDAR with 360 rays at 1-degree spacing would fill in much more of the grid. But even with dense scanning, the occluded region behind an obstacle remains unknown.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
The Problem: Sensor Noise


Real sensors are noisy:

Scan 1 says cell \((5, 2)\) is free
Scan 2 says cell \((5, 2)\) is occupied

A binary grid can only store one value.
Which scan do we trust?
Neither – we need to accumulate evidence over multiple observations.





This is the motivation for moving from binary grids to probabilistic grids. Real LiDAR measurements have noise: the range measurement has a standard deviation of a few centimeters, the angular measurement has small errors, and occasionally you get completely spurious readings (multipath reflections, temporary obstacles like a person walking by). If two scans disagree about a cell, a binary grid has no good way to resolve the conflict – you either overwrite the old value or ignore the new one. What we want is to accumulate evidence: if 9 out of 10 scans say a cell is free and 1 scan says occupied, the cell is probably free (the occupied reading was noise). This requires storing a probability, not just 0 or 1.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
From Binary to Probabilistic
Instead of \(\{0, 1, -1\}\), store a probability \(p(\text{occupied})\) for each cell:



\(p\)
Meaning




0.0
Definitely free


0.5
Unknown (no information)


1.0
Definitely occupied



Update rule (Bayes’ theorem):
\[p(\text{occ} \mid z_{1:t}) = \frac{p(z_t \mid \text{occ}) \cdot p(\text{occ} \mid z_{1:t-1})}{p(z_t)}\]
But repeatedly multiplying small probabilities causes numerical underflow…

The probabilistic approach stores a probability of occupancy for each cell. We start with p = 0.5 (maximum uncertainty – we have no idea). Each new observation updates the probability. If the sensor says “free,” p decreases. If it says “occupied,” p increases. The Bayesian update rule is theoretically correct but computationally problematic: multiplying many numbers between 0 and 1 eventually produces values too small for floating-point representation. We need a transformation that turns these multiplications into additions. That’s the log-odds trick, coming next.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
The Log-Odds Representation


Define the log-odds of a probability:
\[l = \log\frac{p}{1 - p}\]



\(l\)
\(p\)
Meaning




\(-\infty\)
0.0
Certain free


\(-2.2\)
0.1
Likely free


\(0\)
0.5
Unknown


\(+2.2\)
0.9
Likely occupied


\(+\infty\)
1.0
Certain occupied



Inverse: \(p = 1 / (1 + e^{-l})\) (sigmoid)



Key property: Bayesian update becomes addition — no multiplications, no underflow.


Log-odds is a monotonic transformation of probability. It maps [0,1] to (-inf, +inf). The nice thing is that 0.5 maps to 0 (our “unknown” prior), negative values mean “more likely free,” positive values mean “more likely occupied.” Students may recognize the sigmoid function from logistic regression or neural networks – it’s the same thing. The log-odds representation has been standard in occupancy grid mapping since Elfes (1989). The mathematical reason it works: in log-odds space, the Bayesian update becomes a simple addition rather than a multiplication, which is both numerically stable and computationally cheap.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Log-Odds Update Rule
The Bayesian update simplifies to:
\[l_{t} = l_{t-1} + l_{\text{meas}}\]

\(l_{t-1}\) — accumulated log-odds from past observations
\(l_{\text{meas}}\) — log-odds of the new measurement

Typical values: free evidence \(l_{\text{free}} = -0.4\); hit evidence \(l_{\text{occ}} = +0.85\).
That’s it — just add to the current value. No multiplications, no normalization, no underflow.

This is the payoff of the log-odds representation. The full Bayesian update with priors and likelihoods reduces to a single addition per cell. The values l_free = -0.4 and l_occ = +0.85 are tuning parameters that encode how much we trust a single observation. These particular values correspond to: if the ray passes through a cell, we’re about 60% confident it’s free (p = 0.4 = exp(-0.4)/(1+exp(-0.4))); if the ray hits a cell, we’re about 70% confident it’s occupied. The asymmetry (|l_occ| > |l_free|) is intentional: occupied evidence is stronger because a single hit is more informative than a single pass-through. Students can think of l_free and l_occ as “confidence weights” – bigger magnitudes mean more aggressive updates.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Worked Example: Log-Odds Update
A cell starts at \(l_0 = 0\) (unknown, \(p = 0.5\)). Five successive observations:



Obs
Type
\(l_{\text{meas}}\)
\(l_{\text{new}}\)
\(p\)




1
free
\(-0.4\)
\(-0.4\)
0.40


2
free
\(-0.4\)
\(-0.8\)
0.31


3
occupied
\(+0.85\)
\(+0.05\)
0.51


4
free
\(-0.4\)
\(-0.35\)
0.41


5
free
\(-0.4\)
\(-0.75\)
0.32



Computation: \(l_{\text{new}} = l_{\text{old}} + l_{\text{meas}}\), then \(p = 1/(1+e^{-l_{\text{new}}})\).

Walk through each row. Start at l=0 (totally uncertain). First free observation: l drops to -0.4, p drops to 0.40 (slight lean toward free). Second free: l = -0.8, p = 0.31 (more confident it’s free). Third observation is occupied: l jumps from -0.8 to +0.05, p goes back to 0.51 (almost back to uncertain – one occupied reading nearly cancelled two free readings because l_occ > |l_free|). Fourth and fifth are free again, bringing the belief back down.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Worked Example: Takeaways
Result: 4 free + 1 occupied \(\Rightarrow\) \(p = 0.32\) (probably free).

The single occupied reading shifted the belief (jumped from 0.31 to 0.51).
Accumulated free evidence outweighs the one noisy reading.
Asymmetry \(|l_{\text{occ}}| > |l_{\text{free}}|\) means one hit is louder than one pass-through.







Warning


In practice, clamp \(l \in [-5, +5]\) to prevent saturation. Otherwise a cell observed 1000 times as free needs 1000+ occupied observations to change its mind.




This is exactly how the grid handles noisy sensors: evidence accumulates and conflicting observations partially cancel. The clamping range [-5, +5] gives max confidence p ≈ 0.007 (very free) or p ≈ 0.993 (very occupied) – enough for planning, but leaves the door open for new evidence.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Putting It in Code
def update_occupancy_grid(grid, robot_ij, endpoints_ij, l_free=-0.4, l_occ=0.85):
    """Update occupancy grid with one full LiDAR scan."""
    for end_i, end_j in endpoints_ij:
        # Get all cells along the ray
        ray_i, ray_j = line(robot_ij[0], robot_ij[1], end_i, end_j)

        # All cells except last: free evidence
        grid[ray_i[:-1], ray_j[:-1]] += l_free

        # Last cell: occupied evidence
        grid[ray_i[-1], ray_j[-1]] += l_occ

    # Clamp to prevent saturation
    np.clip(grid, -5.0, 5.0, out=grid)

This is the complete occupancy grid update function. Students will implement a version of this in Lab 9. Note the structure: for each ray, get the cells using Bresenham’s algorithm, add l_free to all cells along the ray except the last one, add l_occ to the last cell. The clamp at the end prevents log-odds from growing without bound – without it, a cell observed 100 times as free would have l = -40, and it would take 50+ occupied observations to change the belief. Clamping to [-5, +5] means the maximum confidence is about p = 0.007 (very confident free) or p = 0.993 (very confident occupied). The function modifies the grid in-place for efficiency.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Building the Map: Multiple Scans


As the robot moves and scans from different positions, the unknown region shrinks and the map converges.

Show three panels: (1) after the first scan, most of the grid is unknown except for the area directly visible from the robot’s starting position; (2) after the robot moves and takes a second scan, more area is revealed, and cells observed from both positions have stronger evidence; (3) after several scans, the map is mostly complete with only small occluded pockets remaining unknown. This is exactly how SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) works in practice, except we’re assuming the robot knows its exact pose (from odometry or some external tracking system). In W13, we’ll address what happens when the pose estimate is uncertain.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
section: From Grid to Path Planning (Preview of W11)
text:
From Grid to Path Planning (Preview of W11)


The occupancy grid IS the planner’s input:

Free cells — nodes to visit
Occupied cells — obstacles
Cell adjacency — graph edges

Next week: Dijkstra and A* find the shortest path through this grid.





This is the payoff slide – connecting today’s content to next week’s path planning. The occupancy grid is literally a graph where each free cell is a node and adjacent free cells are connected by edges. Dijkstra’s algorithm and A* search operate on exactly this kind of graph. The path planning problem reduces to: find the shortest sequence of free cells from the start cell to the goal cell, where “shortest” is measured by the number of cells traversed (or the Euclidean distance). The conversion from occupancy grid to graph is trivial: each cell with p < 0.5 is a node, and each node is connected to its 4 or 8 neighbors (4-connected for cardinal directions only, 8-connected to allow diagonal movement). Students will see this in full detail next week.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
The Full Autonomy Pipeline


Every autonomous mobile robot runs some version of this loop. Each block uses concepts from a specific week in our course.

Step back and show the big picture. The full pipeline is: (1) Sense the environment with LiDAR/camera (today, W10); (2) Build/update a map representation (today, W10 – occupancy grid); (3) Plan a path from current position to goal (W11-W12 – Dijkstra, A*, RRT); (4) Execute the path using the kinematic model (W09 – unicycle/diff-drive); (5) Estimate where you actually ended up (W13 – localization/particle filter). Then repeat. This is the sense-plan-act loop from the beginning of the lecture, but now with concrete implementations for each block. The loop runs continuously: the robot senses, updates its map, replans if the map changed, and continues executing. In reality, these steps often run at different rates – sensing at 10Hz, planning at 1Hz, control at 50Hz – but the conceptual loop is the same.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Looking Ahead
What we didn’t cover today:








Topic
Where
Why




3D perception (point clouds, depth cams)
Advanced courses
We kept to 2D


Sensor fusion (LiDAR + camera)
Advanced courses
Needs probabilistic framework


SLAM (mapping + localization)
W13 — localization
The “L” in SLAM


Deep learning for perception
Vision courses
Needs ML background



W13 closes the loop: what if the robot doesn’t know its exact pose? That’s localization.

Be transparent about what we skipped. 3D perception is increasingly important (self-driving cars use 3D LiDAR point clouds) but the math is the same – just one more dimension. Sensor fusion combines multiple sensor modalities (e.g., using camera to classify what LiDAR detects) and requires a probabilistic framework like Kalman filters. SLAM is the holy grail of mobile robotics – building a map while simultaneously figuring out where you are in that map. We’ll touch on the “L” (localization) part in W13 with particle filters. Deep learning has revolutionized perception but requires ML prerequisites that not all students have.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Key Takeaways

Sense-Plan-Act: The robot must perceive the environment (W10) before planning paths (W11) or executing motions (W09)
LiDAR measures distances using time-of-flight. A 2D scan is an array of \((r, \alpha)\) pairs. Convert to Cartesian: \(x = r\cos\alpha\), \(y = r\sin\alpha\)
Cameras provide rich appearance data but no direct depth. A simple threshold + contour pipeline extracts object locations in the image
Occupancy grids discretize space into cells (free / occupied / unknown). Built from LiDAR scans using ray casting (Bresenham’s algorithm)
Log-odds update makes Bayesian fusion simple: just add measurement evidence to each cell. Multiple scans accumulate into a consistent map


Tie each takeaway back to the learning goals from the first slide. The occupancy grid + log-odds update is the most important skill from today – students will implement it in Lab 9 and use the resulting grid as input to path planning in W11. The LiDAR material gives them the data pipeline: raw ranges go in, a grid comes out. The camera section is awareness-level – they should know what cameras can and can’t do, but they won’t implement vision-based algorithms in the labs.

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Next Week
Week 11: Path Planning I – Grid Search

Configuration space (C-space): what it means for a mobile robot
Graph search on occupancy grids
Dijkstra’s algorithm: guaranteed shortest path
A* search: faster with a heuristic
Lab 10: The Maze Solver

The occupancy grid you built today becomes the maze A* will solve next week.

Preview W11 to create anticipation. The occupancy grid from today IS the input to next week’s algorithms. Dijkstra and A* are graph search algorithms that find the shortest path from start to goal on a grid. Students who have taken a data structures or algorithms course may have seen these algorithms on abstract graphs – next week we apply them to a concrete robotics problem. Lab 10 will have students implement A* on an occupancy grid and visualize the search process. The transition from W10 to W11 is one of the cleanest in the course: the output of today (a grid) is literally the input of next week (a graph to search).

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Exit Ticket
A robot at grid cell \((2, 2)\) on a \(5 \times 5\) grid takes a LiDAR scan. Two rays:

Ray A: hits a wall at cell \((4, 2)\) (going right)
Ray B: hits a wall at cell \((2, 4)\) (going up)

The grid uses log-odds with \(l_{\text{free}} = -0.4\), \(l_{\text{occ}} = +0.85\). All cells start at \(l = 0\).
Questions:

After processing both rays, what is the log-odds value of cell \((3, 2)\)?
What is the log-odds value of cell \((4, 2)\)?
Convert cell \((3, 2)\)’s log-odds to a probability. Is this cell likely free or occupied?

title: Week 10: Sensors for Autonomy (HTML Visuals Trial)
text:
Exit Ticket: Solution
Part 1: Cell \((3, 2)\) is along Ray A (between robot and wall).
\[l_{(3,2)} = 0 + l_{\text{free}} = 0 + (-0.4) = -0.4\]
Part 2: Cell \((4, 2)\) is the endpoint of Ray A.
\[l_{(4,2)} = 0 + l_{\text{occ}} = 0 + 0.85 = +0.85\]
Part 3: Convert \(l = -0.4\) to probability:
\[p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(-0.4)}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{0.4}} = \frac{1}{1 + 1.49} = 0.40\]
Since \(p = 0.40 < 0.5\), cell \((3, 2)\) is likely free.

Walk through each part. Part 1: cell (3,2) is on the path of Ray A going from (2,2) to (4,2), so it gets l_free = -0.4. Ray B goes from (2,2) to (2,4), which does NOT pass through (3,2), so only Ray A contributes. Part 2: cell (4,2) is the endpoint of Ray A, so it gets l_occ = +0.85. Part 3: the sigmoid function converts l = -0.4 to p = 0.40. Since 0.40 < 0.5, the evidence suggests this cell is free. Note that this is only slightly below 0.5 – one observation gives weak evidence. Multiple consistent observations would drive the probability further toward 0 (definitely free). This is a 3-minute exit ticket – if students can do this, they understand the core algorithm.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Dijkstra vs A*: Live Comparison


Both find the same optimal path (purple) — but A* visits far fewer cells (slate) than Dijkstra. Drag the green start or orange goal to try different cases.

This is the key takeaway slide. Dijkstra’s explored region (shown in slate gray) expands roughly as a circle around the start — it has no information about where the goal is. A’s explored region is elongated toward the goal because the octile heuristic deprioritizes any node whose g+h exceeds the current best. Both algorithms terminate with the same purple path (they’re both optimal), but the cell counts differ by 3-10x depending on obstacle density. On very large grids this gap can reach 100x, which is why A dominates grid planners in practice. Let students drag the endpoints and watch the difference. A corner case worth demonstrating: when the goal is right next to a wall, both algorithms explore similar numbers of cells because the heuristic can’t see the obstacle.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
It All Connects
This week is the bridge between what the robot sees (W10) and what it does (W09):

W10 — The occupancy grid we built from LiDAR scans is the input to today’s planner
W10 — Bresenham’s line algorithm (used for ray casting) returns today for line-of-sight path smoothing
W02 — Homogeneous transforms place grid cells in the world frame
W09 — The kinematic controller executes the waypoints we output
W12 — When this week’s grid approach breaks down (high-D, narrow passages), we’ll move to sampling







Tip


Today’s output — a list of waypoints — is literally next week’s input after sampling, and next week’s target trajectory for the differential-drive controller from W09.




Step back and show the big picture. The occupancy grid from W10 is a 2D NumPy array with free/occupied/unknown cells. Today we put the robot (a point, thanks to C-space inflation) at the start cell, and we search this array for the cheapest sequence of adjacent free cells ending at the goal. That sequence of cells, converted back to world coordinates via the grid-to-world map from W10, becomes a list of waypoints. Then W09’s unicycle/diff-drive controller takes those waypoints and generates wheel commands. The whole sense-plan-act loop closes.

W12 opens the door: what if grid discretization is hopeless — e.g., a 7-DOF manipulator? Randomly sample the config space and grow a tree (RRT).

Be transparent about what we skipped. D* Lite is the standard for dynamic maps — recompute only the affected portion of the A* tree when new observations invalidate part of the plan. Any-angle search relaxes the grid constraint: instead of moving only in 8 directions, Theta* allows paths that cut across cells at arbitrary angles, producing much smoother trajectories. State lattices are used in self-driving car planning – they discretize the state space in a way that respects kinematic constraints. MPC is a control-theoretic formulation that optimizes over a short horizon while considering dynamics and constraints. Sampling planners are next week.

Why grids fail in high dimensions (curse of dimensionality, revisited)
RRT — grow a tree of random samples rooted at the start

Bidirectional RRT and practical tuning
Guided exercise: trace RRT by hand

Today’s planner handles the 2D mobile-robot case. Next week’s handles everything else.

Preview W12 to create anticipation. RRT is conceptually very different from A: instead of systematically expanding from the start, it grows a tree by repeatedly sampling a random point in C-space and extending the nearest tree node toward it. After enough samples, the tree “explores” the reachable region. RRT adds a rewiring step that makes the path length converge to the optimum as more samples are added. The key insight is that sampling sidesteps the exponential cost of gridding high-dimensional spaces.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Exit Ticket
A mobile robot with radius 0.20 m is on a 2D grid with resolution 0.10 m. Its C-space is 8-connected with octile heuristic.
Start S = (0, 0), goal G = (5, 3) (grid cells).
Questions:

How many cells of obstacle inflation are needed around each wall cell?
Compute the octile heuristic \(h(S)\).
The grid-optimal path length from S to G is \(5 + 3(\sqrt{2} - 1) \approx 6.24\). Is A* with octile guaranteed to find a path of this exact cost? Why?

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Exit Ticket: Solution
Part 1: Inflation radius = robot radius / resolution = \(0.20 / 0.10 = 2\) cells.
Every cell within 2 grid cells of any wall cell becomes occupied in C-space.
Part 2: Octile heuristic between S = (0, 0) and G = (5, 3):
\[h = (\sqrt{2} - 1) \cdot \min(5, 3) + \max(5, 3) = (\sqrt{2} - 1)(3) + 5 \approx 6.24\]
Part 3: Yes. The octile heuristic is admissible and consistent for 8-connected grids with edge costs \(\{1, \sqrt{2}\}\), so A* is guaranteed to find the optimal path. Moreover, \(h(S) = 6.24\) already equals the optimal cost, meaning A* will expand only the cells on the optimal path — zero wasted exploration.

Walk through each part. Part 1 is the C-space step: divide physical radius by grid resolution to get the inflation radius in cells, then mark every cell within that distance of a wall as occupied. Part 2 is a direct application of the octile formula — emphasize that min/max matter, and that the sqrt(2)-1 factor comes from the fact that diagonal moves cost sqrt(2) while saving you one cardinal move per diagonal. Part 3 is the deepest question: why is octile admissible? Because it’s the EXACT shortest-path distance on an 8-connected grid with no obstacles. Any real grid (with or without obstacles) can’t have a shorter path than that. When the heuristic equals the true cost on the optimal path, A* degenerates to following that path directly — this is the best-case behavior.

(2) The expansion log now shows g, h, and f — note how f stays nearly constant for nodes on the optimal path (hallmark of a tight heuristic). (3) Both algorithms find the SAME optimal path with the SAME cost — A* just does it with less wasted exploration. (4) Ask students: what happens if the heuristic overestimates? (A* may find a suboptimal path — admissibility is key.)

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
text:
Heuristics Compared: Why Octile Wins



Each panel colors cells by their heuristic distance from S. Contours mark equal-distance level sets — i.e. the shape the metric thinks is “round.”

Manhattan → diamond (only cardinal moves count)
Chebyshev → square (treats diagonals as cost 1)
Euclidean → circle (straight-line distance)
Octile → octagon (diagonals at cost √2, cardinals at cost 1)


Why we prefer octile on 8-connected grids:

Tight: octile is the exact shortest-path length when there are no obstacles, so \(h(v)\) is as close to the true cost-to-go as any admissible heuristic can be.
Admissible: Manhattan overestimates on 8-connected grids (it ignores cheap diagonals), so A* with Manhattan can return a non-optimal path. Octile never overestimates.
Faster A*: a tighter \(h\) means fewer expanded cells. Chebyshev and Euclidean are admissible but looser, so A* explores more.



Walk through the four panels. Manhattan: the level sets are diamonds because going one step diagonally counts as two unit moves. Chebyshev: squares — it pretends diagonals are free. Euclidean: circles — pure straight-line distance. Octile: an octagon, because the cheapest path uses diagonals (cost √2) until one axis is matched, then cardinals (cost 1) for the rest. The octagon shape literally matches the actual movement cost on an 8-connected grid. That makes octile tight: \(h(v)\) equals the true cost-to-go when there are no obstacles. Tightness matters because A* expands a node only if \(f(n) = g(n) + h(n) \le \text{cost}(\text{optimal path})\) — a tighter \(h\) prunes more aggressively.

title: Week 11: Path Planning I — Grid Search
section: Heuristics Compared on the Same Pair
text:
Heuristics Compared on the Same Pair


Same S and G in every panel. True 8-connected cost: \(4\sqrt{2}+3 \approx 8.66\).







Tight vs. loose heuristic


The gap = (true cost) − \(h(v)\). A tight heuristic has a small gap (close to truth); a loose one has a big gap.
A* expands every cell whose \(f = g + h\) is below the optimal cost. Smaller gap → fewer such cells → less wasted work.





Manhattan → 11, gap = \(-2.34\) (overestimates → ✗ inadmissible).
Chebyshev → 7, gap = \(1.66\) (loose).
Euclidean → 8.06, gap = \(0.60\) (tighter).
Octile → 8.66, gap = \(0\) (✓ exact, tightest possible).









Walk panel-by-panel. Manhattan forbids diagonals so it has to take an L-shape — 7 right + 4 up = 11 moves. That number is BIGGER than the actual 8-connected cost of 8.66, which means Manhattan can mislead A* into thinking a worse path is good — it’s inadmissible on 8-connected grids and A* loses its optimality guarantee. Chebyshev counts each move as 1 even though diagonals really cost √2, so it gives 7 — too low, admissible, but loose. Euclidean draws a straight line: √(7² + 4²) ≈ 8.06 — also too low because the robot can’t actually fly diagonally through cell corners, it has to follow the grid. Octile matches reality: 4 diagonals at √2 each + 3 cardinals at 1 each = exactly the true cost. Tight admissible heuristic = A* prunes maximally = fewest cells expanded.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT*: Choose Best Parent
# After q_new is collision-free...
r = rewire_radius(len(nodes))            # shrinks as tree grows
neighbors = nodes_within(nodes, q_new, r) # candidate parents in ball of radius r

# Start with the nearest node as the default parent (basic-RRT choice)
best_parent = q_near
best_cost = cost[q_near] + dist(q_near, q_new)

# Try every neighbor; keep the one giving the lowest cost-to-come
for n in neighbors:
    c = cost[n] + dist(n, q_new)         # cost if we route through n
    if c < best_cost and collision_free(n, q_new, obstacles):
        best_parent = n                  # cheaper AND reachable -> prefer it
        best_cost = c

# Attach q_new to the winning parent and store its cost
nodes[q_new] = best_parent
cost[q_new] = best_cost

The choose-best-parent step is like looking around the neighborhood when you arrive somewhere new and picking the best route to get there. This is the first difference from basic RRT: instead of always attaching q_new to the nearest node, RRT* attaches it to the neighbor that gives the lowest total cost from the start.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT*: Rewire Neighbors
# Now ask: can q_new serve as a BETTER parent for any neighbor?
for n in neighbors:
    new_cost = cost[q_new] + dist(q_new, n)   # cost if n re-parented to q_new

    if (new_cost < cost[n] and                # shortcut found
        collision_free(q_new, n, obstacles)): # and the edge is valid
        nodes[n] = q_new                      # re-parent: n's parent <- q_new
        cost[n] = new_cost                    # update n's cost-to-come

        # n's children inherit the savings, so propagate the delta down the subtree.
        update_descendant_costs(n)






Note


Rewiring lets the tree repair earlier choices as better connections appear.




The rewire step is like telling nearby nodes “it might be faster to go through me.” If the new node creates a shortcut, the tree restructures itself. In production code, changing a parent also requires propagating the cost change to that node’s descendants; the slide names this bookkeeping explicitly so the pseudocode is not misleading. Both operations require collision checks, making RRT* roughly 2-3x slower per iteration than basic RRT. But the path quality improvement is dramatic and worth it in most applications.

Planner Choice Cheat Sheet


Low-dimensional maps

Use grid search when the state space is small enough to discretize.

Real-time replanning

High-quality path
RRT* + smoothing


Narrow passages
bidirectional RRT



Use sampling when a grid would explode in memory or time.


This decision table is the practical takeaway. Students should be able to look at a planning problem and immediately choose the right algorithm family. The dimension of the C-space is the primary factor. For 2D, always use A* — it’s faster and gives optimal paths. For 3D, it depends on the map complexity and real-time requirements. For anything higher, sampling-based is the only option. Bidirectional RRT (grow a tree from start and from goal, connect when they meet) is particularly effective for narrow passages because both trees can find opposite ends of the passage.

title: Week 12: Path Planning II — Sampling-Based Methods
text:
RRT vs RRT*: Cost Convergence




How to read it:

Shaded band: interquartile range across 20 seeds
RRT finds a feasible path quickly, then plateaus
RRT* descends past RRT’s plateau as rewiring kicks in
Dashed line: best path ever observed (≈ true optimum)



Plot is from real measurements: 20 seeds of each planner on the 3-wall maze, 2000 iterations. Median curve plus IQR band shows the population behavior, not one lucky run. RRT typically finds a feasible path around iteration 90 and plateaus near 19.5. RRT* takes a bit longer to find its first path (around iteration 160) because rewiring filters out more candidates per iteration, but the rewiring lets the best-known cost keep decreasing. By iteration 1000 RRT* is essentially at the asymptote (~14.6), about 25% better than RRT.

text:
RRT: Interactive Expansion



Use this interactive as a slower version of the pseudocode. Each button press runs one RRT iteration. Students should identify q_rand, the nearest existing tree node, the proposed q_new after steering by delta, and whether the edge is accepted or rejected by collision checking. The key lesson is that failed samples are still part of the algorithm: they do not add nodes, but they show that the planner is testing local motions against obstacles rather than blindly connecting every random point.
